title: A Strongly-Subquadratic $(3+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for the Fréchet Distance for Paths in Metric Spaces
comment: To be published in proceedings of ESA 2026
summary:
The Fréchet distance is a well-studied distance measure for paths in a metric space. It is mostly studied for paths in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Here, computing the Fréchet distance between two polylines takes time roughly quadratic in the number of vertices. Assuming the strong exponential time hypothesis (SETH), it cannot be approximated to within a factor less than $3$ in strongly-subquadratic time. Recently, it was shown that for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a randomized algorithm that can compute a $(7+\varepsilon)$-approximation in strongly-subquadratic expected time [Cheng, Huang, and Zhang; STOC'25]. For polylines with $n$ and $m$ vertices in a Euclidean space of constant dimension, where $n \geq m$, their algorithm takes $O(nm^{0.99} \log(n/\varepsilon))$ time in expectation.
  We present a deterministic approximation algorithm that significantly improves upon the approximation factor and running time. Specifically, our algorithm computes a $(3+\varepsilon)$-approximation in $O(nm^{2/3} \log n \cdot \log (\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \log n))$ time. Our algorithm nearly matches the conditional lower bound on the approximation factor implied by SETH. For polylines in $\mathbb{R}$, we present a $3$-approximation algorithm that runs in $O(nm^{2/3} \log^{5/3} n)$ time, and exactly matches the conditional lower bound.
  For our results, we introduce a general strongly-subquadratic time $3$-approximate decision algorithm. This algorithm makes no assumptions on the ambient metric space, and relies only on standard assumptions on the so-called free space of the input paths. Under some mild assumptions, our decision algorithm leads to a $(3+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm in general metric spaces. These assumptions hold automatically for polylines in any metric space $(\mathbb{R}^d, L_p)$ with $p \geq 1$.

AI.tldr: A deterministic 3+ε approximation for Fréchet distance between polylines in Euclidean spaces, with near-subquadratic time; introduces a general 3-approximate decision algorithm based on free-space, enabling extension to general metric spaces under mild assumptions; in 1D, achieves exact 3-approx with slower, but still subquadratic, time; results approach SETH-based lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Improve deterministic approximation factor and running time for Fréchet distance between polylines, surpassing recent randomized subquadratic approximations and aligning with conditional lower bounds; provide a framework via free-space to extend to general metric spaces.
AI.method: Develop a strongly-subquadratic time 3-approximate decision algorithm that relies on free-space structure, then derive a (3+ε)-approximation for polylines in R^d; specialized 1D case yields a 3-approx in O(n m^{2/3} log^{5/3} n); assumptions on free-space lead to general metric-space extension.
AI.result: Deterministic (3+ε)-approximation in O(n m^{2/3} log n · log( (1/ε) log n)) time; 1D case yields a 3-approx in O(n m^{2/3} log^{5/3} n); provides a general 3-approximate decision algorithm; aligns with SETH lower bounds up to factors.
AI.conclusion: Presents a near-optimal deterministic approach under SETH for Fréchet distance on polylines, with potential extension to general metric spaces; tightens the gap between lower bounds and algorithms, especially in 1D.

title: Overlapping Unfoldings of Cones and Convex Polyhedra
comment: 7 pages, 13 figures, 8 references. CCCG 2026, Orillia, Canada, August 12-14, 2026
summary:
Research on Dürer's problem focuses on edge unfoldings of convex polyhedra that avoid overlap. We invert the goal and find unfoldings that overlap at some point to any given thickness t.
  We have two main results. The first is that, if we allow unfolding cuts that do not follow polyhedron edges, then there is a convex polyhedron that can unfold with overlap of any given thickness. The second result is that for any given thickness, there is a convex polyhedron with an edge unfolding that overlaps to that thickness.

AI.tldr: Two existence results for overlap unfoldings of convex polyhedra: (1) with cuts not restricted to edges, there exists a polyhedron whose unfolding overlaps by any prescribed thickness t; (2) for any t>0, there exists a polyhedron with an edge unfolding that overlaps by that thickness.
AI.motivation: Invert Dürer's edge-unfolding problem by studying unfoldings that intentionally overlap, and characterize how overlap thickness can be controlled under different cut models.
AI.method: Two constructive proofs: (i) a convex polyhedron whose non-edge unfolding can realize overlap of any given thickness t; (ii) a convex polyhedron that possesses an edge unfolding with overlap of thickness t for any t>0.
AI.result: Existence theorems: (i) non-edge unfoldings can realize overlap of any prescribed thickness t on some convex polyhedron; (ii) there exists a convex polyhedron with an edge unfolding achieving overlap of any prescribed thickness t.
AI.conclusion: The work reframes Dürer's problem by showing that overlap can be forced to any thickness under two cut regimes, highlighting that the feasibility and magnitude of overlap depend on the allowed cutting scheme and can be tuned arbitrarily.

title: Interval Certifications for Multilayered Perceptrons via Lattice Traversal
summary: In this work we present a rigorous theoretical framework to a foundational problem of AI safety, namely adversarial robustness. In particular, we show that the adversarial robustness problem can be reduced to a lattice traversal problem. Each element of this lattice corresponds to an interval, i.e., an axis-aligned hyper-rectangle, containing an input point $\mathbf{x}$. Consider a multilayered perceptron classifier (MLP). An interval $I$ constitutes a sound certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and $\mathbf{x}$ can be freely perturbed in $I$ without changing the MLP's prediction. Complementarily, an interval $I$ constitutes a complete certification if $\mathbf{x} \in I$ and when $\mathbf{x}$ moves outside of $I$ the MLP's prediction is guaranteed to change. While the sound certification problem corresponds to the well-studied adversarial robustness, complete certifications have not been examined in the literature. We develop lattice traversal operators, which we apply in a refine & verify iterative scheme. Using formal MLP verifiers, sound maximality and complete minimality are guaranteed. Moreover, we examine objective optimization problems. There we discover some interesting asymmetries. For complete certifications, the minimum solution is obtained in polynomial oracle calls. This does not hold for sound certifications, where we prove strong intractability results. Additionally, we examine optimization problems in symmetric intervals (i.e., $\ell_\infty$-spheres), where we provide logarithmic algorithms. Finally, we present an empirical evaluation, using the novel ParallelepipedoNN system.

AI.tldr: Presents a lattice-based framework to adversarial robustness, introducing complete certifications via interval lattices; shows polynomial oracle-time attainment for complete certifications but intractability for sound ones; gives logarithmic algorithms for l∞-intervals and an empirical evaluation with ParallelepipedoNN.
AI.motivation: Adversarial robustness is central to AI safety. Current certifiably robust work focuses on sound certs; the notion of complete certifications (guarantees upon leaving a region) is novel and could provide stronger safety guarantees. The paper frames robustness as a lattice traversal to enable formal verification and optimization.
AI.method: Model robustness as traversal over a lattice of axis-aligned hyperrectangles I containing x. Sound certification: x can perturb within I without changing the MLP’s prediction. Complete certification: moving outside I guarantees a prediction change. Develop lattice traversal operators and a refine & verify iterative scheme. Use formal MLP verifiers to guarantee sound maximality and complete minimality. Analyze objective optimization problems, revealing asymmetries. Study symmetric intervals (ℓ∞-spheres) with logarithmic algorithms. Empirically evaluate via ParallelepipedoNN.
AI.result: Establishes a theoretical reduction from adversarial robustness to lattice traversal. Proves that complete certs admit polynomial oracle-time solutions, while sound certs are strongly intractable. Provides logarithmic algorithms for ℓ∞-intervals and demonstrates practicality through an empirical evaluation using ParallelepipedoNN.
AI.conclusion: Offers a rigorous framework for both sound and complete certifications in neural networks, highlighting fundamental asymmetries between them. Introduces new traversal-based algorithms and verifier-based guarantees, and demonstrates feasibility with a prototype system (ParallelepipedoNN).

title: AgenticFocus: Object-Preserving Mixed Reality Synthesis from Human FPV Video for Dexterous Humanoid Learning
summary: Human egocentric video is a scalable supervision source for humanoid policy learning, but current pipelines struggle with hand-object occlusion, oversimplified motion, or specialized capture hardware. We introduce AgenticFocus, a Mixed Reality synthesis pipeline that converts ordinary first-person-view human videos into robot-trainable demonstrations by restoring occluded object geometry, reconstructing full-hand motion, and retargeting it to a humanoid embodiment through camera-relative alignment and layered compositing. The resulting dataset pairs focused visual observations with synchronized robot actions and states. AgenticFocus achieves lower trajectory error and smoother wrist motion than cross-embodiment baselines, with SPARC scores of -5.18 versus -5.56 and -6.05.

AI.tldr: AgenticFocus is a Mixed Reality pipeline that converts first-person videos into robot-demonstrations by restoring occluded objects, reconstructing full-hand motion, and retargeting to a humanoid; it yields smoother wrist motion and lower trajectory error than baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome egocentric video limitations for humanoid policy learning, specifically occlusions, oversimplified hand motion, and reliance on specialized capture hardware.
AI.method: Restore occluded object geometry, reconstruct full-hand motion, and retarget to a humanoid embodiment using camera-relative alignment and layered compositing to produce paired datasets of focused observations with synchronized robot actions and states.
AI.result: AgenticFocus achieves lower trajectory error and smoother wrist motion compared with cross-embodiment baselines. Reported SPARC scores: -5.18 (AgenticFocus) versus -5.56 and -6.05 for baselines.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline demonstrates the practicality of converting ordinary egocentric videos into robot-training demonstrations, improving motion quality and enabling scalable humanoid policy learning.

title: StereoSplat+: Feed-Forward Stereo Gaussian Splatting with Diffusion-Assisted Progressive Inference
comment: 8 pages, accepted as a conference paper for IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS2026)
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled high-quality, render-ready scene representations for novel-view synthesis. However, most existing 3DGS pipelines rely on multi-view observations (or non-causal access to future frames) to achieve sufficient coverage, which is often unavailable in on-device robotics and AR settings where sensing is restricted to a single stereo rig. Recovering a high-quality 3DGS scene from one stereo observation, therefore, remains challenging due to occlusions, limited field of view, and missing geometry. We present StereoSplat+, a diffusion-enhanced feed-forward framework that enables causal reconstruction from a single stereo pair. Our method builds on two key components. First, we propose StereoSplat, an input-invariant feed-forward 3D Gaussian estimator that takes a variable number of posed stereo pairs as input and predicts high-quality 3D Gaussians. StereoSplat fuses complementary geometry cues via a cost-volume branch and a triplane-based 3D volume branch and leverages continuous pose encoding to generalize across view counts and camera configurations. Second, since multiple posed stereo pairs are typically unavailable at inference time, we introduce a diffusion-enhanced one-shot progressive inference scheme called StereoSplat+: starting from one stereo pair, we render novel stereo views from the predicted 3DGS, refine them with a one-step diffusion enhancer, and feed them back as additional inputs to update the 3DGS. Experiments on the KITTI-360 dataset show that StereoSplat+ improves novel-view rendering quality and geometry accuracy, especially in occluded regions and under strong view extrapolation, outperforming recent feed-forward 3DGS baselines.

AI.tldr: StereoSplat+ enables causal 3D Gaussian Splatting from a single stereo pair by combining a feed-forward stereo-based estimator with a diffusion-enhanced progressive refinement loop, improving novel-view render quality and geometry in occluded regions.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) typically requires multi-view observations; single stereo data presents occlusions, limited field of view, and missing geometry. For on-device robotics/AR with sensing restricted to a single stereo rig, a causal, single-shot method is needed to reconstruct high-quality 3DGS.
AI.method: StereoSplat is an input-invariant feed-forward 3D Gaussian estimator that accepts a variable number of posed stereo pairs and fuses geometry cues from a cost-volume branch and a triplane-based 3D volume branch, using continuous pose encoding to generalize across view counts and camera setups. StereoSplat+ is a diffusion-enhanced one-shot progressive inference: starting from one stereo pair, render novel stereo views from the predicted 3DGS, apply a one-step diffusion enhancer, and feed them back as additional inputs to update the 3DGS.
AI.result: On KITTI-360, StereoSplat+ yields higher novel-view rendering quality and tighter geometry estimates, particularly in occluded regions and under strong view extrapolation, outperforming recent feed-forward 3DGS baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables causal reconstruction of high-quality 3D Gaussian scenes from a single stereo observation, reducing reliance on multi-view data and bringing 3DGS closer to real-time, on-device deployment.

title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Models via Interactions
summary: Despite the success of knowledge distillation (KD) in Large Language Models (LLMs), the underlying mechanism behind its efficacy remains unclear. In this paper, we propose a unified approach to explore the common mechanism of various KD methods using interactions. Specifically, we decompose the output score of the LLM into the sum of numerous interactions. Each interaction represents a nonlinear relationship involving a set of input variables (e.g., words). Based on the decomposed interactions, we discover that the common mechanism underlying various KD methods is the sparsification of interactions, i.e., student models retain fewer interactions for inference while suppressing other interactions to zero effects. Furthermore, we discover that the performance variance across different KD methods arises from their capabilities in handling complex interactions. A KD method typically yields better performance if it enables the student model to achieve higher sparsity of complex interactions. Motivated by these insights, we propose a plug-and-play loss function called Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) to explicitly enforce the sparsity of complex interactions during the distillation process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating CIP consistently improves the performance of diverse KD methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Unified view of KD via interaction sparsity; CIP enforces sparsity of complex interactions to boost KD across methods and domains.
AI.motivation: Clarify why KD works and why methods vary by identifying a common mechanism in interaction sparsity.
AI.method: Decompose LLM outputs into a sum over nonlinear interactions among input variables; analyze sparsity of these interactions; propose Complex Interaction Penalty (CIP) as a plug-and-play loss to enforce sparsity of complex interactions during distillation; evaluate across diverse KD methods on in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.result: Demonstrates sparsification of interactions as the shared mechanism; better KD performance correlates with ability to induce sparsity of complex interactions; CIP yields improvements across methods and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Sparse complex interactions underpin KD efficacy; CIP provides a practical, generalizable approach to enhance KD by promoting sparsity of complex interactions.

title: CogniConsole: Externalizing Inference-Time Control as a Formal Abstraction for Reliable LLM Interactions
comment: Revised version focusing on the CogniConsole system architecture and empirical evaluation of inference-time control probes (N=489)
summary: Reliability in large language model (LLM) systems is typically framed as a function of model capability. We challenge this by demonstrating that reliability is significantly influenced by \emph{inference-time control} -- the computational layer governing task framing and context selection. We introduce \emph{CogniConsole}, an architectural instantiation that externalizes this control into a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Through \emph{controllability-oriented probes} ($N=489$) in a multi-step interactive environment, we show that increasing structural scaffolding -- from unstructured to fully scaffolded -- \textbf{systematically reduces output variance and failure rates under a fixed model architecture}. Our results indicate that many observed failure modes, such as context drift and inconsistent constraint adherence, arise from under-specified control rather than insufficient capability. This work provides an empirical basis for treating inference-time control as a first-class abstraction, opening new directions for designing and evaluating LLM systems beyond scaling alone.

AI.tldr: Increasing inference-time control structure reduces LLM output variance and failures, challenging the idea that reliability depends solely on model scaling.
AI.motivation: To show that reliability in LLMs is strongly influenced by the computational layer that frames tasks and selects context, not just model capability.
AI.method: Introduce CogniConsole, an architecture that externalizes inference-time control via a structured interface combining programmatic coordination with bounded prompt-based reasoning. Use controllability-oriented probes (N=489) in a multi-step interactive setting, comparing levels of scaffolding from unstructured to fully scaffolded.
AI.result: Increasing structural scaffolding systematically reduces output variance and failure rates at a fixed model architecture. Failure modes such as context drift and constraint adherence are attributed to under-specified control rather than model capability.
AI.conclusion: Treat inference-time control as a first-class abstraction in LLM system design and evaluation, enabling robust behavior beyond scaling and opening new directions for system design.

title: FlowDAgger: Human-in-the-Loop Adaptation of Generative Robot Policies in Latent Space
summary: Pretrained generative robot policies based on flow matching and diffusion have achieved impressive results across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Yet real-world deployments routinely expose failure modes outside the pretraining distribution. Closing these gaps typically requires large-scale data collection or online reinforcement learning on physical hardware, which is impractical for rapid and safe adaptation. We present FlowDAgger, a sample- and compute-efficient method for adapting frozen generative robot policies from human interventions in latent space. Our key idea is action inversion: each human expert action is mapped to the noise that would have produced it under the frozen base policy, using reverse-time integration followed by local refinement. The resulting inverted noise provides supervision for a lightweight latent policy that steers the base model at deployment time, enabling rapid skill acquisition while preserving its behavioral priors. We evaluate FlowDAgger in simulation and on real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation, adapting both action-head VLAs and world-action models from a handful of interventions. FlowDAgger outperforms supervised fine-tuning and latent-space RL baselines and preserves pretrained skills on held-out tasks, offering a practical path for adapting robot foundation models in the real world. Website: https://microsoft.github.io/FlowDAgger

AI.tldr: FlowDAgger provides a sample- and compute-efficient method to adapt frozen generative robot policies by converting human actions into inverted latent noise and training a lightweight latent policy to steer the base model during deployment, enabling rapid adaptation with few interventions.
AI.motivation: Real-world failures lie outside pretraining distribution, and large-scale data collection or online hardware RL is impractical; there is a need for practical, data-efficient adaptation of robot foundation models.
AI.method: Action inversion: map each expert action to the noise that would have produced it under the frozen base policy via reverse-time integration and local refinement; use the inverted noise to supervise a lightweight latent policy that conditions the base model at deployment; evaluate via human interventions in simulation and real-world bimanual/single-arm tasks; compatible with action-head VLAs and world-action models.
AI.result: FlowDAgger outperforms supervised fine-tuning and latent-space RL baselines; preserves pretrained skills on held-out tasks; demonstrated in both simulation and real-world experiments with a handful of interventions.
AI.conclusion: FlowDAgger enables rapid skill acquisition while preserving pretrained priors by leveraging latent-space inversions to guide adaptation, offering a practical path for updating robot foundation models with minimal data and compute.

title: Mixture of Probes: Learning from Privileged Modalities in Multimodal LLMs Through Probing
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are typically designed under the assumption that all modalities available during training will also be accessible at inference. However, many real-world settings violate this assumption, requiring models to operate under a privileged modality setting, where auxiliary modalities are available only during training. While these modalities contain valuable information, existing MLLMs largely fail to leverage them effectively, as they treat modalities as interchangeable inputs rather than sources of complementary supervision. We propose Mixture of Probes (MoP), a novel framework that disentangles modality-specific and modality-general signals within the MLLM, allowing the model to preserve modality-dependent structure while learning transferable representations across modalities. At its core, MoP achieves this through a structured probing mechanism that extracts and organizes information from intermediate representations of a shared modality encoder, rather than relying only on final-layer alignment as done in existing MLLMs. To support this disentanglement, we further introduce MoP Cross-modal Training (MoP-X), a training strategy for MoP centered around a probe disentanglement loss that prevents probe collapse and encourages cross-modal learning. We evaluate MoP across two domains spanning eight tasks and four modalities under a comprehensive evaluation protocol tailored to the privileged modality setting, where each modality is independently treated as the sole input at inference time. MoP consistently outperforms strong MLLM baselines, achieving up to 65% relative improvement, demonstrating that auxiliary modalities, even when unavailable at inference, can provide substantial gains when effectively leveraged during training. Code, model checkpoints, and evaluation protocols will be made available at https://github.com/Sony/MoP.

AI.tldr: Mixture of Probes (MoP) disentangles modality-specific vs modality-general signals via intermediate-probe supervision and cross-modal training (MoP-X) to leverage privileged training-time modalities; yields strong gains across 8 tasks and 4 modalities, with up to 65% relative improvement.
AI.motivation: Real-world settings often provide auxiliary modalities only during training; current MLLMs underutilize such privileged information by treating modalities as interchangeable; leveraging them can yield better transferable representations.
AI.method: Introduce structured probes placed on intermediate representations of a shared modality encoder to separate modality-specific and modality-general information. Train with MoP-X, including a probe disentanglement loss to prevent collapse and promote cross-modal transfer. Evaluate under privileged modality setting by treating each modality as the sole input at inference; use a two-domain, eight-task, four-modality design.
AI.result: MoP outperforms strong MLLM baselines, achieving up to 65% relative improvement, demonstrating that auxiliary modalities provide substantial gains even when unavailable at inference.
AI.conclusion: Structured probing and disentangled cross-modal training enable learning transferable representations from privileged modalities, improving MLLM performance under restricted inference; code and checkpoints will be released.

title: iLENS: Interpretable LLM-Guided Mixture-of-Experts for Neuroimaging Survival Analysis
summary: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder that continues to impact millions of people worldwide. Predicting AD conversion during the prodromal stage remains critical for disease understanding and patient care. As such, survival models are widely used for AD risk prediction, yet they are typically static predictors with limited interpretability and no capacity for natural language reasoning. In this work, we propose iLENS, an interpretable large language model (LLM) guided framework based on mixture-of-experts (MoE) for survival prediction in AD conversion. Our approach uses LLM to synthesize structured neuroimaging measurements and unstructured information to guide expert routing. Our framework demonstrates competitive predictive performance and capability in patient subtyping. Furthermore, our framework provides transparent, biologically grounded rationales for its routing decisions, bridging the gap between high-performance survival analysis and interpretable clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts survival model (iLENS) using an LLM-guided routing to predict Alzheimer’s conversion by integrating structured neuroimaging and unstructured data, enabling patient subtyping and rationale-based decisions.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer’s prodromal prediction requires dynamic, interpretable risk modeling. Traditional survival models are static and opaque and lack natural language reasoning for clinical actionability.
AI.method: iLENS applies an LLM-guided mixture-of-experts framework. The LLM synthesizes structured neuroimaging measurements and unstructured information to route among experts, yielding survival predictions and interpretable biologically grounded rationales for routing decisions.
AI.result: The approach achieves competitive predictive performance, supports patient subtyping, and provides transparent, biologically anchored rationales for expert routing.
AI.conclusion: iLENS advances interpretable, high-performing survival analysis in AD and demonstrates how LLM-guided MoE can bridge predictive accuracy with clinical interpretability and decision support.

title: GATS: Graph-Augmented Tree Search with Layered World Models for Efficient Agent Planning
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise in multi-step planning tasks, but existing approaches like LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) and ReAct rely heavily on LLM inference during planning, leading to high computational costs and stochastic behavior. We present \textbf{GATS} (Graph-Augmented Tree Search), a planning framework that combines systematic UCB1-based tree search with a layered world model to eliminate LLM calls during inference while achieving superior planning performance. Our three-layer world model integrates: (L1) exact symbolic action matching, (L2) statistics learned from execution logs, and (L3) LLM-based prediction for unknown actions. On synthetic planning tasks with branching paths and dead-ends, GATS achieves \textbf{100\% success rate} compared to 92 % for LATS and 64\% for ReAct. On a comprehensive stress test spanning 12 challenging scenarios -- including coding workflows, web navigation, and long-horizon tasks -- GATS maintains \textbf{100\% success} while LATS drops to 88.9 % and ReAct to 23.9%. GATS requires \textbf{zero LLM calls per task} during planning (vs. 37 per task for LATS) and produces deterministic plans with zero variance across runs. Our results demonstrate that systematic search with learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning.

AI.tldr: GATS: Graph-Augmented Tree Search combining UCB1-tree search with a three-layer world model to eliminate LLM inference during planning, achieving zero LLM calls and deterministic plans with superior performance vs LATS and ReAct on synthetic and stress-test tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce computational costs and stochasticity of LLM-driven planning (e.g., LATS, ReAct) by removing runtime LLM calls during planning while maintaining or improving planning performance.
AI.method: Three-layer world model integrated with UCB1-based tree search: (L1) exact symbolic action matching; (L2) statistics learned from execution logs; (L3) LLM-based prediction for unknown actions. Planning uses the learned model to guide search without consulting the LLM, yielding deterministic plans.
AI.result: Synthetic planning tasks: GATS 100% success vs 92% (LATS) and 64% (ReAct). Stress test (12 scenarios: coding, web navigation, long-horizon): GATS 100% vs 88.9% (LATS) and 23.9% (ReAct). Zero LLM calls per task during planning (0) compared to 37 for LATS. Plans are deterministic with zero variance across runs.
AI.conclusion: Systematic search augmented with layered, learned world models can substantially outperform LLM-guided exploration for agent planning, achieving zero reliance on LLM inference during planning and stable, high-performance results.

title: SplatCtrl: Perception-Action Coupling via Gaussian Scene Representations and Reactive Robot Control
comment: Published in 2026 International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). 8 pages, 8 figures
summary: Robotic manipulators excel in structured environments but face substantial challenges in unstructured and dynamic settings. This paper presents SplatCtrl, a unified framework for real-time scene reconstruction and reactive robot motion generation to enable collision-free robotic arm control in previously unseen and continuously changing environments. Building on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS), we introduce a hybrid voxel-based filtering and dynamic Gaussian relocation strategy that supports efficient scene reconstruction from RGB-D streams while accommodating environmental changes. For safe and reactive control, we further propose a method for deriving continuous signed distance functions from isotropic Gaussians, providing stable and differentiable collision probability estimates that bridge classical distance fields with the modern implicit representation. These continuous distance metrics are incorporated into control barrier functions, resulting in a unified perception-action coupling framework that supports smooth and reliable real-time motion generation in response to scene changes. Experimental validation in simulation, on physical robot, and within shared human-robot workspace demonstrates the framework's effectiveness, achieving integrated scene reconstruction and reactive control in uncertain, and dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: A real-time, unified perception-action framework (SplatCtrl) for collision-free robotic arm control in dynamic, unseen environments, built on 3D Gaussian Splatting with continuous distance fields and control barrier integration.
AI.motivation: Robots excel in structured settings but struggle in unstructured/dynamic ones due to perception gaps and safety concerns; there is a need for real-time scene reconstruction from RGB-D data and reactive, safe motion generation.
AI.method: 1) Use 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) for scene representation; 2) employ a hybrid voxel-based filtering and dynamic Gaussian relocation to enable efficient reconstruction from RGB-D streams and to adapt to environmental changes; 3) derive continuous signed distance functions from isotropic Gaussians to obtain stable, differentiable collision probability estimates; 4) fuse these distance metrics into control barrier functions to couple perception with action for smooth, real-time motion generation; 5) validate in simulation, on a real robot, and in a shared human-robot workspace.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates integrated scene reconstruction and reactive control in uncertain and dynamic environments, achieving collision-free, real-time motion in changing scenes across simulation and physical experiments.
AI.conclusion: SplatCtrl bridges classic distance-field concepts with modern implicit representations, enabling a unified perception–action pipeline for safe, real-time manipulation in dynamic, unseen environments, with demonstrated transfer from simulation to real hardware.

title: Secure-by-Disguise: A Systematic Evaluation of Image Disguising for Confidential Medical Image Modeling
summary: Cloud-based deep learning enables large-scale medical image analysis but raises significant privacy concerns when sensitive patient images are outsourced for model development. Image disguising has recently emerged as a promising privacy-enhancing technology (PET) that transforms images into visually unintelligible representations while preserving information for downstream learning. We established a unified framework to evaluate representative methods, DisguisedNets and NeuraCrypt, across four datasets involving classification and semantic segmentation tasks. Our analysis assessed predictive utility, efficiency, and robustness against reconstruction attacks. Results showed that image disguising performance varies significantly between tasks; while methods preserved utility for medical image classification, they caused substantial degradation in dense semantic segmentation. Specifically, Randomized Multidimensional Transformation (RMT) offered the optimal balance of performance and security, whereas AES-based disguising severely impacted utility. Furthermore, regression-based reconstruction attacks effective on natural images proved considerably less successful on realistic medical images. These findings provide a systematic assessment of PET suitability for confidential medical AI applications.

AI.tldr: RMT-based disguising offers the best trade-off between privacy, utility, and security for medical AI; disguising methods show task-dependent performance—classification retains utility, dense segmentation degrades; AES-based disguising harms utility; reconstruction attacks are less effective on medical images than natural images.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate privacy-enhancing disguising methods for cloud-based medical AI across tasks and datasets, focusing on utility, efficiency, and robustness to reconstruction attacks.
AI.method: Unified framework evaluating representative PET methods (DisguisedNets, NeuraCrypt) on four medical imaging datasets spanning classification and semantic segmentation; compare RMT and AES disguising; assess predictive utility, computational efficiency, and resilience to reconstruction attacks.
AI.result: Utility preserved for classification under disguising; substantial degradation observed in semantic segmentation. Randomized Multidimensional Transformation (RMT) offers the best overall balance between accuracy and security; AES-based disguising markedly reduces utility. Regression-based reconstruction attacks effective on natural images are considerably less successful on realistic medical images.
AI.conclusion: PET can be suitable for confidential medical AI, particularly for classification tasks; for dense tasks like semantic segmentation, existing disguising methods may be insufficient. Task-specific evaluation is essential; RMT is recommended for general use, with ongoing research into more robust attacks and defenses.

title: Signed Symmetric Quantization for Few-Bit Integers
summary: The signed integer alphabet contains one more negative representable value than positive. Yet, by convention, the standard symmetric integer quantizer fixes its scale to be strictly positive, which assigns this extra representable value to the negative tail and can force clipping of positive outliers. In this work, we show that, at few-bit precision, such clipping is a non-trivial source of quantization error. Asymmetric quantization addresses this problem with a zero point, shifting the grid toward the observed data range; however, this flexibility is well-known to carry a runtime penalty. For example, in llama.cpp on an AMD EPYC(TM) "Turin" CPU, a 4-bit symmetric format uses up to 9% less memory with up to 2.45$\times$ higher throughput than its asymmetric counterpart. We highlight signed symmetric quantization as a third option that retains the runtime profile of symmetric quantization without the penalty of the asymmetric format: our signed absmax grid places the extra representable value on the dominant-outlier tail through a principled and lightweight sign selection rule while keeping the zero point at zero. Our theoretical analysis offers two main results. First, we establish the signed absmax grid as conditionally bound-optimal on $\ell_2$ quantization error, and show that the condition holds for 88-99% of weight groups across pre-trained large language models (LLMs) at low bit widths. Second, we show that negating the scale of a standard symmetric quantizer is analytically equivalent to a unit zero point shift on the same signed integer alphabet. We empirically validate our proposal on models from the Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and Llama3 families, and observe improvement in perplexity and downstream few-shot accuracy over the standard unsigned symmetric quantizer at no extra inference cost

AI.tldr: Proposes a signed absmax grid for low-bit quantization that retains zero at zero and places the extra representable value on the dominant tail, offering near-optimal L2 error and runtime parity with symmetric quantization, validated on large language models with empirical gains.
AI.motivation: Address quantization error from clipping in few-bit symmetric quantization and the runtime penalty of fully asymmetric quantization. Provide a middle-ground that preserves symmetric runtime while reducing error.
AI.method: Introduce a signed absmax grid with a principled sign selection rule to allocate the extra representable value to the dominant tail. Prove conditional bound-optimality for L2 quantization error and show equivalence between negating scale and a unit zero-point shift. Empirically validate on Qwen3, Qwen3.5, and Llama3 models, comparing perplexity and few-shot accuracy, with analysis of memory/throughput in related implementations (e.g., llama.cpp).
AI.result: The signed absmax grid is conditionally bound-optimal for L2 error across 88–99% of weight groups at low bit-widths. Negating the scale of a standard symmetric quantizer is equivalent to a unit zero-point shift analytically. Empirical tests show improved perplexity and few-shot accuracy over unsigned symmetric quantization without additional inference cost, aligning runtime with symmetric quantization and avoiding asymmetric penalties.
AI.conclusion: A practical and theoretically grounded middle-ground for low-bit quantization that preserves symmetric-runtime efficiency while reducing quantization error by optimally placing the extra representable value on the dominant tail; broadly applicable to pre-trained LLMs with substantial empirical gains.

title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench: Testing the Limits of Agents on Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks with Dense Reward-Based Grading
summary: AI agents have become capable of autonomously completing short, well-specified tasks. However, existing terminal benchmarks largely focus on simple problems that finish within minutes and are evaluated only by their final outcome. This setup overlooks intermediate progress and partial solutions, yielding sparse reward signals and an incomplete picture of agent capability. We introduce Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench, a terminal benchmark of 46 long-horizon tasks spanning nine categories, including experiment reproduction, software engineering, multimodal analysis, interactive games, and scientific computing. Each task follows a Terminal-Bench-style setup with a reference solution or simulation engine, but is further decomposed into fine-grained graded subtasks. This design enables dense intermediate rewards and partial credit, allowing evaluation to capture not only whether an agent reaches the final goal, but also how far it progresses on open-ended workflows. Tasks in Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench typically require hundreds of episodes and minutes to hours of execution, stressing long-horizon planning, long-context management, and iterative debugging rather than one-shot problem solving. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find that agents consume on average 9.9M tokens per task, with roughly 231 episodes and 85.3 minutes of execution time per run, making Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench more demanding than prior terminal-based benchmarks. Even the strongest tested model achieves 15.2% pass@1 at a partial-reward threshold of 0.95 and 10.9% at a perfect-reward threshold of 1.0, while the mean pass rate across models is 4.3% and 1.7% under the two thresholds, respectively. These results reveal headroom for improvement. We further analyze failure modes and error patterns, and release Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench to support future progress on long-horizon terminal agents.

AI.tldr: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench introduces 46 long-horizon, graded terminal tasks across 9 categories, enabling dense intermediate rewards and partial credit to evaluate progress, not just final outcomes.
AI.motivation: Fills a gap where existing terminal benchmarks emphasize final outcomes with sparse rewards, overlooking intermediate progress, learning curves, and debugging for long-horizon agents.
AI.method: Construct 46 tasks with reference solutions or simulation engines, decompose into fine-grained graded subtasks, measure dense intermediate rewards, and evaluate 15 frontier models across multiple episodes, tokens, and time.
AI.result: The benchmark reveals low pass rates even for strong models (best ~15.2% pass@1 at partial reward 0.95; ~10.9% at perfect 1.0; mean 4.3% and 1.7%), with high resource use (avg ~9.9M tokens/task, ~231 episodes/run, ~85.3 minutes).
AI.conclusion: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench enables tracking progress on long-horizon terminal tasks, diagnosing failure modes, and advancing long-horizon planning, context management, and debugging in AI agents; the authors release the benchmark for future research.

title: CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Adaptation via Language-Action Grounding
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic capabilities from pretrained VLMs, yet large-scale post-training on robot data and architectural modifications can reshape the backbone so extensively that it becomes difficult to isolate what the VLM contributes to control. Directly converting pretrained VLMs into VLAs with minimal architectural change offers a more transparent path to understanding how VLM capabilities transfer across model scales. The core obstacle is output-distribution mismatch: predicting actions as bare numeric token sequences moves generation away from the VLM's pretrained language distribution, degrading the capabilities we seek to preserve. To address this, we propose CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction), which prepends each numeric action sequence with a natural-language action description, causally conditioning precise action-token prediction on a language-action plan without modifying the backbone architecture. With single-epoch fine-tuning alone, 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO (+14.9 pt over VLA-0) and improves robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations. We will release CLAP at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B as an open-weight, multi-scale compact VLA family from a single VLM lineage, enabling controlled analysis of VLM-to-VLA capability transfer.

AI.tldr: CLAP uses causal language-action planning by prefixing numeric actions with natural-language descriptions to align VLA action generation with the pretrained language distribution, enabling transparent transfer from VLMs with minimal fine-tuning; achieves 90.8% LIBERO on 2B; to be released at 0.8B/2B/4B.
AI.motivation: Isolate the VLM's contribution to control in VLAs and elucidate transfer of capabilities across model scales by avoiding large architectural changes and post-training on robot data; address the output-distribution mismatch between bare action tokens and the VLM's language prior.
AI.method: For each numeric action sequence, prepend a natural-language action description to causally condition action-token prediction on a language-action plan; no backbone modification; single-epoch fine-tuning; evaluate across LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO; plan to release open-weight models at multiple scales.
AI.result: 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO ( +14.9 points vs VLA-0 ); improved robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations.
AI.conclusion: CLAP enables controlled, transparent analysis of VLM-to-VLA capability transfer across scales without changing the backbone; open-weight, multi-scale VLA family from a single VLM lineage for systematic study.

title: Decoupled Illumination Priors for Spatially Controllable Multi-View Indoor Scene Relighting
summary: Indoor scene relighting demands photorealism, precise spatial control, and strict multi-view consistency. While diffusion-based image editing models enable semantic lighting manipulation via text prompts, enforcing exact 3D light placement often disrupts their generative priors. We propose Lume-Palette, a progressive framework that leverages semantic lighting priors for spatially controllable multi-view indoor relighting. The approach decouples relighting into two stages: (1) illumination distillation, which extracts canonical illumination palettes from a pretrained diffusion model to preserve realistic material-light interactions, and (2) illumination casting, which explicitly maps target spatial lighting conditions defined from coarse 3D geometry. To efficiently handle dense multi-view and multi-modal inputs, we introduce an asymmetric multi-view conditioning strategy that selectively injects essential spatial context. Experiments on diverse synthetic scenes and real-world scenes demonstrate that Lume-Palette produces photorealistic, spatially controllable, and multi-view consistent relighting results. Project Page: https://cjeen.github.io/lumepalette

AI.tldr: Two-stage diffusion-based indoor relighting framework (Lume-Palette) that distills canonical lighting priors from a pretrained diffusion model and then casts target lighting under coarse 3D geometry, using asymmetric multi-view conditioning to achieve photorealistic, spatially controllable, and multi-view-consistent results.
AI.motivation: Enforcing exact 3D light placement within diffusion-based editing often disrupts realism; need precise spatial control and multi-view consistency for indoor relighting while preserving material–light interactions.
AI.method: 1) Illumination distillation: extract canonical illumination palettes from a pretrained diffusion model to preserve realistic material–light interactions. 2) Illumination casting: map target spatial lighting defined from coarse geometry. 3) Asymmetric multi-view conditioning: selectively inject essential spatial context to handle dense multi-view and multi-modal inputs.
AI.result: Evaluations on diverse synthetic and real-world scenes show photorealistic, spatially controllable, and multi-view consistent relighting results.
AI.conclusion: Lume-Palette effectively decouples relighting into distillation and casting stages, enabling controllable, geometry-guided indoor relighting while preserving realism through diffusion priors.

title: Sticky Routing: Training MoE Models for Memory-Efficient Inference
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a sparse subset of experts per token, yet consecutive tokens frequently activate different experts -- causing constant weight swapping between slow storage and fast memory on edge devices. Existing remedies are either system-level (caching heuristics) or post-hoc (router fine-tuning), leaving the root cause unchanged during pretraining. We propose StickyMoE, a differentiable routing consistency loss that penalises abrupt expert switches between adjacent tokens, encouraging the router to maintain the same expert assignment across semantically coherent spans. StickyMoE requires no architectural changes, adds a single hyperparameter lambda, and unlike post-hoc methods, allows expert representations and routing decisions to co-adapt from the first training step. Experiments on small-scale MoE language models show that StickyMoE reduces the expert switch rate by up to 60% with less than 4% perplexity degradation, Pareto-dominating post-hoc fine-tuning on the quality-locality frontier. Routing temporal locality is most efficiently instilled at training time.

AI.tldr: Differentiable routing consistency loss (StickyMoE) reduces per-token expert switches in Mixture-of-Experts models during pretraining, achieving up to 60% switch reduction with <4% perplexity loss, and Pareto-dominates post-hoc fine-tuning on the quality-locality frontier.
AI.motivation: MoE models trigger sparse expert utilization per token, but successive tokens often switch experts, causing costly memory traffic on edge devices. Existing fixes are system-level or post-hoc and do not address the root cause during pretraining.
AI.method: Introduce a differentiable routing consistency loss that penalizes abrupt switches between adjacent tokens. Encourages the router to assign the same expert across semantically coherent spans. No architectural changes; adds a single hyperparameter lambda. Enables co-adaptation of expert representations and routing from the first training step.
AI.result: Reduces expert switch rate by up to 60% with less than 4% perplexity degradation. Outperforms post-hoc fine-tuning on the quality-locality Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Training-time routing temporal locality can be efficiently instilled without architectural changes, using a simple differentiable loss and minimal hyperparameter tuning; potential for better edge deployment and overall model efficiency.

title: A Formalization of the Mean-Field Derivation of the Vlasov Equation: AI-Assisted Lean Formalization as a Strategy Game
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures. Lean 4 development, blueprint site, and agent logs: https://github.com/Hydrodynamical/Vlasov_Meanfield_Formalization
summary: We formalize a research result in the Lean 4 proof assistant by having a mathematician direct an AI system, and frame the activity as a formalization game. The objective is to turn a LaTeX document into Lean. The game is won when the development compiles, contains no sorry, and a machine check shows the target theorems rest on Lean's foundational axioms alone. Reuse is a second check, by a definition we introduce: whether the development yields a self-contained layer of general mathematics the wider library could absorb. The case study is a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin's mean-field route -- existence, uniqueness, the stability estimate and mean-field limit, and a short-window superposition principle (weak solutions are Lagrangian). The human's role was to direct, not to write proofs: to scope the definitions, steer the decompositions, and triage the library's gaps; the AI agent executed. The formalization certifies the proof of each statement as written; whether the written statement is the intended theorem stays the mathematician's judgment. The optimal-transport machinery that fell out of the build (in particular, properties of the Wasserstein-1 metric and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality theorem) separates into a self-contained layer that compiles against Mathlib alone: about a sixth of the development (49 of 299 declarations), behind a 22-declaration interface with no reverse dependency. The headline theorems ran in about a week, the full development in about a month. We report the quantitative claims as observations of one game, not as general laws. The game's rules name no particular system, so the methodological framing is meant to outlast the tools of any one run.

AI.tldr: A human-guided AI formalization game converts a LaTeX document into Lean 4, demonstrated on a complete, axiom-clean formalization of well-posedness for the nonlinear Vlasov equation via Dobrushin’s mean-field route; shows a modular, reusable library structure with a self-contained optimal-transport layer that compiles against Mathlib; timeline: headline theorems in ~1 week, full development in ~1 month; results suggest a general, tool-agnostic methodology for AI-assisted formalization.
AI.motivation: To explore feasibility, reproducibility, and library-design implications of AI-assisted formalization of mathematics. The work frames formalization as a game, separates human directive roles from AI execution, and seeks self-contained, reusable library layers that can be absorbed by broader mathematical libraries.
AI.method: Formalization game: a mathematician scopes definitions, decompositions, and gaps; an AI agent performs the formalization proofs. Success criteria include compiling with no sorries and ensuring statements rest only on Lean’s axioms. A self-contained layer for optimal transport (Wasserstein-1 and Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality) is extracted, modularized with a 22-declaration interface and no reverse dependencies. Case study formalizes well-posedness of the Vlasov equation via Dobrushin’s mean-field route: existence, uniqueness, stability, mean-field limit, and a weak soln principle.
AI.result: Approximately one-sixth of the development (49 of 299 declarations) forms a self-contained layer; the optimal-transport portion isolates into a module that compiles against Mathlib with a 22-declaration interface and no reverse dependencies. Headline theorems run in about a week; full development in about a month. The formalization certifies the proofs as written; the mathematical intent lies in the human judgment of the theorems themselves.
AI.conclusion: The framework is methodology-agnostic and tool-agnostic beyond one run; it yields a practical, reusable library architecture and demonstrates that AI-assisted formalization can produce coherent, axiom-clean developments within a bounded timeline. Observations are based on a single study and serve as a pilot for broader applicability.

title: Dec-MARVEL: Decentralized Multi-Agent Exploration without Communication under Budget Constraints
summary: Multi-UAV exploration is often constrained by unreliable communication, limited field-of-view sensing (e.g., lightweight onboard camera), and finite travel budgets that require each robot to reserve enough budget to return to its base. We present Dec-MARVEL, a decentralized budget-aware exploration framework for communication-free teams with directional sensing. Rather than exchanging maps, goals, or messages, each robot coordinates through its incidental observations: any teammate trajectory within its field of view serves as a coordination signal. A graph-attention actor fuses local frontier geometry, teammate motion, and budget features to select return-feasible waypoint-heading actions. The actor is trained with phase-conditioned critics, a training-only task-oriented privileged critic, and a mixture-based budget curriculum. Across 900 held-out trials spanning three team sizes (2, 4, 8 robots) and three travel budgets (720, 800, 1024 meters) against four baselines, Dec-MARVEL achieves the highest or tied-highest exploration rate and lowest sensing overlap across all nine team-size budget configurations. Under our tightest 720m budget, it reaches 53%, 94%, and 100% success for 2, 4, and 8 robots, versus 37%, 83%, and 99% for the strongest baseline. Physical-robot experiments demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer and real-world deployment of Dec-MARVEL.

AI.tldr: Dec-MARVEL introduces a decentralized, budget-aware exploration framework for multi-UAV teams with directional sensing that coordinates via incidental observations, using a graph-attention actor and phase-conditioned training to achieve robust exploration under limited communication, with sim-to-real transfer and strong empirical results across multiple team sizes and budgets.
AI.motivation: Unreliable communication, limited field-of-view sensing, and finite travel budgets necessitate autonomous, coordination-efficient exploration without exchanging maps or messages.
AI.method: Decentralized coordination relying on incidental observations; a graph-attention actor fuses frontier geometry, teammate motion, and budget features to select return-feasible waypoint-heading actions. Training uses phase-conditioned critics, a training-only privileged critic, and a mixture-based budget curriculum. Evaluation on 900 trials across team sizes 2, 4, 8 and budgets 720/800/1024 m against four baselines.
AI.result: Dec-MARVEL achieves the highest or tied-highest exploration rate and the lowest sensing overlap across configurations. Under 720 m budget, success rates are 53%, 94%, and 100% for 2, 4, and 8 robots (vs 37%, 83%, 99% for the strongest baseline). Sim-to-real transfer demonstrated with physical robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: Dec-MARVEL effectively enables decentralized, budget-aware exploration in communication-free teams with directional sensing, scalable to up to 8 robots, robust across budgets, and capable of sim-to-real transfer, outperforming baselines on multiple metrics.

title: HAT Super-Resolution and a PARSeq+CLIP4STR Voting Ensemble for Extreme In-the-Wild License Plate Recognition
comment: 2 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the IEEE ICIP 2026 Grand Challenge on Extreme In-the-Wild License Plate Super-Resolution (XLPSR). Top-8 finalist
summary: We describe our entry to the ICIP 2026 Grand Challenge on Extreme In-the-Wild License Plate Super-Resolution (XLPSR), which scored 9.73 wECR on the public validation leaderboard. The system pairs a Hybrid Attention Transformer super-resolution (HAT) front-end with an ensemble of two scene-text recognisers (PARSeq-S and CLIP4STR-B) and a confidence-weighted character-voting scheme that abstains on uncertain positions. We treat XLPSR as a recognition task gated by image legibility: the SR step exists to lift characters out of sub-pixel territory, and the asymmetric scoring rule (+2 / -1 / 0) is exploited explicitly through abstention. Our pipeline runs in 1.7 s per sequence on RTX 3090 (max 2.7 s, p99 2.4 s), well under the 60 s/sequence Docker budget.

AI.tldr: Fast XLPSR pipeline combining HAT SR front-end with an ensemble of two scene-text recognisers and a confidence-weighted voting/abstention scheme; achieves 9.73 wECR on public validation and ~1.7s per sequence on RTX 3090, under a strict 60s budget.
AI.motivation: Frame XLPSR as a recognition task gated by image legibility, leveraging SR to lift characters from sub-pixel territory and abstention to exploit the asymmetric scoring rule, while maintaining practical latency.
AI.method: Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT) SR front-end; ensemble of two recognisers (PARSeq-S and CLIP4STR-B); confidence-weighted character voting with abstention for uncertain positions; evaluation uses an asymmetric scoring rule (+2 / -1 / 0).
AI.result: Public validation leaderboard score: 9.73 wECR. Runtime: 1.7 s per sequence on RTX 3090 (max 2.7 s, p99 2.4 s), well under the 60 s/sequence Docker budget.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a fast, recognition-gated XLPSR pipeline that benefits from SR uplift of legibility and ensemble voting with abstention, achieving strong performance within tight latency constraints.

title: Reward Transport: Property Control in Flow Matching via Noise-Space Alignment
summary: The coupling in flow matching -- the rule pairing noise vectors with data points -- is typically treated as a computational choice. We show that this coupling can instead serve as an alignment interface: by matching noise and data according to a target molecular property, it embeds controllable structure directly into the learned flow field. Building on this view, we introduce Reward Transport, which uses optimal transport coupling at training time to align a scalar noise-space coordinate with molecular rewards; at inference, varying this coordinate steers the generated distribution without requiring an oracle, reward model, gradient guidance, or additional computation. In the coupling-preserving limit, thresholding this coordinate recovers the Cross-Entropy Method's truncated reward distribution, providing a principled, continuously adjustable distribution-level control knob. Empirically, on ZINC-250K and GuacaMol, sweeping the scalar induces monotone control of logP and consistent QED control over its operating range; most tellingly, the same knob produces opposite structural responses for different targets, growing molecules for logP but shrinking them for QED, which rules out a generic size bias. The interface is complementary to classifier-free guidance and conditional flow matching, while a negative result under epsilon-prediction diffusion clarifies where coupling-level alignment is structurally absent. Code: https://github.com/KehanGuo2/reward-transport

AI.tldr: Reward Transport reframes the flow-matching coupling as a controllable alignment interface, using optimal transport to align a noise-space coordinate with molecular rewards; this yields a continuous distribution-level control knob for property-directed generation, with empirical monotone logP and QED control on ZINC-250K and GuacaMol and a negative result clarifying diffusion limitations.
AI.motivation: To transform the coupling from a computational convenience into an alignment mechanism that embeds controllable molecular structure into the learned flow, enabling property-driven steering without external guidance or extra compute.
AI.method: Introduce Reward Transport: train with optimal-transport coupling that aligns a scalar noise coordinate with molecular rewards; at inference, vary this coordinate to steer the generated distribution; in the coupling-preserving limit, thresholding recovers the Cross-Entropy Method’s truncated reward distribution, providing a principled, continuous control knob; code provided.
AI.result: Empirically, sweeping the scalar achieves monotone control of logP and consistent QED control over its operating range; the same knob yields opposite structural responses for different targets (increase for logP, decrease for QED), ruling out a generic size-bias; the interface complements classifier-free guidance and conditional flow matching, while epsilon-prediction diffusion yields a negative result clarifying where coupling-level alignment is structurally absent.
AI.conclusion: Reward Transport offers a principled, continuous, distribution-level control mechanism for property-directed generation via coupling alignment, demonstrating how to embed target properties into the flow field and providing a concrete path for property-conditioned generation without relying on an explicit reward model or gradient guidance.

title: ARCANA: A Reflective Multi-Agent Program Synthesis Framework for ARC-AGI-2 Reasoning
summary: We present ARCANA, a collaborative multi agent framework for solving ARC AGI 2 tasks under strict test time and hardware constraints. ARCANA decomposes each task into iterative perception, hypothesis generation, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement. A perceptual grounding agent builds object centric scene graphs from raw grids, a latent program policy proposes diverse DSL programs, a symbolic executor verifies candidates on demonstrations, and a reflective agent synthesizes failure driven feedback for the next turn. These agents communicate through a shared differentiable blackboard and are scheduled by a learned meta controller. The design combines structured program search with adaptive multi turn correction, improving reasoning efficiency and solution quality on challenging abstract transformation tasks.

AI.tldr: ARCANA is a cooperative multi-agent framework for ARC AGI 2 tasks that operates under strict test-time and hardware constraints using perception, DSL-based program search, symbolic execution, and reflective refinement on a differentiable blackboard.
AI.motivation: Address strict resource constraints and the challenge of abstract transformation reasoning by integrating structured program search with adaptive, multi-turn collaboration.
AI.method: Four agent roles: a perceptual grounding agent builds object-centric scene graphs from raw grids; a latent program policy proposes diverse DSL programs; a symbolic executor verifies candidates against demonstrations; a reflective agent generates failure-driven feedback for the next turn. Agents share a differentiable blackboard and are scheduled by a learned meta-controller, enabling iterative refinement and hybrid reasoning.
AI.result: The architecture aims to improve reasoning efficiency and solution quality on challenging abstract transformation tasks by combining structured program search with adaptive, multi-turn correction in a cooperative setting.
AI.conclusion: ARCANA demonstrates that integrating structured program search with multi-turn feedback on a differentiable blackboard can achieve robust, efficient reasoning under tight constraints.

title: Vascular Geometry Characterization for AI-Based Endovascular Navigation
summary: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is a time-critical intervention for acute ischemic stroke; however, access remains limited due to a shortage of neuroradiologists and specialized centers. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers potential to automate endovascular navigation and improve accessibility, yet current models lack standardized frameworks to assess navigation difficulty for model training and evaluation. This study aims to identify vascular metrics associated with navigation difficulty and to develop an automated pipeline for quantitative vascular feature extraction, enabling future complexity grading. Vascular trees were segmented from computed tomography angiograms from 61 patients, and vascular metrics including aortic arch type, presence of bovine arch, vessel length, tortuosity, take-off angle, number of reverse curves, were measured using a custom pipeline. A Soft Actor-Critic RL algorithm was used for 120 s autonomous navigation. Outcomes were analyzed using both mixed effects linear and logistic regression. On the left side, the presence of a bovine arch and aortic arch type II/III increased navigation time by 30.19 s and 37.92 s, respectively, while greater tortuosity (\b{eta} = 118.20) further prolonged the procedure and reduced success probability. On the right side, type II/III arches extended procedure time by 45.94 s, while each additional reverse curve was associated with 3.96 s longer navigation time and lower probability of success. These findings demonstrate for the first time that MT agent navigation difficulty is strongly influenced by vascular geometry. The proposed automated pipeline enables objective and quantitative characterization of vascular features, providing a foundation for future development of standardized complexity grading and RL model evaluation, without aiming to demonstrate clinically generalizable autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: RL-based autonomous navigation for mechanical thrombectomy is strongly influenced by vascular geometry; authors develop an automated pipeline to extract quantitative vascular features from CTA for standardized complexity grading and RL model evaluation; key findings show arch type, bovine arch, tortuosity, and reverse curves affect navigation time and success probability; study emphasizes groundwork rather than clinical generalizability.
AI.motivation: MT access is limited by a shortage of neuroradiologists and specialized centers. RL could automate endovascular navigation, but there is no standardized framework to quantify navigation difficulty for model training and evaluation. The study aims to identify vascular metrics linked to navigation difficulty and to create an automated pipeline for quantitative feature extraction to enable standardized complexity grading and model evaluation.
AI.method: Vascular trees segmented from CT angiograms of 61 patients. Measured metrics: aortic arch type, presence of bovine arch, vessel length, tortuosity, take-off angle, and number of reverse curves using a custom pipeline. Applied Soft Actor-Critic RL algorithm for 120 s of autonomous navigation. Analysis via mixed effects linear and logistic regression.
AI.result: On the left side, bovine arch and arch type II/III increased navigation time by 30.19 s and 37.92 s, respectively; greater tortuosity (beta = 118.20) further prolonged the procedure and reduced success probability. On the right side, arch type II/III increased time by 45.94 s; each additional reverse curve added 3.96 s to navigation time and lowered probability of success. Findings indicate that MT agent navigation difficulty is strongly influenced by vascular geometry. The automated pipeline enables objective, quantitative characterization of vascular features, supporting future development of standardized complexity grading and RL model evaluation; the study does not claim clinical generalizability of autonomous navigation.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline provides objective quantification of vascular features relevant to navigation difficulty, establishing a foundation for standardized complexity grading and RL evaluation in MT navigation research, while not asserting clinical generalizability of autonomous navigation at this stage.

title: Vision Transformers Learn Gestalt-Like Figure-Ground Cues from Natural Images
summary:
Figure-ground organization in the human visual system relies on several shape-based cues, including surroundedness, convexity, and symmetry. While these cues have been extensively studied using abstract stimuli, little is known about how they operate under natural conditions or how they arise from the statistics of natural scenes. Deep neural networks offer a promising path forward: a model that relies on the same figure-ground cues as humans would provide tractable experimental access to the underlying mechanisms. In this study, we evaluate shape-based figure-ground organization in Vision Transformers (ViTs), for which prior work has demonstrated the emergence of object-based grouping. We test 25 ViTs spanning supervised and self-supervised training objectives, by fitting linear probes to predict figure-ground assignment from intermediate patch representations using both natural images and controlled artificial stimuli that isolate individual cues. Our results show that ViTs robustly encode surroundedness and convexity, and that probes trained on natural images generalize zero-shot to artificial stimuli across several models. For symmetry we observe mixed results: the cue is encoded for uniformly colored but not for textured regions. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Gestalt-like figure-ground cues can be learned from natural scene statistics and position ViTs as a compelling model system for studying the computational mechanisms of perceptual organization.
  Code and data is available at https://github.com/mtangemann/mlvbench

AI.tldr: ViTs encode Gestalt-like figure-ground cues (surroundedness, convexity, symmetry) from natural scene statistics; linear probes predict figure-ground assignment from patch representations; surroundedness and convexity robust across models and generalize zero-shot to artificial stimuli; symmetry is cue-dependent (uniform color yes, texture no); 25 ViTs across supervised and self-supervised objectives; proposes ViTs as model for perceptual organization.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether human-like figure-ground cues emerge in Vision Transformers and whether they can be studied using natural scene statistics and probing methods.
AI.method: Evaluate 25 ViTs (supervised and self-supervised) by fitting linear probes to intermediate patch representations to predict figure-ground assignment. Test on natural images and controlled artificial stimuli that isolate individual cues for surroundedness, convexity, and symmetry.
AI.result: ViTs robustly encode surroundedness and convexity. Probes trained on natural images generalize zero-shot to artificial stimuli across several models. Symmetry is encoded for uniformly colored regions but not for textured regions.
AI.conclusion: Gestalt-like figure-ground cues can be learned from natural scene statistics. Vision Transformers are a suitable model system for studying computational mechanisms of perceptual organization.

title: Director: Accelerating Distributed MoE Serving via Online Proactive Expert Placement
summary: Expert parallelism has become the prevailing paradigm to serve Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Its efficiency depends on the communication and computation latencies of the GPUs, which are linked to the placement of experts in the GPUs. Existing works for optimizing expert placement focus on leveraging past requests' expert activation patterns. However, they demonstrate deficiencies facing diverse and rapidly changing request patterns, calling for an online, proactive approach. Implementing such an approach requires addressing several challenges: the uncertainty associated with incoming requests' expert activation, the cost of expert migration, and the NP-hard complexity in optimization. Therefore, we present Director, a new distributed MoE serving system that minimizes end-to-end latency via prediction-driven, online expert placement. Director uses either a lightweight cascaded predictor or a low-bit quantized replica for expert activation patterns of incoming requests. An online migration module then enacts the changes with near-zero downtime by executing migrations in compute-bound phases, keeping disruption bounded. At its core, a relaxation-based expert placement optimizer operates under capacity constraints, runs in polynomial time, and achieves a $(1+ε)$ approximation ratio. Finally, we implement a prototype and demonstrate, through extensive experiments, a reduction in end-to-end latency of $11\sim55\%$ for popular MoE models (e.g., Mistral, DeepSeek and Qwen) compared to existing work.

AI.tldr: Director: a prediction-driven online expert placement system for MoE models that minimizes end-to-end latency via light-weight predictions, online migrations, and a polynomial-time 1+ε optimizer; shows 11–55% latency reduction on Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen.
AI.motivation: MoE serving efficiency hinges on expert placement across GPUs; existing methods rely on historical activation patterns and fail under diverse/rapidly changing requests; need online proactive approach accounting for activation uncertainty, migration cost, and NP-hard optimization.
AI.method: Two prediction modules (lightweight cascaded predictor or low-bit quantized replica) for expert activation; online migration module executing migrations in compute-bound phases to bound downtime; a relaxation-based expert placement optimizer under capacity constraints with polynomial-time complexity and (1+ε) approximation; prototype implementation.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation shows end-to-end latency reductions of 11% to 55% on popular MoE models (Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) versus prior work.
AI.conclusion: Prediction-driven online expert placement is effective for reducing latency in distributed MoE serving, balancing activation uncertainty and migration costs; the approach is practical with provable approximation guarantees and real-world latency gains.

title: Neuro-Agentic Control: A Deep Learning-based LLM-Powered Agentic AI Framework for Controlling Security Controls
summary: Cyberattacks on operational technology are increasingly causing costly downtime and physical damage, exposing the limitations of traditional rule-based monitoring in industrial IoT environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have strong semantic reasoning abilities to assist in decision support, their hallucinatory nature presents unacceptable safety liabilities for closed-loop control. This paper introduces a neuro-agentic control framework, a novel architecture that couples an LLM-based planner (i.e., such as Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) with a pre-trained Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM), to achieve physics-grounded autonomous defense. The paper introduces a ``Counterfactual Physics Injection'' mechanism that simulates the impact of LLM-proposed interventions within the numerical latent space of the foundation model before actuation, while allowing the system to reject hallucinatory or unsafe actions. Evaluated on an industrial dataset (e.g., the Secure Water Treatment (SWaT)) in the context of stochastic attack scenarios, the framework exhibited better performance compared to LSTM and TCN baselines. The Neuro-Agentic Loop prevented five breaches (33.3%) below the threshold versus LSTM (26.7%) and TCN (13.3%), with zero physically invalid (hallucinated) actions executed. These results demonstrate the efficacy of using foundation models as deterministic ``Sentinels'' to safeguard agentic AI in critical infrastructure.

AI.tldr: A neuro-agentic control framework that combines an LLM-based planner with a Time-Series Foundation Model (TimesFM) and a Counterfactual Physics Injection mechanism to simulate and validate LLM interventions in latent space before actuation, enhancing safety in industrial OT without hallucinated actions.
AI.motivation: Address the safety risks of using LLMs for closed-loop control in industrial IoT, where hallucinations can cause unsafe actions and physical damage; leverage physics-grounded foundation models to serve as deterministic sentinels for autonomous defense.
AI.method: Architectural integration of an LLM-based planner (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) with a pre-trained TimesFM.
