- Visual-evidence rewards help only if verification is reliable: keyword checks increase hacking; VLM-as-judge semantic verification reduces hacking.
- Overall, reward hacking is a systematic consequence of optimizing imperfect rewards; robust alignment requires rewards and verifiers that remain reliable under optimization pressure.
AI.conclusion: Reward design and verification strategies must be jointly robust to optimization pressure in multimodal RL. Merely improving proxy rewards or scaling models is insufficient; rely on verifiers that maintain reliability as rewards are optimized, and consider algorithm-specific vulnerabilities to mitigate reward hacking.

title: DemoBridge: A Simulation-in-the-Loop Toolkit for Single-View Human Demonstration Retargeting
summary: We present DemoBridge, an toolkit that turns a single-view RGB stereo recording of a human hand demonstration into an executable, physics-validated robot-arm trajectory. Retargeting across the embodiment gap is hard. A robot arm reaches a target with a long, articulated body whose links carry far more collision volume than a hand. Solving inverse kinematics for the mapped end-effector pose often yields no collision-free solution, and a trajectory imposes this at every waypoint. A single view adds noise, leaving the demonstrated reference inaccurate. At the core of DemoBridge is a single collision-aware planner. It optimizes the whole joint trajectory at once, reasoning jointly over alternative grasp poses, whole-arm and grasped-object collision, and fidelity to the demonstrated path. A physics simulator runs in the loop. It validates each phase as it is produced and backtracks on failure, so a demonstration that cannot be reproduced as given is re-planned rather than discarded. The resulting action sequence is dynamically stable and faithful to the demonstrated manipulation. It also doubles as a ready-to-use simulation rollout for policy learning. Grasp timing is inferred automatically, and the perception backends, robot, and pipeline stages are swappable from configuration. We evaluate whole-pipeline retargeting on three real-demonstration tasks and the planner on a controlled synthetic benchmark. Our code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/u0123974/demo-bridge/ .

AI.tldr: A collision-aware, physics-validated retargeting pipeline (DemoBridge) converts single-view hand demonstrations into executable, faithful robot-arm trajectories via joint-trajectory optimization and looped physics validation.
AI.motivation: Transferring human hand manipulation to a robotic arm is challenged by embodiment gaps, noisy single-view observations, and collision constraints; a unified planner that optimizes the full trajectory with fidelity to the demonstration and checks via physics can improve reproducibility and policy-learning data.
AI.method: A single collision-aware planner optimizes the entire joint trajectory, jointly reasoning over alternative grasp poses, whole-arm and object collisions, and fidelity to the demonstrated path. A physics simulator runs in the loop to validate phases and backtrack on failure rather than discarding the demonstration. Grasp timing is inferred automatically. Perception backends, robot, and pipeline stages are swappable via configuration. Evaluated on three real-demonstration tasks and a controlled synthetic benchmark.
AI.result: The approach yields dynamically stable, faithful trajectories that can be executed by a robot arm and serve as ready-to-use simulation rollouts for policy learning. It re-plans on failure instead of discarding demonstrations, and code is released for reuse.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end retargeting with a unified, physics-validated planner is feasible and practical for converting hand demonstrations into executable robot trajectories. The looped validation improves reproducibility and enables policy learning; the pipeline remains modular and adaptable, though remaining challenges include single-view noise, computational cost, and generalization to more complex manipulation scenarios.

title: Subtoken Vision Transformer for Fine-grained Recognition
summary: We present Subtoken Vision Transformer (SubViT), a selective image tokenization method for fine-grained visual recognition. Standard Vision Transformers compress each fixed-size patch into a single token, although fine-grained distinctions often depend on localized variations within only a few patches. SubViT addresses this mismatch by representing discriminative patches with multiple subtokens while retaining the original token sequence for global context, thereby allocating additional capacity where it is most needed. Since attention heads encode complementary semantics and extracting attention maps at inference requires an extra backbone forward, we adopt a two-stage training strategy. Stage 1 fine-tunes the ViT using subdivision regions sampled from random attention heads, exposing the model to diverse subdivision patterns. Stage 2 identifies informative attention maps through feature-degradation distances and distills them into a lightweight single-map router, which directly predicts deterministic token-importance scores without a separate attention forward. We evaluate SubViT on Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), a challenging task requiring both fine-grained discrimination and generalization to unlabeled novel categories. Across CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, SubViT improves the average novel-category accuracy of DINOv2 from $81.3\%$ to $84.7\%$, with only $0.50$ ms additional latency and $3.4\%$ more FLOPs, while reducing latency by $73.8\%$ relative to Retina Patch. Results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 demonstrate its broader applicability.

AI.tldr: SubViT introduces selective tokenization for ViTs by using multiple subtokens for discriminative patches and a light router to assign token importance, achieving improved novel-category accuracy on GCD with small latency overhead and broader applicability.
AI.motivation: To address the mismatch between fixed patch tokens in ViTs and fine-grained discriminative cues that reside in localized regions; allocate extra representation capacity to a subset of patches while preserving global context.
AI.method: A two-stage training pipeline: Stage 1 fine-tunes ViT using subdivision regions sampled from random attention heads to expose diverse subdivision patterns; Stage 2 identifies informative attention maps via feature-degradation distances and distills them into a lightweight single-map router that directly predicts deterministic token-importance scores without requiring a separate attention forward.
AI.result: On Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), SubViT improves the average novel-category accuracy of DINOv2 from 81.3% to 84.7% across CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars, with only 0.50 ms additional latency and 3.4% more FLOPs, and reduces latency by 73.8% relative to Retina Patch. Additional results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 demonstrate broader applicability.
AI.conclusion: SubViT effectively reallocates model capacity to discriminative patches via selective tokenization and an efficient routing mechanism, delivering accuracy gains with modest computational overhead and showing generalization to broader fine-grained recognition tasks.

title: Training, Reading, and Editing Legible Transformers
summary: A transformer can be built from operators that are legible by construction -- bounded, named units that read as fuzzy set operations rather than dense activations -- but legibility must be pressed for during training, and the pressure has a failure mode. A crispness penalty meant to sharpen a bounded operator into a decisive detector instead collapses it into a dead constant. An identity, E[v(1-v)] = mu(1-mu) - var, shows why -- the penalty is a variance-minimizer blind to the difference between a live detector and a constant -- and names the fix: a per-channel variance floor, the target legibility metric written as a loss, which recovers both legibility and quality. A learned per-unit fraction then retires the hand-set reserved-GELU partition of prior work: given the choice the model keeps no unit as pure GELU and routes 87% of its load-bearing computation through crisp operators. The result is the most legible transformer we have built -- 78% of its feed-forward operands and 50% of its attention value channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors, and per-head legibility rises from 18% in shallow layers to 78% in deep ones. Read in the correct rotated per-layer frame, these units separate a clean detection (what a unit responds to) from a harder naming (what its output decodes to); and because the objective makes each unit crisp and sparse, edits to them are far more local -- 50-184x in the deep layers where the edit sites concentrate -- and can target explicit conjunctions a single neuron cannot express. Finally, a between-unit decorrelation pressure exposes a legibility dial: it trades a circuit's reuse for independence at no quality cost, turning concepts into single, surgically editable units and a prediction into a short explanation read off a handful of named operations. Quality holds at parity with a conventional baseline throughout.

AI.tldr: Proposes a legible transformer built from bounded, named operators; introduces a per-channel variance floor loss to preserve legibility; learns per-unit fraction to retire fixed GELU partitions; achieves high legibility and editability with maintained accuracy; decorrelation pressure yields independent, surgically editable units.
AI.motivation: Enhance interpretability and editability of transformers by using legible, bounded operators and minimizing reliance on opaque dense activations; fix a failure mode of crispness penalties that collapse operators to dead constants.
AI.method: Introduce a per-channel variance floor as a loss term to enforce legibility without collapsing to constants; learn per-unit fractions to determine the mix between crisp operators and GELU-like behavior, replacing hand-crafted partitions; route most computation through crisp operators; apply a per-layer rotated frame to separate what a unit detects from how it is named; apply a decorrelation pressure to promote independence among units; evaluate legibility metrics (percent of feed-forward operands and attention channels that are crisp) and edit locality.
AI.result: The model achieves high legibility: about 78% of feed-forward operands and 50% of attention value channels are crisp-and-contextual detectors; per-head legibility grows from 18% in shallow layers to 78% in deep ones; 87% of load-bearing computation routed through crisp operators; edits are 50–184x more local in deep layers; quality parity with a conventional baseline maintained.
AI.conclusion: A legible transformer can be built and edited more easily without sacrificing accuracy by enforcing a per-channel variance floor and learned per-unit gating, leading to highly interpretable, sparse units and modular explanations via named operations.

title: Shared Selective Persistent Memory for Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Agentic LLM systems that generate code through multi-turn tool use face a fundamental context problem: each session starts from zero, discarding the configuration choices, domain constraints, data schemas, and tool-use patterns that made previous sessions productive. Naively persisting entire conversation histories is token-inefficient and counterproductive: irrelevant context degrades generation quality. We introduce shared selective persistent memory, an architecture that identifies and retains four categories of reusable context (task specifications, data schemas, tool configurations, and output constraints) while discarding session-specific reasoning traces. Crucially, this memory is shared: workspaces encapsulating selective memory can be transferred across users with role-based access control, enabling collaborative reuse without redundant specification. We implement it in a deployed collaborative workspace platform where LLM agents produce, edit, and maintain git-versioned artifacts (dashboards, reports, and data-driven documents) from heterogeneous sources (CSV, SQL, REST APIs, and MCP servers). A complementary zero-token data refresh mechanism decouples generated programs from runtime data, enabling artifact reuse without re-invocation. Across three enterprise scenarios, shared selective persistent memory achieves 96% task completion (vs. 79% without memory and 71% with full history). Zero-token refresh eliminates LLM re-invocation for recurring updates (14x task-time reduction), while summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data injection. A replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability, with zero-token refresh succeeding in 12/12 trials. Notably, naive full-history persistence actively degrades completion by biasing the agent with stale traces, while selective memory outperforms both extremes.

AI.tldr: A shared selective persistent memory architecture preserves reusable context across LLM sessions, enabling collaborative reuse and data-schema/tool-config retention, with zero-token data refresh; it improves task completion and efficiency across enterprise scenarios and public datasets.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLMs that code through multi-turn tool use lose productive context when sessions reset. Persisting full histories is token-inefficient and can bias with stale traces. There is a need to retain four reusable context categories (task specs, data schemas, tool configs, output constraints) while discarding reasoning traces, and to share this memory across users via role-based access control to enable collaboration.
AI.method: Introduce shared selective persistent memory that stores four reusable context categories and discards session-specific traces. Implement in a deployed collaborative workspace platform where LLM agents generate and maintain git-versioned artifacts from heterogeneous sources. Include a zero-token data refresh mechanism that decouples generated programs from runtime data, enabling reuse without re-invocation. Use workspaces with RBAC and test across three enterprise scenarios and replication on public datasets.
AI.result: Shared memory yields 96% task completion vs 79% without memory and 71% with full history. Zero-token refresh reduces task time by 14x. Summary-driven generation cuts per-invocation token cost by 97x versus raw data. Replication on four public datasets confirms generalizability; zero-token refresh succeeds in 12/12 trials. Naive full-history persistence degrades completion due to stale traces; selective memory outperforms both extremes.
AI.conclusion: Selective, shared persistent memory effectively preserves reusable context, enabling collaborative reuse and significant efficiency gains. It outperforms full-history persistence and memoryless baselines, and generalizes across datasets; a zero-token refresh and summary-driven generation further enhance performance and cost efficiency.

title: How Mobile Gas Sensor Trajectories Govern Hydrogen Leak Detection: A Safety Gap in Manual Leak Inspection of Hydrogen System Components
summary: The integrity of hydrogen infrastructure relies on reliable leak detection, performed almost exclusively via manual tracer gas sniffing in electrolyzer manufacturing. Although mandated by standards, the lack of spatial probe guidance instructions leaves detection reliability entirely to operator execution, further compromised by sensor signal delays. This study quantifies how sniffer trajectory kinematics affect detection reliability at small-scale pipes and fittings, a near-field regime largely neglected by macroscopic dispersion research. Using a robotically guided test bench to eliminate operator variability, static concentration fields and dynamic trajectory passes were acquired across representative geometries under standardized leak rates (5 vol% hydrogen in nitrogen) and varying scanning velocities. Results demonstrate that scanning velocity and spatial probe orientation strongly dictate detectability. Conventional linear trajectories frequently miss leaks under dynamic conditions, causing severe false negatives. Conversely, geometry-specific routing, such as circumferential plunging paths around sealing points, maintains a high safety margin. From these observations, geometry-specific routing rules and a reduction-factor model for dynamic signal loss are derived. The findings reveal that current standard operating procedures pose a tangible safety risk. To operationalize these rules, a proof-of-concept software pipeline is presented, generating validated trajectories directly from 3D models for visualization in assistance systems.

AI.tldr: Robotically guided sniffing study shows trajectory geometry and speed critically affect hydrogen leak detectability in near-field piping; conventional linear scans under dynamic conditions miss leaks; geometry-specific routes and a reduction-factor model improve reliability; a software pipeline converts 3D models into validated sniffing trajectories.
AI.motivation: Leak detection in electrolyzer hydrogen infrastructure relies on manual tracer gas sniffing; lack of spatial guidance leads to operator-dependent reliability and safety issues due to sensor delays; there is a need for geometry-aware sniffing strategies in small-scale geometries.
AI.method: A robotically guided test bench eliminates operator variability. The study collects static concentration fields and dynamic trajectory passes across representative geometries under standardized leak rates (5 vol% H2 in N2) and varying scanning velocities. It derives geometry-specific routing rules and a dynamic signal-loss reduction-factor model, and presents a proof-of-concept software pipeline that generates validated trajectories from 3D models for visualization in assistance systems.
AI.result: Scanning velocity and spatial probe orientation strongly affect detectability. Conventional linear trajectories frequently miss leaks under dynamic conditions. Geometry-specificRouting (e.g., circumferential plunging paths around sealing points) maintains higher safety margins. Derived routing rules and a reduction-factor model quantify dynamic signal loss.
AI.conclusion: Current standard operating procedures pose a tangible safety risk. Geometry-aware sniffing routes and a reduction-factor model are proposed to improve reliability; a proof-of-concept software pipeline demonstrates generation of validated trajectories from 3D models for deployment in assistance systems.

title: DETRAM: End-to-end DEtection, Tracking and Recovery of HumAn Meshes
summary: In the task of human mesh recovery (HMR), multi-person scenes are particularly difficult to handle due to the many entities that appear and occlusions between them over time. In particular for video inputs, there is a need to track each entity reliably and consistently. Existing methods rely on pretrained human detection modules, increasing their runtime and limiting the number of tracked entities. We present DETRAM, a unified framework for multi-person HMR and tracking that simultaneously detects, reconstructs, and tracks humans across time, both automatically and via user prompts. DETRAM uses a single transformer decoder with an identity-consistent set of learnable query embeddings that persist across frames: detection queries discover new people, tracking queries maintain pose and shape for existing individuals, and prompt queries follow user-specified identities. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art tracking results on PoseTrack21, 3DPW, BEDLAM, and MuPoTS-3D, and competitive reconstruction accuracy on BEDLAM and 3DPW, while uniquely supporting prompt-based tracking of individuals in multi-person scenes. To our knowledge, this is the first method to unify promptability and multi-person HMR with tracking in an end-to-end trainable framework, enabling user-directed human analysis in videos.

AI.tldr: DETRAM unifies detection, reconstruction, and tracking of multiple humans in video using a single transformer decoder with persistent query embeddings; supports prompt-based tracking and achieves SOTA on several datasets.
AI.motivation: Reduce runtime and dependence on pretrained detectors in multi-person HMR/tracking, enabling end-to-end analysis and user-directed prompts across video sequences.
AI.method: Single transformer decoder with three types of learnable queries—detection queries for new people, tracking queries for existing individuals, and prompt queries for user-specified identities—plus identity-consistent embeddings that persist across frames, enabling automatic and prompt-guided tracking.
AI.result: State-of-the-art tracking on PoseTrack21, 3DPW, BEDLAM, and MuPoTS-3D; competitive reconstruction accuracy on BEDLAM and 3DPW; uniquely supports prompt-based tracking in multi-person scenes in an end-to-end trainable framework.
AI.conclusion: First method to unify promptability, multi-person HMR, and tracking in an end-to-end trainable framework, enabling user-directed human analysis in videos.

title: FairSelect: A Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Level and Intersectional Algorithmic Fairness
comment: 15 pages, 5 tables, Submission to Health Informatics Knowledge Management Conference 2026
summary: Algorithmic fairness methods are increasingly used to identify and mitigate bias in machine learning models, yet most approaches are evaluated in isolation and along single demographic axes. This limits practical guidance for selecting fairness strategies, where disparities may arise across intersectional subgroups and across multiple stages of the modeling lifecycle. This work presents FairSelect, a toolkit for systematically evaluating fairness mitigation strategies applied individually and in combination across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages. FairSelect supports multiple model architectures, intersectional subgroup evaluation, and comparison of fairness utility tradeoffs across baseline, single method, and multi level configurations. The framework was validated using synthetic clinical datasets designed to represent specific bias mechanisms and a real-world replication of two-year stroke risk prediction among patients with atrial fibrillation. Synthetic experiments showed that targeted fairness methods generally reduced intended subgroup disparities, while combined strategies produced larger average fairness improvements with modest utility tradeoffs. In the clinical prediction task, mitigation effects were highly variable, with some combinations improving both fairness and predictive performance while others were ineffective or counterproductive. These findings demonstrate that fairness interventions interact in nonadditive and context dependent ways. FairSelect provides a practical framework for systematically identifying fairness strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical machine learning.

AI.tldr: FairSelect is a toolkit to systematically evaluate fairness mitigation strategies across preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing, including intersectional subgroups; validated on synthetic clinical data and real-world stroke risk data; reveals nonadditive interactions and context-dependent effects; helps identify strategies that improve equity with minimal loss of model performance.
AI.motivation: There is a need for comprehensive, cross-stage, and intersectional evaluation of fairness interventions. Most work tests methods in isolation and across a single demographic axis, limiting guidance for real-world deployment where multiple biases interact.
AI.method: Introduce FairSelect, a modular framework supporting various model architectures and enabling evaluation of fairness mitigation strategies applied at preprocessing, inprocessing, and postprocessing stages. It compares baseline, single-method, and multi-level configurations across intersectional subgroups. Validates using synthetic datasets designed to instantiate bias mechanisms and a real-world two-year stroke risk prediction dataset in atrial fibrillation.
AI.result: Targeted fairness methods generally reduce disparities for targeted subgroups; multi-method configurations yield larger average fairness gains with modest utility tradeoffs. In the clinical task, mitigation effects are highly variable: some combinations improve both fairness and predictive performance, others are ineffective or counterproductive, indicating nonadditive, context-dependent interactions.
AI.conclusion: FairSelect provides a practical framework for identifying fairness strategies that improve subgroup equity while preserving model performance in clinical ML, highlighting the nonadditive interaction of interventions and the importance of cross-stage evaluation.

title: SAGEAgent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Cost-Aware Modality Acquisition in Multimodal Survival Prediction
summary: Does every cancer patient truly need a complete diagnostic workup for accurate survival prediction? In multimodal clinical oncology, diagnostic modalities follow a clinically mandated order of escalating burden -- from demographics collected at intake to genomic profiling requiring specialized tissue analysis. Current multimodal survival methods either assume all modalities are available or passively handle missing data, but none actively reason about whether acquiring the next modality is justified for a given patient along this ordered workflow. We formulate this as a sequential decision problem and propose SAGEAgent (Sequential Acquisition Guided by Experience), a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that decides which diagnostic modalities to acquire for each patient, balancing predictive accuracy against clinical invasiveness. SAGEAgent reasons about each patient's evolving diagnostic state through clinical tools that translate numerical predictions into text, an episodic memory that retrieves similar past cases, and a semantic memory that accumulates reusable decision patterns from experience. Experiments on a glioma cohort combining TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, and BraTS with four diagnostic modalities demonstrate that SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average acquisition burden by 55%.

AI.tldr: A sequential acquisition framework (SAGEAgent) enables an LLM-based clinical agent to decide which diagnostic modalities to obtain for each patient, balancing accuracy and invasiveness, and reducing diagnostic burden by 55% while preserving survival prediction performance.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal oncology workflows burden patients with sequentially escalating diagnostics and treat missing modalities inadequately. There is a need for active, cost-conscious decision-making that determines whether acquiring the next modality is warranted.
AI.method: Formulates diagnostic acquisition as a sequential decision problem and introduces SAGEAgent, a self-evolving LLM-based clinical agent that (1) translates numerical predictions into text via clinical tools, (2) uses episodic memory to retrieve similar past cases, and (3) employs semantic memory to accumulate reusable decision patterns. Evaluated on a glioma cohort (TCGA-LGG, TCGA-GBM, BraTS) with four modalities.
AI.result: SAGEAgent achieves competitive survival prediction accuracy while reducing average modality acquisition burden by 55%.
AI.conclusion: Active, experience-guided acquisition can match predictive performance while substantially lowering diagnostic burden in multimodal oncology; memory components enable reuse and adaptation across patients.

title: Task-Adaptive Design of Modular Aerial Manipulators Under Airflow Exposure Constraints
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: Aerial manipulation with multirotor platforms enables physical interaction in complex environments, but rotor-induced airflow remains a critical limitation for tasks involving airflow-sensitive targets or surroundings. This paper presents an optimization-based design framework for modular aerial manipulators that jointly considers task wrench feasibility, end-effector placement, and airflow exposure constraints. We first introduce a novel categorization of target-side airflow tolerance and formulate the corresponding exposure requirements as geometric constraints. To efficiently model rotor-induced airflow, we introduce a compact cone-sphere envelope that approximates the spreading structure of a quadrotor's airflow while preserving computational tractability for optimization. Building on this formulation, we propose a reconfiguration optimization that adapts a modular aerial manipulator to diverse task wrench requirements while enforcing both target-side airflow exposure and intra-platform airflow interference constraints. Unlike prior designs that assume a fixed end-effector location, the proposed framework optimizes the end-effector placement together with the platform configuration. Scalability experiments and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: An optimization-based framework for modular aerial manipulators that jointly optimizes end-effector placement and platform configuration while enforcing rotor-induced airflow exposure constraints via a cone-sphere envelope, enabling task wrench feasibility across diverse targets and validating with scalability and ablation studies.
AI.motivation: Rotor-induced airflow from multirotor platforms imposes constraints on interaction with airflow-sensitive tasks and surroundings. There is a need for a configurable, end-effector–aware design that jointly accounts for wrench feasibility, placement, and airflow exposure.
AI.method: Categorize target-side airflow tolerance; formulate geometric exposure constraints; introduce a cone-sphere envelope to approximate rotor airflow; develop a reconfiguration optimization that enforces airflow exposure, intra-platform airflow interference, and joint end-effector placement with platform configuration.
AI.result: The approach enables adaptable modular configurations that satisfy airflow exposure and wrench requirements, with validation via scalability experiments and ablation studies showing effectiveness and component contributions.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of end-effector placement and platform configuration under airflow constraints is feasible and beneficial for modular aerial manipulators, outperforming fixed-location designs.

title: Beyond Time Shifts: Adapting Omni-LLM as a Reference-Free Evaluator for Generative Audio-Visual Models
summary: As audio-visual generative models evolve into world simulators, cross-modal synchronization stands as a critical proxy for assessing the consistency of world dynamics and causality in generated content. However, existing evaluation metrics presume structural correctness, reducing synchronization to mere temporal alignment. Consequently, they fail on generative outputs, especially when exhibiting structural hallucinations and asymmetric cross-modal relations, which currently \textbf{mandate expert human annotation to assess synchronization.} This dependency introduces a critical paradox: \emph{human evaluators rely on relative, reference-dependent comparisons, whereas automated metrics require reference-free, absolute scalars.} We resolve this paradox by proposing a framework that distills relative human perception into a continuous, globally consistent metric. First, we introduce SynthSync, a dataset of generative failures ranked via pairwise human annotations. Second, we adapt the Omni-LLM equipped with a continuous latent projection to translate relative human rankings into continuous absolute values. Third, we propose Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization ($\mathbb{R}$-GRPO) to internalize the global causal structure of synchronization via listwise score distributions. Empirically, our metric achieves state-of-the-art human preference alignment. We leverage this estimator to establish a standardized benchmark, advancing AV-Gen assessment from low-level signal correlation to visually grounded causality.

AI.tldr: Proposes SynthSync, Omni-LLM-based latent mapping, and Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO) to create a continuous, globally consistent metric for audio-visual synchronization, aligning with human judgments and enabling a reference-free AV-Gen benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current metrics assume structural correctness and rely on temporal alignment, failing on outputs with structural hallucinations or asymmetric cross-modal relations. They require expert human annotation, creating a paradox between relative human judgments and absolute, reference-free metrics. A global, continuous metric would fuse human perception with automated evaluation for AV-Gen synchronization.
AI.method: (1) Build SynthSync, a dataset of generative failures ranked via pairwise human annotations. (2) Use Omni-LLM with a continuous latent projection to convert relative human rankings into continuous absolute scores. (3) Introduce Real-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO) to model global synchronization causality through listwise score distributions.
AI.result: Empirically achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human preferences; provides a standardized benchmark, shifting AV-Gen assessment from low-level signal correlation to visually grounded causality.
AI.conclusion: A framework for a globally consistent, reference-free metric of cross-modal synchronization that harnesses human perception and an automated latent mapping, enabling robust AV-Gen evaluation and benchmarking.

title: Eluna: An Agentic LLM System for Automating Warehouse Operations with Reasoning and Task Execution
summary: Warehouse operations are governed by Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that encode complex, multi-system decision logic, which must be executed reliably under strict time constraints, yet LLM agents lack mechanisms to enforce procedural compliance and degrade under the context overload full SOP specifications introduce. We present Eluna, a production-deployed agentic system for reliable SOP execution. Eluna is a graph-guided, multi-agent framework that encodes SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure and delegates independent tasks to parallel sub-agents, each with persistent code execution and live data access. To meet production latency and accuracy needs, we use asymmetric episodic distillation where a strong teacher is improved through episodic error memories, then a smaller student is fine-tuned on the corrected trajectories with memory stripped, internalizing corrections without inference-time overhead. On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, our fine-tuned models match or exceed their teacher, beat all larger off-the-shelf baselines, and reach 94% expert agreement on the ticket processing application.

AI.tldr: Eluna presents a production-grade graph-guided multi-agent system for reliable SOP execution, encoding SOPs as DAGs, enabling parallel sub-agents with persistent execution and live data, augmented by asymmetric episodic distillation to meet latency/accuracy constraints; on a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, it matches or surpasses the teacher and beats larger baselines, achieving 94% expert agreement on ticket processing.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to enforce procedural compliance and degrade under context overload when processing full SOPs under production latency; there is a need for reliable, scalable SOP execution.
AI.method: Encode SOPs as directed acyclic graphs with progressive disclosure; delegate tasks to parallel sub-agents; maintain persistent code execution and live data access; employ asymmetric episodic distillation: a strong teacher is improved via episodic error memories, while a smaller student is fine-tuned on corrected trajectories with memory stripped to internalize corrections without inference-time overhead.
AI.result: On a 13-task benchmark and two production applications, fine-tuned models match or exceed the teacher; beat larger off-the-shelf baselines.
AI.conclusion: The approach delivers production-reliable SOP execution with reduced latency and overhead, demonstrating a scalable graph-guided multi-agent architecture and memory-efficient distillation for SOP-driven operations.

title: Beyond Fixed Representations: The Vocabulary and Verifier Gaps in Open-Ended AI
summary:
Modern AI systems are increasingly being evaluated for their ability to reason, code, prove theorems, use tools, and long-horizon research tasks. These are powerful capabilities, but they share a structural limitation: the representational frame within which the model operates, including its conceptual vocabulary, the space of admissible solutions it can search, and the criteria by which success is evaluated, is typically fixed and supplied in advance. This paper argues that building stronger intelligent systems capable of open-ended innovation requires additional classes of operations: the creation, stabilization, and reuse of new representational primitives, which alter the space being searched rather than simply searching within it.
  We characterize the distance between current AI systems and genuinely open-ended intelligence through two gaps. The first is the vocabulary gap, the difficulty of inventing and stabilizing new representational primitives rather than merely recombining existing ones. The second is the verifier gap, the difficulty of judging the value of a new primitive when its full payoff may be visible only after future reuse. We interpret both gaps through a unified framework of intelligence as cognitive discrepancy reduction. By viewing intelligent behaviors as a sequence of cognitive transformations, we distinguish intra-space transformations which operate within a fixed representational frame, from generative transformations which may modify the frame itself. On this basis, we propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and outline several directions for advancing open-ended AI, including objectives that reward useful representational change, persistent memory architectures for invented primitives, and adaptive verification mechanisms capable of evolving alongside the representations they evaluate.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework and research agenda for open-ended AI by enabling creation and stabilization of new representational primitives, addressing vocabulary and verifier gaps.
AI.motivation: Current AI systems search within fixed representations; open-ended intelligence requires altering representations themselves, not just using them.
AI.method: Introduce a unified framework of cognitive discrepancy reduction, distinguishing intra-space (within-frame) vs. generative transformations (frame-changing); identify two gaps (vocabulary and verifier); propose a ladder of innovation autonomy and directions for advancing open-ended AI.
AI.result: Conceptual blueprint with actionable directions: reward representational change, persistent memory for invented primitives, and adaptive verification that co-evolves with representations.
AI.conclusion: Open-ended AI hinges on agents capable of inventing and stabilizing new primitives; progress requires architectures that support representational change and verification mechanisms that adapt alongside those representations.

title: CORAL-AUV: CFD Oriented Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles
summary: Fine grain control and positioning of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) is critical for sampling, maintenance, and survey applications. Traditional control methods for AUVs are labor intensive and are not robust to changes in the vehicle configuration or environmental conditions. Reinforcement learning (RL) promises rapid controller development while handling a range of deployment parameters via domain randomization (DR). However, DR is still limited by the capacity of the underlying simulation to model real physics. In particular, drag physics are difficult to model and are a large contributor to sim-to-real gaps. Meanwhile, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) provides high fidelity drag models but is challenging to leverage within reinforcement learning frameworks due to its computational overhead. Thus, in this paper we exploit the idea of training surrogate approximations of CFD models of a given vehicle, enabling fast inference within RL pipelines. We are the first to successfully deploy a zero-shot RL policy on a 6-DOF AUV in which policy training is performed on surrogate drag models (SDMs) trained on CFD data. We find 31% lower energy usage compared to a controller using simplified physics while traversing between waypoints 11% faster with 19% less error. Our SDM based RL controller better predicts zero-shot transfer and is more robust across reward shaping design choices. When using DR to complete a task with perturbed parameters, we find that the CFD policy is the only controller that successfully transfers. The policies are evaluated in a controlled tank environment and in the field providing extensive testing of the policies' capabilities.

AI.tldr: Surrogate CFD-based drag models for RL-controlled 6-DOF AUVs enable zero-shot transfer with improved efficiency and robustness over simplified-physics baselines.
AI.motivation: Address the sim-to-real gap in RL for AUV control by replacing crude drag models with CFD-informed surrogate models that enable fast yet accurate drag predictions during policy training.
AI.method: Train surrogate drag models (SDMs) on CFD data to emulate high-fidelity drag for a 6-DOF AUV. Use these SDMs within a reinforcement learning pipeline with domain randomization to train policies in simulation, then deploy zero-shot to real AUVs without further training. Compare to baselines using simplified physics under various reward shapes and with parameter perturbations. Validate in tank and field tests.
AI.result: SDM-based RL achieved 31% lower energy usage, 11% faster traversal, and 19% reduced waypoint error compared to simplified-physics controller. The CFD-informed policy showed better zero-shot transfer and robustness to reward shaping. Under DR with perturbed parameters, the CFD policy was the only one to transfer successfully.
AI.conclusion: CFD-informed surrogate drag models enable effective zero-shot RL for 6-DOF AUVs, reducing energy, time, and error while improving transfer robustness; SDMs allow leveraging CFD fidelity with RL without prohibitive compute, and improve generalization in varied deployment conditions.

title: A Coreset Selection Framework with Ensemble Aggregation for Image Classification
summary: The rapid growth of image data has produced large-scale datasets, raising concerns about the time and memory costs of model training. Selecting representative training subsets, however, remains challenging: individual sample contributions are unclear, and model behavior varies across datasets and runs. We address these challenges with a framework that combines coreset selection with an ensemble aggregation over multiple runs. For coreset selection, we propose SCOre-Stratified Selection (SCOSS), which partitions the training data into intervals based on a chosen score and samples from each interval. The ensemble combines predictions from multiple runs, each performed on an independently sampled training subset. As baselines, we use moderate and random selection, each in original and class-balanced versions. We assess the framework with Simple Graph Convolution (SGC) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers under different sampling ratios. Experiments show that SCOSS is competitive with baselines, often the best choice for SGC, and enables favorable trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. On the fine-grained dataset, SGC with SCOSS outperforms SVMs when using fewer labeled samples. The code and supplementary materials are publicly available at http://scoss.lucasvalem.com.

AI.tldr: SCOSS introduces coreset stratified selection for efficient training by partitioning data into score-based intervals and sampling from each, combined with an ensemble of multiple runs. It yields competitive accuracy with favorable efficiency trade-offs, especially for SGC, and can outperform SVM with fewer labels on a fine-grained dataset; code is provided.
AI.motivation: Large-scale image datasets incur high time and memory costs in model training. Subset selection remains difficult due to unclear per-sample contributions and sample- and run-variance across datasets. A robust, scalable subset selection method is needed to balance accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: SCOSS partitions training data into intervals based on a chosen score, then samples from each interval to form a coreset. An ensemble aggregates predictions from multiple runs, each trained on independently sampled subsets. Baselines include moderate and random selection, in original and class-balanced forms.
AI.result: SCOSS is competitive with baselines and often best for Simple Graph Convolution (SGC); it enables favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. On a fine-grained dataset, SGC+SCOSS outperforms SVMs when labeled samples are limited. Public code and supplementary materials are provided at the stated URL.
AI.conclusion: Coreset stratified selection with an ensemble can achieve strong accuracy with reduced labeling and training costs, showing robustness across models and datasets and offering practical guidance for data-efficient learning.

title: NL-PAC: Specification Ambiguity and Certified Minimax Risk Floors in LLM-Mediated Supervision
summary: Large language models increasingly provide labels, evaluations, and feedback for tasks specified in natural language. When a specification admits multiple readings but the supervision channel does not reveal which is operative, additional labels reduce sampling error without resolving the resulting identification problem. We introduce Natural Language PAC (NL-PAC), a framework that uses a fixed model's thresholded decoding law to define admissible labels and candidate targets. The probability that multiple labels are admissible equals the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class, and under target-blind supervision every learner incurs worst-case risk of at least half this diameter, at every sample size; the exact randomized minimax risk over this class is attained by a data-independent strategy. Finite-sample confidence bounds make these quantities certifiable from held-out unlabeled inputs. In a frozen Qwen~2.5--3B audit, one prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate, whereas a paraphrase and exact-rule controls yield zero. A held-out bridge audit finds that supplied candidate reading clauses fail the admissibility condition needed to transfer the certificate to coherent readings. The guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution; extending it to human interpretations requires external validation.

AI.tldr: NL-PAC provides a minimax framework for learning with multiple admissible readings from fixed LLM decoding, yielding guarantees under target-blind supervision and model/prompt-dependent certificates.
AI.motivation: When supervision cannot reveal the operative readings of a natural-language specification, labels reduce sampling error but cannot resolve identification; a rigorous framework is needed to quantify risk and certifiability.
AI.method: Define admissible labels via a fixed model's thresholded decoding; quantify the diameter of the pointwise-admissible target class; show that under target-blind supervision every learner incurs worst-case risk at least half this diameter; provide the exact randomized minimax strategy that attains the bound; derive finite-sample confidence bounds to certify quantities from held-out unlabeled inputs.
AI.result: The bound: worst-case risk ≥ half the diameter at every sample size; the minimax strategy is data-independent; finite-sample bounds enable certifiability; in a frozen Qwen 2.5-3B audit, a prespecified prompt yields a positive model-relative certificate while paraphrase controls yield zero; a held-out bridge audit shows supplied candidate clauses fail the admissibility condition; the guarantee is specific to the audited model, prompt, threshold, and input distribution.
AI.conclusion: The guarantee is model/prompt/input specific; extending it to human interpretations requires external validation.

title: Knowledge Graphs and Explainable AI as Complementary Resources for Urban Mining
comment: Accepted for presentation at the AISE Workshop @ IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Pre-demolition assessment, the regulated audit process at the heart of urban mining, is an information process in which AI support must serve qualified auditors who remain accountable for the decisions taken. The relevant unit of value is not prediction accuracy alone, but the defensibility of the supported decisions: their legibility, plausibility, sourcing, and contestability. Explainable AI techniques and domain knowledge graphs each address parts of this requirement, and existing taxonomies have catalogued their integration. The literature is descriptively rich but structurally under-specified: what remains less developed is a structural account of why specific integrations produce artefacts neither resource can provide alone. This paper offers a complementarity-theoretic interpretation grounded in the IS resource-based tradition. We propose four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, and Revising), each defined as a typed operation over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrate structures. Each mode unlocks a distinct property of defensibility and contributes to the kind of regulatory artefact pre-demolition assessment demands. A fire-door example from the urban-mining process illustrates the modes using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.

AI.tldr: Proposes four KG-XAI integration modes (Lifting, Constraining, Typing, Revising) within an IS resource-based framework to improve defensibility in pre-demolition assessments; illustrated with a fire-door example using W3C Linked Building Data.
AI.motivation: Defensible decisions in urban mining require legibility, sourcing, and contestability; existing taxonomies are descriptively rich but structurally under-specified; a complementarity-theoretic account grounded in the IS resource-based view is needed.
AI.method: Define four consolidated KG-XAI integration modes as typed operations over XAI artefacts and knowledge-graph substrates; grounded in the IS resource-based tradition; illustrated by a fire-door process using the W3C Linked Building Data stack and valuation extensions.
AI.result: Each mode unlocks a distinct defensibility property and contributes to the regulatory artefacts demanded by pre-demolition assessment; clarifies how KG and XAI artefacts complement each other and provides a structured integration framework.
AI.conclusion: The four-mode KG-XAI integration framework offers a principled, structural account for designing defensible, auditable regulatory artefacts in urban mining, demonstrated through a concrete example.

title: CoDiMAD: Diffusion-Based Privileged Distillation for Communication-Free Multi-Robot Coordination
summary: Decentralized multi-robot coordination under partial observability remains challenging, especially in communication-free settings where agents must act solely from local sensor observations. Privileged policy distillation provides a promising approach by transferring knowledge from a globally informed oracle to sensor-constrained students. However, in multi-agent systems, the same local observation may correspond to multiple global configurations requiring qualitatively different cooperative actions, making the conditional action distribution inherently multi-modal. Standard deterministic distillation collapses these modes to their mean, often yielding invalid or hesitant actions. To address this issue, we propose CoDiMAD, a three-stage framework that trains a privileged oracle with MAPPO, constructs an offline dataset of local-observation-oracle-action pairs, and distills the oracle into decentralized students parameterized as conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models. By approximating the conditional oracle-action distribution through the diffusion reverse process, CoDiMAD samples decisive actions from coherent coordination modes rather than averaging across them. Theoretical analysis characterizes the mode-averaging failure of deterministic distillation and the distributional recovery property of diffusion-based distillation. Experiments on three cooperative tasks show that CoDiMAD consistently outperforms direct local MARL and deterministic distillation baselines. The source code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: CoDiMAD uses diffusion-based distillation to handle multi-modal, locally-observed actions in decentralized MARL by preserving coordination modes rather than averaging, outperforming deterministic distillation and direct local MARL in three cooperative tasks.
AI.motivation: Tackle mode-averaging failure in privileged policy distillation under partial observability, where the same local observation can map to multiple global configurations requiring different cooperative actions.
AI.method: Three-stage pipeline: 1) train a privileged global oracle with MAPPO; 2) build an offline dataset of local-observation, oracle-action pairs; 3) distill into decentralized students parameterized as conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic models, using the diffusion reverse process to sample actions from coherent coordination modes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on three cooperative tasks show CoDiMAD consistently outperforms direct local MARL and deterministic distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: Distributional distillation via diffusion recovers multi-modal action distributions and yields decisive coordination actions; code will be released publicly after acceptance.

title: Equivariant Filter for High Performance Image Tracking using an Event Camera
summary: Image tracking is the problem of estimating the transformation that relates a moving image of a scene to an original reference image. The problem is important in control of autonomous vehicles or robots, where the image encodes information about the motion of the camera or environment, as well as in pure computer vision applications. In this paper, we present an equivariant filter design for high performance tracking of planar image transformations using an event camera. The design exploits the Asynchronous Event Blob (AEB) tracker (Wang et al., 2024) to extract feature-position measurements from the raw event stream, and an equivariant filter to compute an affine image translation and rotation using the special Euclidean group symmetry. The equivariant filter incorporates an equivalent-measurement update step that de-correlates the (highly temporally correlated) feature-position measurements provided by the AEB tracker. We evaluate the design experimentally using two datasets involving general and fast rotational motion. We benchmark results against direct optimisation (estimating the relative transformation from the raw blob tracks), and a covariance intersection approach for overcoming data correlation. Our design provides smooth image tracking for features moving up to 7000 pixels per second on the image plane.

AI.tldr: Introduces an SE(2) equivariant filter for affine image tracking with event cameras, integrating AEB-derived feature measurements and an equivalent-measurement update to decorrelate temporally correlated data; achieves smooth, high-speed tracking and outperforms direct optimization and covariance-intersection baselines on two datasets.
AI.motivation: Need for accurate, high-temporal-resolution tracking of planar image transformations from event-camera data in autonomous robotics, where rapidly changing scenes and correlated measurements challenge traditional frame-based methods.
AI.method: Leverage the Asynchronous Event Blob (AEB) tracker to extract feature-position measurements from the raw event stream. Apply an SE(2) equivariant filter to estimate affine image translation and rotation, incorporating an equivalent-measurement update to decorrelate highly temporally correlated measurements. Compare against direct optimization from blob tracks and a covariance-intersection approach; evaluate on two datasets with general and fast rotational motion.
AI.result: Demonstrates smooth image tracking for features moving up to 7000 pixels per second on the image plane. Benchmark results show improved stability and tracking quality relative to the direct optimisation and covariance-intersection baselines on the tested datasets.
AI.conclusion: The work validates the combination of AEB-based measurements with SE(2) equivariant filtering as a viable approach for fast, robust event-based planar image tracking, with potential for real-time high-speed applications. Limitations and extensions (e.g., 3D motion, broader transformation classes) are natural avenues for future work.

title: Stochastic Linear Bandits with Partially Observed Actions
summary: The stochastic linear bandit, where actions are represented as vectors and rewards are linear, is a central paradigm for sequential decision making. We study a partially observed variant of this problem in which the learning agent only sees a random subset of coordinates for each action. Such partial observability arises naturally in settings like recommendation and healthcare, where full action descriptions can be expensive or even impossible to obtain. In general, this makes sublinear regret information-theoretically impossible. However, we show that this barrier can be overcome when the action vectors have low intrinsic dimension. We propose an algorithm, TOFU-POV, that estimates the latent action subspace using the masked actions, imputes current actions using an epoch-wise frozen representation, and runs OFUL in the resulting low-dimensional coordinates. Our theory shows that TOFU-POV enjoys a $\sqrt{T}$ regret that scales with the intrinsic action subspace dimension as opposed to the ambient dimension and quantifies the interaction between these quantities and the missingness, decision set size, and subspace conditioning. We also devise a rank-adaptive algorithm that does not require the knowledge of the intrinsic dimension. We complement these guarantees with a lower bound based on a novel product construction that separates usual reward-learning uncertainty from a missingness-dependent cost intrinsic to partial observation. Synthetic and real data experiments support our theory and show that TOFU-POV can substantially improve upon natural baselines in this challenging problem.

AI.tldr: Partially observed stochastic linear bandits with low intrinsic action dimension: a new method (TOFU-POV) that imputes masked features, estimates a latent subspace, and runs OFUL in reduced coordinates, achieving sqrt(T) regret depending on intrinsic dimension; includes a rank-adaptive variant and a lower bound; validated on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: In many domains, full action descriptions are costly or unavailable, leading to partial observability that prevents sublinear regret. If the action space has a low intrinsic (latent) dimension, this structure can be exploited to recover near-optimal learning performance.
AI.method: Estimate the latent action subspace from masked actions, imput current actions with an epoch-wise frozen representation, and apply OFUL in the resulting low-dimensional coordinates. Introduce a rank-adaptive variant that does not require the intrinsic dimension. Provide a lower bound via a product construction to separate reward-learning uncertainty from missingness costs. Support results with synthetic and real-data experiments.
AI.result: TOFU-POV achieves a sqrt(T) regret that scales with the intrinsic subspace dimension rather than ambient dimension. The bounds reveal the interaction between missingness, decision set size, and subspace conditioning. The rank-adaptive variant removes the need to know the intrinsic dimension. A new lower bound highlights the cost of partial observability. Empirical results show substantial improvements over natural baselines.
AI.conclusion: Partial observability need not preclude sublinear regret when the action space has low intrinsic dimension. TOFU-POV effectively learns in the latent subspace and demonstrates strong theoretical and empirical performance, with practical extensions via a rank-adaptive variant.

title: TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework (ARC): Risk-Tiering Internally Created Agentic AI Systems
comment: This is a working paper on our risk classification tool, with iterations currently underway
summary: The proliferation of agentic AI systems across enterprise and public-sector contexts has outpaced the capacity of general-purpose AI risk frameworks to classify and govern them. In this paper, we introduce the TrustX Agent Risk Classification Framework, a structured, repeatable instrument that can be applied to seven types of agentic AI systems and is grounded in foundational pre-existing AI governance frameworks. At the core of the framework is a twelve-dimension scoring rubric that robustly quantifies the risk. This rubric is combined with other components, such as the GPA + IAT classification model and the five-level autonomy framework derived from existing literature. These inputs produce a three-tier governance output with mapped control recommendations. A specialised Coding Assistant extension is also included to account for nuances specific to this type of agentic AI system. We then use an illustrative example to show our framework in practice. ARC is intended for AI governance practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators, and it will regularly undergo iteration as we continue to expand it and make it more robust. The community can access the interactive framework here: https://arc.responsible.ai/

AI.tldr: Introduces the TrustX Agent Risk Classification (ARC) Framework for agentic AI risk governance, featuring a 12-dimension risk rubric, integration with GPA+IAT and a five-level autonomy model, producing a three-tier governance output with control recommendations; includes a Coding Assistant extension and an illustrative example; intended for practitioners and regulators with ongoing iteration and community access.
AI.motivation: Address the gap between the rapid deployment of agentic AI systems and the limited reach of general AI risk frameworks; provide a repeatable, robust governance instrument grounded in established frameworks.
AI.method: Develop a structured instrument (ARC) applicable to seven types of agentic AI systems) built around a 12-dimension scoring rubric; integrate with the GPA + IAT classification model and a five-level autonomy framework; generate a three-tier governance output with mapped controls; include a Coding Assistant extension; illustrate with an example; offer an interactive framework for community use.
AI.result: A practical, repeatable risk-classification framework (ARC) with a quantitative 12-dimension rubric, multi-model inputs, and a tiered governance output, along with an extension tool and an illustrative demonstration; publicly accessible interactive platform.
AI.conclusion: ARC is designed as an evolving governance tool for AI practitioners, risk officers, developers, and regulators, with plans for iterative improvements and broader adoption across agentic AI types.

title: PAC-ACT: Post-training Actor-Critic for Action Chunking Transformers
summary: Precision industrial contact manipulation requires reliable robot policies under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints. Vision-language-action models offer broad generalization but often introduce high inference latency and GPU-memory cost, while vision-action chunking policies are more suitable for real-time industrial control. However, these policies are usually trained by behavior cloning and suffer from distribution shift in contact-rich tasks. This paper proposes PAC-ACT, a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies. PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning. Experiments on industrial precision-contact benchmarks show that PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage. On the Contour task, PAC-ACT significantly reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations further show that the proposed behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.

AI.tldr: RL post-training framework PAC-ACT improves pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies for precision industrial contact manipulation by chunk-level RL, an ACT-based actor-critic, and a behavior-prior constraint, achieving better performance with low latency and memory.
AI.motivation: Address distribution shift and latency/memory challenges in vision-language-action or chunk-based policies for contact-rich manipulation; enable real-time control with reliable performance under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints.
AI.method: Post-training RL at chunk level; introduces ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture; hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning.
AI.result: Improved task success, contact stability, and force safety; maintained low latency and GPU memory; Contour task: peak contact force reduced; force readings >60N decreased by 46x; sparse-reward ablations show improved exploration with behavior-prior.
AI.conclusion: PAC-ACT demonstrates effective, efficient fine-tuning of chunk-based policies for precision industrial manipulation and suggests behavior-prior constraints as a practical tool for mitigating distribution shift during RL fine-tuning.

title: Integrating Large Language Models and Graph Convolutional Networks for Semi-Supervised Image Classification
summary: While the growing availability of image data has driven significant advances, labeling datasets remains costly and time-consuming. Therefore, semi-supervised approaches such as Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which learn from both labeled and unlabeled data, have emerged as a promising solution. One of the primary challenges in applying GCNs to image classification is graph construction, since, unlike in citation networks or similar domains, images typically do not come with a predefined structural representation. For visual data, most studies construct graphs based on the similarity between feature vectors from pretrained deep learning backbones, typically by employing kNN or reciprocal kNN algorithms. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capability in capturing high-level semantics, their integration with GCNs for image classification remains underexplored. Aiming to fill this gap, our approach uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to generate textual image descriptions, which are then processed by an LLM to estimate semantic similarity scores between connected images. These scores guide the pruning of edges in kNN and reciprocal kNN graphs, filtering out semantically irrelevant neighbors. Experimental results reveal that leveraging LLMs for graph refinement can improve classification accuracy, particularly for kNN graphs and some backbones. The source code is publicly available at http://gcnllm.lucasvalem.com.

AI.tldr: LLM-guided refinement of kNN graphs for GCN-based image classification improves accuracy by pruning semantically irrelevant edges using VLM-generated image descriptions and an LLM to estimate similarities.
AI.motivation: Labeling datasets for image classification is costly, and effective GCNs require meaningful graphs. Traditional graph construction relies on feature similarity, which may not capture semantic relationships; integrating LLMs/vision-language models can refine graph structure to improve semi-supervised learning.
AI.method: Generate textual descriptions for images with a Vision-Language Model, use an LLM to estimate semantic similarity scores between connected images, prune edges in kNN/reciprocal kNN graphs accordingly, then train GCNs on the refined graphs across backbones; public code provided.
AI.result: Edge pruning via LLM-guided semantic similarity improves classification accuracy, particularly for kNN graphs and some backbones; performance gains demonstrated; source code available at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven graph refinement is a promising direction for semi-supervised image classification with GCNs, showing that semantic-edge pruning can enhance performance and that LLMs can complement traditional feature-based graphs.

title: Federated Low-Rank Koopman Learning for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection in IoT Systems
summary: Distributed IoT systems generate multivariate time-series streams for monitoring physical assets, servers, and embedded sensing platforms. Detecting abnormal temporal behavior is critical for fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, and security. However, practical IoT anomaly detection is hindered by decentralized and non-IID data, limited bandwidth, and the constrained computation and memory of edge devices. This paper proposes FedKAD, a resource-efficient federated Koopman anomaly detection framework for distributed IoT multivariate time series. Unlike deep-learning-based anomaly detectors that require training and communicating large neural models, FedKAD learns normal temporal dynamics through lightweight sliding-window Koopman representations. Federated training is formulated as a low-rank consensus problem, where raw sensor streams and local reduced dynamics remain on device while only compact subspace variables are exchanged with the server. To optimize the shared representation under orthonormality constraints, we develop a federated Stiefel-ADMM algorithm and provide convergence and stationarity analysis under partial client participation. During inference, each client detects anomalies locally by measuring the prediction residual between observed future trajectories and the learned Koopman dynamics. Experiments on four widely used multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show that FedKAD maintains or improves detection performance compared with federated deep-learning baselines. More importantly for IoT deployment, FedKAD provides up to $2.1\times10^3$ faster training, $80\times$ lower communication, and $79\times$ lower inference latency than neural baselines, confirming its suitability for resource-constrained edge devices.

AI.tldr: FedKAD is a resource-efficient federated Koopman-based anomaly detection framework for distributed IoT multivariate time series, enabling on-device training and local inference with compact communication and competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: IoT anomaly detection is hindered by decentralized and non-IID data, limited bandwidth, and constrained edge computation/memory. Deep learning baselines are powerful but costly for edge deployment; a lightweight, privacy-preserving approach is needed.
AI.method: Learn normal dynamics using sliding-window Koopman representations. Formulate federated training as a low-rank consensus problem where raw data and local dynamics stay on-device; exchange compact subspace variables. Optimize the shared representation under orthonormal constraints via a federated Stiefel-ADMM algorithm with convergence analysis under partial client participation. Inference is conducted locally by measuring prediction residuals between observed futures and learned Koopman dynamics.
AI.result: Experiments on four multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show FedKAD matches or outperforms federated deep-learning baselines in detection performance, while delivering large efficiency gains: up to 2.1×10^3 faster training, 80× lower communication, and 79× lower inference latency, making it well-suited for resource-constrained IoT edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: FedKAD provides a scalable, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient anomaly detection framework for distributed IoT systems, achieving competitive detection accuracy with substantial reductions in training time, communication, and latency compared to neural baselines.

title: Agora: Enhancing LLM Agent Reasoning Via Auction-Based Task Allocation
summary: Enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents requires effective orchestration of diverse expert models and tools. However, existing frameworks typically call APIs based on coarse-grained matching between tasks and the functions of expert models or tools, while overlooking critical factors such as performance variability and cost efficiency among functionally similar alternatives. To address this, we propose Agora, a framework that introduces an incentive-compatible auction mechanism for dynamically allocating tasks to expert models and tools. By treating reasoning steps as tradeable items, Agora enables agents to bid based on their rectified competence-ensuring that critical logic is routed to the most capable solver rather than the most overconfident one. Evaluations across five benchmarks show that Agora improves over matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, while exposing a controllable cost-quality trade-off through a single auction parameter.

AI.tldr: Agora introduces an incentive-compatible auction to dynamically allocate reasoning tasks to expert models/tools, treating each reasoning step as a tradable item and routing critical logic to the most capable solver while controlling cost-quality trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Address performance variability and cost differences among functionally similar tools in LLM agent reasoning. Move beyond coarse-grained task-function matching to ensure critical logic is solved by the best solver rather than just the cheapest or most confident.
AI.method: Propose an auction-based framework where reasoning steps are treated as tradeable items. Candidates bid according to their rectified competence, enabling incentive-compatible allocation that prefers the most capable solver. Evaluate on five benchmarks against matched models, routing, and cascade baselines under comparable candidate pools, with a single auction parameter controlling cost-quality trade-off.
AI.result: Agora outperforms matched single-model, routing, and cascade baselines across five benchmarks under similar candidate pools, and offers a controllable cost-quality trade-off via a single auction parameter.
AI.conclusion: An auction-based, rectified-competence allocation mechanism can substantially improve reasoning quality and cost efficiency in LLM agent orchestration, with a tunable parameter to balance resource use and performance.

title: B-spline Policy: Accelerating Manipulation Policies via B-spline Action Representations
summary: In this work, we present B-spline Policy (BSP), an action representation designed for accelerating robot manipulation policies. Rather than predicting discrete-time action chunks, BSP parameterizes actions as continuous B-spline curves defined by a set of knots and control points. This representation yields smooth, time-continuous trajectories that can be temporally scaled and executed by low-level controllers at higher frequencies and speeds. We show that B-spline-parameterized actions can be seamlessly integrated into standard policy learning pipelines by directly predicting B-spline parameters. Experiments on simulated and real-world tasks demonstrate that BSP significantly reduces task completion time, achieving substantial improvements over baseline methods while maintaining strong success rates. More results: https://b-spline-policy.github.io

AI.tldr: B-spline Policy (BSP) treats actions as continuous B-spline curves instead of discrete action chunks, yielding smooth, time-continuous trajectories that can be executed at higher frequencies and scaled in time.
AI.motivation: Discrete action chunks can produce non-smooth, slower trajectories and limit high-frequency control. A continuous-time action representation can accelerate policy execution while remaining compatible with standard learning pipelines.
AI.method: Parameterize actions with B-spline curves defined by knots and control points. The policy directly predicts B-spline parameters; the resulting trajectories are smooth and time-continuous and can be temporally scaled. These actions are compatible with standard policy-learning pipelines and low-level controllers operating at higher frequencies.
AI.result: Experiments in simulation and on real robots show substantial reductions in task completion time with BSP, outperforming baselines while maintaining high success rates.
AI.conclusion: B-spline parameterization is an effective action representation for accelerating robot manipulation policies, enabling faster execution without sacrificing performance and integrating smoothly into existing learning workflows.

title: Event Stream based Multi-Modal Video Anomaly Detection: A Benchmark Dataset and Algorithms
summary: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is critical for automated surveillance but remains fragile under challenging conditions such as illumination variations, fast motion, and complex backgrounds when relying solely on visible light videos. To address these limitations, we propose EVAD, an event enhanced VAD framework that jointly exploits conventional video and event streams captured by bio inspired event cameras. Event sensors asynchronously capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution, offering robustness to motion blur and extreme lighting, and providing motion salient cues complementary to video based visual information. To support multi modal VAD research, we construct a large scale visible event benchmark comprising 6.3 billion events and 376,368 video frames collected under diverse illumination levels, motion patterns, and background complexities, filling the gap of realistic and scalable datasets for event based anomaly detection. Building upon this dataset, we design a contrastive multi modal pretraining framework to learn discriminative event representations by aligning semantic embeddings across event streams, visible videos, and textual descriptions. An adaptive fusion module then dynamically integrates event based temporal cues with video based spatial semantics, improving robustness to environmental disturbances. Experiments on benchmarks and the proposed TJUTCM Pha dataset demonstrate that E VAD consistently outperforms methods, validating the effectiveness of event-based sensing for VAD in real world scenarios.

AI.tldr: EVAD introduces an event-camera–assisted video anomaly detection framework that fuses high-temporal-resolution event streams with conventional video, backed by a large-scale visible-event benchmark and a contrastive multi-modal pretraining pipeline with adaptive fusion for robust VAD.
