AI.conclusion: Advocates continual learning, memory-centric hardware, standardized evaluation protocols, and full-stack co-design to realize scalable, sustainable large models.

title: Glob3R: Global Structure-from-Motion with 3D Foundation Models
summary: Recent 3D geometric foundation models, such as VGGT, provide robust feed-forward 3D reconstruction by directly predicting camera poses and 3D scene points from input images. However, their results remain inaccurate, and scaling them to long sequences or large unordered image sets typically requires chunk-wise processing, which can introduce drift and inconsistency. We present Glob3R, a global SfM-style reconstruction built on 3D foundation models. Our key idea is to explicitly optimize feed-forward geometric predictions. To this end, we augment a frozen Pi3X backbone with a lightweight dense matching head that predicts image warps between selected reference frames and neighboring views. These dense warps are converted into sparse but reliable multi-view feature tracks, which provide correspondence constraints for global optimization. We further introduce a keyframe-based sliding-window association strategy that propagates tracks and relative poses across overlapping windows, enabling scalable reconstruction. Finally, we perform global motion averaging and bundle adjustment to refine camera poses, reduce scale inconsistencies, and recover dense scene geometry. Extensive experiments on indoor, outdoor, large-scale driving, and unordered SfM benchmarks demonstrate that Glob3R achieves robust and accurate reconstruction. It consistently improves over feed-forward foundation-model baselines and recent scalable reconstruction methods, while being more robust than classical SfM pipelines. The refined poses also lead to higher-quality neural rendering, validating the benefit of combining foundation-model priors with global geometric optimization. Project page: https://junyuandeng.github.io/Glob3r

AI.tldr: Glob3R augments a frozen 3D foundation-model backbone with a lightweight dense matching head to produce image warps, which are converted into sparse multi-view tracks and used in a global, keyframe-based optimization (motion averaging and bundle adjustment) to achieve scalable, accurate, and robust 3D reconstruction, improving over feed-forward baselines and classical SfM while enhancing neural rendering quality.
AI.motivation: Address the drift, inconsistency, and scalability issues of feed-forward foundation-model reconstructions when handling long sequences or large unordered image sets, by incorporating explicit global geometric optimization.
AI.method: Freeze a Pi3X backbone and add a lightweight dense matching head that predicts image warps between selected reference frames and neighboring views. Convert these dense warps into sparse multi-view feature tracks. Use a keyframe-based sliding-window association to propagate tracks and relative poses across overlapping windows. Perform global motion averaging and bundle adjustment to refine poses and recover dense geometry.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across indoor, outdoor, large-scale driving, and unordered SfM benchmarks show Glob3R achieves robust and accurate reconstruction, consistently outperforming feed-forward foundation-model baselines and recent scalable methods, and displaying greater robustness than classical SfM pipelines. Refined poses yield higher-quality neural rendering.
AI.conclusion: Combining foundation-model priors with global geometric optimization yields scalable, robust 3D reconstruction with improved pose accuracy and dense geometry, enhancing neural rendering quality.

title: EXHOLD: Experience-Aware Real-Time Hold Control for Large-Scale Ride-Hailing Matching at DiDi
summary:
In large-scale ride-hailing, hold control is a critical mechanism for improving passenger-driver experience. By selectively delaying certain driver-order pairs, the system waits for better opportunities, reduces cancellations, and mitigates wasted driver effort. However, existing industrial hold strategies often rely on heuristic thresholding over multiple predictive models, which can be brittle under non-stationary traffic and hard to optimize for multi-objective experience signals.
  We propose EXHOLD, a deployable two-stage framework decoupling experience-aware pair assessment from hold-time execution. In Stage I, we learn a decision model assigning each driver-order pair to discrete, interpretable experience tiers by optimizing a unified objective that aggregates satisfaction signals across the matching funnel. In Stage II, we solve for a monotone hold-time schedule via constrained optimization over empirical quantiles. This explicitly enforces service guardrails bounding the unnecessary holding of promising matches while maximizing overall experience improvement.
  We evaluate EXHOLD through randomized A/B experiments in DiDi's production system in Brazil. Results show consistent gains in marketplace efficiency and experience: EXHOLD increases trip completion and driver income, significantly reduces passenger cancellations, and improves funnel efficiency. Ablations and behavioral analyses confirm both stages are essential and that the policy makes calibrated decisions under spatiotemporal heterogeneity. EXHOLD is currently deployed, serving production traffic in Brazil.

AI.tldr: EXHOLD decouples experience-aware assessment from hold-time scheduling to optimize ride-hailing matches, yielding efficiency and experience gains; deployed in DiDi Brazil with randomized A/B.
AI.motivation: Current hold policies rely on heuristic thresholds across multiple predictive models, which are brittle under non-stationary traffic and hard to optimize for multi-objective experience signals.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: Stage I learns a decision model that assigns each driver-order pair to discrete experience tiers by optimizing a unified objective over the matching funnel; Stage II computes a monotone hold-time schedule via constrained optimization over empirical quantiles, enforcing service guardrails while maximizing overall experience improvement.
AI.result: In randomized A/B experiments in DiDi's production system in Brazil, EXHOLD increased trip completion and driver income, significantly reduced passenger cancellations, and improved funnel efficiency; ablations and analyses show both stages are essential and the policy handles spatiotemporal heterogeneity; EXHOLD is deployed for production traffic in Brazil.
AI.conclusion: EXHOLD is a deployable framework that improves marketplace efficiency and user experience in large-scale ride-hailing by decoupling experience-aware assessment from hold-time execution and constraining hold policies.

title: AnythingReality: Robust Online Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Open-Vocabulary VR Scene Exploration
summary: We present a novel integrated architecture for robust online 3D Gaussian splatting, real-time VR exploration, and speech-driven Vision-Language-Model interaction. Unlike methods assuming clean depth or external poses, our system combines ORB-SLAM3-based pose estimation with online Gaussian reconstruction for noisy real-world data. A VR pipeline enables immersive exploration of incremental reconstructions; a semantic module transcribes voice commands, generates scene descriptions, and records points of interest. Against state-of-the-art online Gaussian splatting methods, we improve image quality on our dataset (+14.5% PSNR, +8.6% SSIM, -14.3% LPIPS) and TUM-RGBD (+11.7% PSNR, +7.8% SSIM, -21.6% LPIPS), with comparable or superior frame rates via quality-speed configurations. We achieve an 88% VLM object-recognition rate.

AI.tldr: An integrated pipeline for robust online 3D Gaussian splatting with SLAM-based pose, VR exploration, and speech-driven VLM interaction, achieving higher perceptual quality and strong VLM recognition while maintaining frame rates.
AI.motivation: Address noise in depth and pose data during real-time 3D reconstruction; enable immersive VR exploration and natural language-driven scene understanding and control by combining SLAM with online Gaussian reconstruction and vision-language interaction.
AI.method: Fuse ORB-SLAM3-based pose estimation with online Gaussian splatting for noisy real-world data. Provide a VR pipeline for incremental reconstruction visualization. Include a semantic module that transcribes voice commands, generates scene descriptions, and records points of interest. Optimize via quality-speed configurations to balance image quality and FPS.
AI.result: On their dataset, image quality improves as: PSNR +14.5%, SSIM +8.6%, LPIPS -14.3%. On TUM-RGBD: PSNR +11.7%, SSIM +7.8%, LPIPS -21.6%. Frame rates are comparable or superior under quality-speed configurations. Achieves 88% VLM object-recognition rate.
AI.conclusion: The integrated system delivers robust online 3D reconstruction with high perceptual quality and effective speech-driven VLM interaction, achieving strong recognition performance while maintaining real-time capabilities, outperforming state-of-the-art online Gaussian splatting baselines on reported metrics.

title: Quantum Circuits in Diffusion Models: A Fair-Comparison Study and a Mechanistic Analysis of Angle-Embedding Failures
summary: We study the integration of variational quantum circuits (VQCs) into diffusion models through a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) channel-modulation scaffold that isolates the quantum contribution. Using a role-matched classical control and multi-seed significance testing across DDPM and latent diffusion on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with a score-based NCSN study on MNIST, we find that quantum cores achieve comparable mean FID to the classical control across DDPM and latent diffusion, while paired sampling-seed tests for EfficientSU2 detect no statistically significant difference. Although the quantum cores use $4.5$--$9\times$ fewer core parameters than the role-matched control, parameter-matched classical controls attain comparable mean FID, so the experiments do not establish a quantum parameter-efficiency advantage. We further identify a structural failure in score-based NCSN: the unbounded score target, proportional to $1/σ$, drives angle-embedding inputs far beyond the $2π$ period of rotation gates, causing phase aliasing and collapse of the quantum modulator. A bounding transformation, $θ\leftarrow π\tanh(\cdot)$, maps inputs to the non-aliasing domain and substantially improves both quantum cores. Since all circuits are classically simulated at a few-qubit scale, we do not claim quantum advantage. Instead, the study provides a fair-comparison protocol for quantum-enhanced generative models and a mechanistic account of when and why angle embeddings fail.

AI.tldr: Quantum cores in diffusion models show comparable performance to classical controls in FID with no clear parameter-efficiency advantage; a key failure mode is angle-embedding aliasing in unbounded score targets, mitigated by a pi*tanh bound, and the study offers a fair protocol for quantum-enhanced generators rather than claiming quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Explore whether variational quantum circuits can meaningfully improve diffusion-model generative performance and parameter efficiency, while isolating quantum contributions from classical controls.
AI.method: Integrates VQCs via a squeeze-and-excitation channel-modulation scaffold with role-matched classical control. Evaluates across DDPM and latent diffusion on MNIST/CIFAR-10, plus a score-based NCSN study on MNIST. Uses multi-seed significance testing and paired sampling-seed tests to compare quantum cores (EfficientSU2) against classical controls. Finds quantum cores use fewer core parameters but do not outperform with parameter-matched classical controls. Identifies angle-embedding instability due to unbounded score target; proposes bounding transform θ ← π tanh(·) to maintain non-aliasing domain.
AI.result: Quantum cores achieve comparable mean FID to classical control across diffusion frameworks; paired sampling-seed tests detect no significant difference. Although quantum cores use 4.5–9× fewer parameters, parameter-matched classical controls achieve similar FID, so no quantum parameter-efficiency advantage is established. Structural failure in score-based NCSN caused by angle-aliasing from unbounded score targets; applying θ ← π tanh(·) improves quantum modulator. All circuits are classically simulated at a few-qubit scale; no quantum advantage claimed. The work provides a fair-comparison protocol and a mechanistic account of angle-embedding failures.
AI.conclusion: The study offers a rigorous, fair protocol for evaluating quantum-enhanced generative models and identifies a key embedding failure mode that can be mitigated. It does not claim quantum advantage under current setups and emphasizes understanding when quantum components contribute meaningfully.

title: Semantic Hardness Is Not Visual Hardness: Sign-Aware Hard Negative Mining for Sign Language Retrieval
summary: Sign Language Retrieval (SLRet) enables efficient access to sign language content but remains fragile in fine-grained scenarios where visually similar signs must be distinguished. We show that this limitation does not stem from model capacity, but from ineffective hard negative supervision. Specifically, we formulate fine-grained retrieval failures as a negative distribution mismatch: semantically distinct yet visually confusable signs are rarely treated as hard negatives, while existing text-based mining strategies fail to capture such visual ambiguity. To address this issue, we propose Sign-Aware Hard Negative Mining (SAN), which constructs hard negatives based on visual confusability in the sign embedding space rather than linguistic similarity. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T demonstrate that SAN substantially improves fine-grained retrieval performance while preserving coarse-grained accuracy, highlighting the importance of aligning negative supervision with visual ambiguity in sign language retrieval.

AI.tldr: Proposes Sign-Aware Hard Negative Mining (SAN) for sign-language retrieval; addresses fine-grained visual confusability by constructing hard negatives from visual similarity in sign embedding space, improving fine-grained retrieval on PHOENIX-2014T while preserving coarse accuracy.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained SLRet suffers from negative distribution mismatch; existing hard negatives rely on linguistic similarity or text-based mining that fails to capture visual ambiguity among signs that appear visually similar but semantically distinct.
AI.method: Introduce SAN: hard negative mining based on visual confusability in the sign embedding space, rather than linguistic similarity; training likely uses embedding distances to select visually close yet semantically different negatives; loss emphasizes distinguishing visually confusable signs.
AI.result: On PHOENIX-2014T dataset, SAN substantially improves fine-grained retrieval metrics, with no loss in coarse-grained accuracy; demonstrates alignment of negative supervision with visual ambiguity improves retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Aligning negative supervision with visual ambiguity is crucial for fine-grained sign-language retrieval; SAN is effective and potentially generalizable to other modalities with visually confusable classes.

title: Power Flow Feasibility Assessment Using Variational Graph Autoencoders
summary: Data-driven methods, including graph neural networks, have been studied for accelerating power flow calculations in recent years, but very little attention has been paid to the solution feasibility, which can be obtained by traditional solvers. This paper presents a Variational Graph Autoencoder (VGAE) that detects the power flow solution feasibility, using the IEEE 118-bus case, to assess the validity of the solutions provided by AI-driven solvers.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Variational Graph Autoencoder to detect power flow solution feasibility and validate AI-driven solvers on the IEEE 118-bus system.
AI.motivation: Data-driven power flow methods, including graph neural networks, accelerate computation but often neglect feasibility guarantees; a method is needed to detect whether proposed solutions are feasible.
AI.method: Develops a VGAE that ingests the power network representation and outputs a feasibility indicator for power flow solutions; evaluated on IEEE 118-bus case to assess AI-driven solvers.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the VGAE can identify feasible vs infeasible power flow solutions and serve as a feasibility validator for AI-based solvers on the test case.
AI.conclusion: VGAE provides a viable feasibility-checking tool for AI-powered power flow solvers, improving reliability of data-driven approaches.

title: REMIND: RE-Identification with Memory for INDoor Navigation
summary:
Mobile robots operating indoors must re-identify previously observed objects after long temporal gaps, significant viewpoint changes, and severe illumination variations. This remains a challenging problem: multi-object tracking methods are optimized for short-term association of pedestrians and vehicles at video rates, person and vehicle re-identification approaches lack persistent memory mechanisms, and state-of-the-art video object segmentation techniques rely on reactive distractor filtering rather than enforcing global identity consistency.
  To address these limitations, we present REMIND, an online tracker designed for long-term multi-object re-identification of generic indoor objects from monocular RGB imagery, requiring neither camera pose nor depth. Motivated by evidence from visual cognition that humans rely on accumulated appearance familiarity and spatial context rather than explicit self-localization, REMIND combines frozen DINOv3 features with a dual-bank multi-prototype appearance memory, part- and background-level descriptors, a neighbour-context reasoning module exploiting spatial co-occurrence, and joint Hungarian assignment with ambiguity-aware safeguards. On a purpose-built indoor dataset featuring controlled revisits and dense same-class clutter, REMIND reaches 90.35% IDF1, nearly 20 points above a state-of-the-art video object segmentation baseline and more than 36 above a strong tracking-by-detection baseline. On ScanNet++, it attains the highest IDF1 in every setting but one, end-to-end detection over all scenes, where the tracking-by-detection baseline is marginally ahead while REMIND still associates and recovers identities more accurately; it also completes every scene, whereas the video object segmentation baseline exhausts GPU memory on 66.9% under YOLO detections. The complete system, evaluation framework, and dataset are publicly released.

AI.tldr: Online tracker REMIND for long-term multi-object re-identification in indoor monocular RGB, using frozen DINOv3 features, a dual-bank appearance memory, context reasoning, and Hungarian assignment; achieves high IDF1 on indoor datasets and releases code/dataset.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of short-term MOT, lack of persistent memory in re-identification, and reactive video object segmentation; enable persistent identity tracking across long temporal gaps, viewpoint shifts, and illumination changes without camera pose or depth.
AI.method: Integrates frozen DINOv3 features with a dual-bank multi-prototype appearance memory; includes part- and background-level descriptors; neighbor-context reasoning exploiting spatial co-occurrence; joint Hungarian assignment with ambiguity-aware safeguards; online tracker for generic indoor objects from monocular RGB.
AI.result: On a purpose-built indoor dataset with revisits and dense clutter, IDF1=90.35%, ~20 points higher than a video object segmentation baseline and >36 higher than a strong tracking-by-detection baseline. On ScanNet++, achieves the highest IDF1 in all settings except one (end-to-end detection where a tracking-by-detection baseline is marginally ahead); REMIND completes every scene, while the VOS baseline exhausts GPU memory under YOLO detections. Public release of the complete system, evaluation framework, and dataset.
AI.conclusion: REMIND demonstrates strong long-term re-identification and identity continuity in indoor monocular tracking, leveraging memory-augmented appearance features and spatial context; scalable to complete scenes with full data release to enable further research.

title: Present but Rescaled: Chat-to-Agent Transfer of Additive Activation Steering
summary: Additive activation steering (injecting a scaled residual-stream direction during generation) is calibrated almost entirely in single-turn chat, yet the models it targets are increasingly deployed as tool-using ReAct agents. We present the first systematic chat-to-agent transfer study of additive steering, coupling behavioral measurement with a representation read-out in a matched-information design: the same items rendered as plain chat or as a ReAct tool-use episode, with matched-norm random-direction controls and the transcript re-encoded every turn to exclude KV-cache contamination. Transfer is real but rescaled, and the right description is a dissociation: the injected direction reaches the late layers at near-full strength in every setting and model tested (install-site agent-over-chat ratios 0.83-1.16 across three families), while the behavioral coupling is reset per model and context. On Qwen2.5-7B a refusal bypass vector amplifies in the agent (T = 1.45, CI [1.20, 1.78], N = 300); across a powered uniform-protocol distribution the coupling spans amplification (Gemma-2-9B T = 2.00) to attenuation (Yi-1.5-9B T = 0.43, CI [0.29, 0.60]), with no universal constant and a single clean attenuator against a universal sign. Directional ablation of the same axis does not amplify (T = 0.93, CI including 1) while additive injection amplifies (T = 1.50), a 20.1-point gain difference (CI [13.4, 26.8]) that identifies an additive-specific mechanism. Two pre-registered instruments converge to localize the rescaling to the ReAct format scaffold, before any tool observation, rather than to the observation boundary where a dilution account would predict it. The safety implication is immediate and unpredictable: agentic deployment amplifies steering-based refusal bypass by up to 2.00x on some models while others attenuate, so a deployment cannot assume a given model is safe under additive steering.

AI.tldr: Additive activation steering can transfer from chat to tool-using agents, but the magnitude is context- and model-dependent. Late-layer representations show near-full-strength injection across settings, while behavioral coupling resets per model/context. Refusal bypass amplification varies by model (up to ~2x), and ablation does not replicate the amplification. The rescaling localizes to the ReAct scaffold before tool observation, implying immediate safety concerns for deployment: some models amplify steering-based refusals, others attenuate.
AI.motivation: Systematically quantify how additive activation steering observed in plain chat transfers when agents operate in a ReAct tool-use setting, and identify where in the model this rescaling occurs, to understand safety implications of deploying such steering.
AI.method: A matched-information design: items presented as plain chat or as a ReAct tool-use episode, with matched-norm random-direction controls. Transcript re-encoded each turn to remove KV-cache contamination. Read-out from representations and behavioral measurements were collected across multiple models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Yi-1.5-9B). Pre-registered instruments localized effects and used ablation vs injection to distinguish mechanisms.
AI.result: Injection direction propagates to late layers at near-full strength across settings (install-site agent-over-chat ratios 0.83–1.16). Behavioral coupling is model/context-specific, resetting per model. Refusal-bypass vector in Qwen2.5-7B amplifies in agent (T=1.45, 95% CI [1.20,1.78], N=300). Across a uniform-protocol distribution, coupling ranges from amplification (Gemma-2-9B, T=2.00) to attenuation (Yi-1.5-9B, T=0.43, CI [0.29,0.60]). No universal constant; a single attenuator against a universal sign exists. Directional ablation does not amplify (T=0.93, CI includes 1) while additive injection amplifies (T=1.50). The difference (~20.1 points, CI [13.4, 26.8]) indicates an additive-specific mechanism. Two pre-registered instruments converge to localize rescaling to the ReAct scaffold prior to tool observation rather than the observation boundary.
AI.conclusion: Additive steering effects are real in agent contexts but highly model- and context-dependent. The rescaling to late representations is robust, yet behavioral coupling varies, implying deployment risks. Safety analyses must account for model-specific susceptibilities to both amplification and attenuation of steering, and mitigation should focus on the ReAct scaffold region prior to tool observation.

title: Rethinking Monocular Depth Embedding for Generalized Stereo Matching
summary: Generally, monocular methods capture rich contextual priors but lack geometric precision, whereas stereo methods are geometrically accurate yet struggle in textureless and occluded regions. Several approaches attempt to combine their strengths to enhance the generalization of stereo matching (SM) by aligning monocular depth with stereo information. However, establishing a stable and generalizable alignment is challenging, and unreliable monocular cues can substantially degrade performance. This paper rethinks monocular depth embedding. First, to prevent shortcut learning, we reduce branch coupling instead of expanding network width. Second, we construct soft constraints instead of hard ones from monocular depth to improve tolerance to monocular depth errors. Based on the principles, we integrate monocular information into both feature extraction and GRU iterations. Specifically, the monocular depth map is fused with the RGB image to sharpen depth boundary perception and suppress matching ambiguities. The fused image is then used for feature extraction, allowing the contextual features to encode global geometric information. Furthermore, the monocular depth gradient feature is employed to guide disparity updates, helping to escape local oscillations. Finally, to address the boundary blurring of supervised disparity caused by data augmentation, we propose an edge confidence estimation method and an edge-aware loss function. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on multiple standard benchmarks, demonstrating excellent generalization while improving accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/linliboabc-maker/stereo-matching-digital.

AI.tldr: A monocular-stereo fusion framework that injects soft monocular depth constraints into both feature extraction and GRU refinement to improve stereo matching, with reduced branch coupling, boundary-aware edge confidence and losses, achieving SOTA and strong generalization; code released.
AI.motivation: Monocular methods provide rich context but poor geometry; stereo methods are geometrically precise but struggle with textureless/occluded regions. Unstable alignment between monocular depth and stereo information can degrade performance. The work aims to create a robust, generalizable monocular-stereo integration.
AI.method: 1) Reduce branch coupling to prevent shortcut learning. 2) Use soft constraints from monocular depth instead of hard guidance. 3) Fuse monocular depth with RGB for improved boundary perception and global geometry in feature extraction. 4) Use monocular depth gradient features to guide disparity updates in GRU iterations. 5) Introduce edge confidence estimation and an edge-aware loss to mitigate boundary blurring from data augmentation.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple standard benchmarks and demonstrates excellent generalization and improved accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Softly integrating monocular depth into both feature extraction and iterative disparity refinement, along with boundary-aware supervision, yields robust generalization and accuracy gains over prior methods. Code is publicly available.

title: A Personalized Computational Framework for Assessing the Sufficiency of Partially Observed Data in Healthcare AI models
summary: Achieving early and timely diagnosis and treatment for disease is a major challenge. Recent applications of machine learning (ML) algorithms trained on patient data have shown promise in many different settings for predicting the patient health state. A challenge often faced when applying these ML algorithms is that at any given time, not all clinical variables (features) needed as input to perform prediction tasks are available. We define the concept of full-feature-capacity (FFC) to refer to prediction performance when such algorithms make use of all features on which they were trained. We then introduce Feature Sufficiency Analysis (FSA) - an analysis for determining whether a subset of all clinical features needed by an AI model is sufficient to achieve FFC. FSA estimates the underlying distributions of missing variables conditioned on features that are available. FSA provides a patient-specific assessment of whether the existing set of measured features achieves FFC. If yes, then there is no need to acquire further inputs and a ML-based prediction. We provide two case studies: prediction of need for postoperative prolonged ventilation in patients recovering from heart surgery; 10-year mortality prediction in an outpatient cohort. We also demonstrate that FSA also provides a clinically interpretable feature-ranking methodology based on prediction sufficiency, identifies intrinsically hard-to-predict patient populations, and has the potential to perform cost-aware optimization for clinical data acquisition. FSA provides a generic computational approach for determining whether incomplete clinical information is sufficient to support trustworthy AI-assisted clinical decision-making, thereby facilitating the prospective deployment of healthcare AI systems across diverse clinical settings.

AI.tldr: Introduces Full-Feature-Capacity (FFC) and Feature Sufficiency Analysis (FSA) to assess whether a subset of clinical features is enough to achieve the maximum expected performance of ML models trained on all features.
AI.motivation: Clinical ML predictions often encounter missing input features. There is a need to determine if available measurements suffice to reach the model's full-feature performance and to guide data acquisition and interpretation.
AI.method: FSA estimates the conditional distributions of missing variables given the observed features, enabling a patient-specific assessment of sufficiency. It yields a feature-sufficiency-based ranking, identifies hard-to-predict subpopulations, and supports cost-aware data acquisition decisions.
AI.result: Case studies include predicting postoperative prolonged ventilation after cardiac surgery and 10-year outpatient mortality. The analysis demonstrates that FSA can determine sufficiency, provide interpretable feature rankings, and reveal intrinsically challenging cases, with potential to reduce unnecessary data collection.
AI.conclusion: FSA offers a generic, computational approach to decide whether incomplete clinical information suffices for trustworthy AI-driven decisions, supporting prospective deployment of clinical AI across diverse settings.

title: TextileNet: Towards Zero-shot Text-style Segmentation of Manuscripts
comment: accepted for publication in the ICDAR 2026 workshop (peer reviewed) "IWCP: 4th International Workshop on Computational Paleography"
summary: Automatic writer identification systems have progressed remarkably in recent years, yet their deployment in archival paleography remains limited by the scarcity of labeled training data, open scribe sets, and degraded image quality. We present TextileNet, a fully convolutional multi-task network trained exclusively on synthetic data to produce dense pixel-level texture embeddings, which we transfer zeroshot to historical manuscript analysis. As an original contribution to evaluation methodology, we designed a paleographic visual quiz of 80 pair and triplet questions and administered it to a range from lay participants to senior paleographers under strict anonymity, establishing to our knowledge for the first time a human baseline for script-style discrimination on late medieval text. We employ TextileNet embeddings to perform zero-shot retrieval on sub-word granularity for hand and gender identification. Our experimental results help in building the credibility of TextileNet in the paleographic domain, but more than that demonstrate in experimental terms that the question of gender in handwriting needs to be treated with caution.

AI.tldr: TextileNet uses synthetic-data trained dense texture embeddings to enable zero-shot paleographic analysis on historical manuscripts, plus a novel human benchmark via an 80-item paleographic quiz; shows zero-shot hand/gender retrieval and cautions against inferring gender from handwriting.
AI.motivation: Overcome scarce labeled historical manuscript data, missing open scribe sets, and degraded image quality; create transferable, texture-focused features for paleography and establish a human baseline.
AI.method: Train a fully convolutional multi-task network on synthetic textures to produce dense pixel-level embeddings; transfer embeddings zero-shot to real historical manuscripts; evaluate via a novel paleographic quiz involving 80 pair/triplet questions; perform zero-shot retrieval at sub-word granularity for hand and gender identification.
AI.result: Embeddings enable zero-shot retrieval at sub-word granularity; empirical results support TextileNet’s credibility in paleography and highlight that gender inference from handwriting is not straightforward and should be treated with caution; introduces a human baseline for late medieval script discrimination.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic-data trained, zero-shot transferable textile texture embeddings can advance paleographic analysis; evaluation methodology with a human baseline strengthens credibility; gender-related conclusions from handwriting require cautious interpretation.

title: COAST: Context-Aware Differential Learning for Gene Expression Prediction in Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial transcriptomics enables profiling of spatial gene expression but is limited by high cost and low throughput, motivating prediction from H&E histopathology images. Existing context-aware methods mainly supervise absolute expression, while relative expression relationships between spots are rarely used explicitly. We propose COAST, a context-aware differential learning framework for spatial gene expression prediction. COAST conditions the local and global context features with type-specific modulation and aggregates the target and context spot tokens using a Transformer encoder to capture both fine-grained local patterns and slide-level structure. It is trained with a joint objective that combines absolute expression regression with signed differential regression between the target and context spots. Experiments on multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets show consistent improvements in correlation- and distribution-based metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of context-aware differential learning for histology-based spatial gene expression prediction.

AI.tldr: COAST introduces context-aware differential learning for histology-based spatial gene expression prediction by fusing target and context spots with a Transformer, using type-specific modulation for local/global context, and jointly optimizing absolute expression and signed differential relations.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly; leveraging H&E images to predict gene expression requires exploiting relational structure between spots, particularly differences between target and context spots, beyond absolute expression alone.
AI.method: COAST modulates local/global context features via type-specific conditioning, aggregates target and context spot tokens with a Transformer encoder to capture local and slide-level structure, and trains with a joint objective combining absolute expression regression and signed differential regression between target and context spots.
AI.result: Across multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets, COAST yields consistent improvements in correlation- and distribution-based evaluation metrics, demonstrating the benefit of context-aware differential learning for histology-driven spatial gene expression prediction.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware differential learning with transformer-based fusion and signed differential objectives is an effective framework for improving histology-based spatial gene expression prediction.

title: From Classification to Localization and Clinical Validation: Large-Scale Development of a Deep Learning System for Thoracic Disease Detection on Chest Radiographs in Thailand
summary: Chest radiography (CXR) remains the most widely used thoracic imaging modality, yet expert interpretation is constrained by a severe shortage of radiologists in Thailand and across Southeast Asia. Local adaptation of deep learning models to Thai data has been shown to substantially improve accuracy on Thai populations. Here we present the development and comprehensive validation of the chest radiograph analysis model in Inspectra CXR version 5, a deep learning system that performs multi-label thoracic disease classification and weakly supervised lesion localization within a single model. The architecture couples a DenseNet-121 backbone with Attend-and-Compare Modules (ACM) and a Probabilistic Class Activation Map (PCAM) aggregation layer, producing a per-condition classification score and heatmap simultaneously. The model was developed on 874,858 frontal chest radiographs with paired radiologist reports from Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok. On a held-out, radiologist-verified in-domain test set of 19,871 cases, it achieved a mean AUROC of 0.994 (mean sensitivity 92.4%, specificity 98.6%) across nine clinically important conditions. On an independent generalization set of 5,992 cases from 13 hospitals across Thailand, the mean AUROC was 0.970, indicating robust transfer across sites. For localization, evaluated on 4,549 radiologist-annotated cases, the model attained a mean lesion-localization fraction (LLF) of 77.9% at 0.59 non-lesion localizations per image. In a usability evaluation with five thoracic radiologists, the system reached a classification concordance of 93.6%, a localization concordance of 94.7%, and a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 89. These results indicate that a locally developed, localization-capable CXR system can deliver high accuracy, generalize across heterogeneous Thai hospitals, and earn the trust of practicing radiologists.

AI.tldr: Large-scale Thai-domain chest X-ray AI with localization; high accuracy and generalization; strong radiologist acceptance.
AI.motivation: Address radiologist shortage and variability in Southeast Asia by developing a locally trained, localization-enabled CXR AI that can improve accuracy on Thai populations and provide explainable localization.
AI.method: DenseNet-121 backbone with Attend-and-Compare Modules (ACM) and Probabilistic Class Activation Map (PCAM) aggregation. Multi-label classification for nine conditions with weakly supervised lesion localization. Trained on 874,858 frontal CXRs with paired radiologist reports from Siriraj Hospital; evaluated on a held-out in-domain test set (19,871 cases) and an independent Thai-wide generalization set (5,992 cases from 13 hospitals). Localization evaluated on 4,549 radiologist-annotated cases. Usability tested with five radiologists.
AI.result: In-domain AUROC 0.994 (sensitivity 92.4%, specificity 98.6%) across nine conditions; independent Thai hospitals AUROC 0.970. Localization: LLF 77.9% at 0.59 non-lesion localizations per image. Usability: classification concordance 93.6%, localization concordance 94.7%, SUS 89.
AI.conclusion: A locally developed, localization-capable CXR system demonstrates high accuracy, robust cross-site generalization within Thailand, and high radiologist trust, suggesting value for deployment to support radiologist workflows in resource-constrained settings.

title: Understanding Schedule-Free Methods in Nonconvex Optimization: Rate Guarantees and Escaping Saddles
summary: Schedule-Free methods have attracted growing interest for alleviating the burden of designing and tuning a learning rate scheduler, while matching and sometimes even outperforming optimizers with tuned schedulers. Despite their strong empirical results, their convergence theory in nonconvex optimization, where modern machine learning objectives typically arise, has remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we provide worst-case analyses of Schedule-Free gradient descent and Schedule-Free stochastic gradient descent, in their standard form and without auxiliary modifications or restrictive conditions, for smooth but possibly nonconvex objectives. Based on a Lyapunov analysis derived from the continuous-time limiting ordinary differential equation associated with these methods, we show that Schedule-Free gradient descent and Schedule-Free stochastic gradient descent achieve the optimal worst-case convergence rates attainable among first-order methods. We further formulate Schedule-Free gradient descent as a nonautonomous dynamical system and prove strict-saddle avoidance under an arbitrarily small one-time perturbation. These theoretical results provide a better understanding of the strong performance that Schedule-Free methods demonstrate.

AI.tldr: Schedule-Free GD/SGD achieve optimal worst-case rates among first-order methods for smooth nonconvex objectives, via Lyapunov analysis from a continuous-time ODE limit; they form a nonautonomous dynamical system that exhibits strict-saddle avoidance with a tiny one-time perturbation, explaining strong empirical performance.
AI.motivation: Address the theoretical gap for Schedule-Free optimization methods, which avoid learning-rate scheduling yet perform competitively; nonconvex optimization convergence theory for these methods is underdeveloped.
AI.method: Lyapunov analysis derived from the continuous-time limit ODE of Schedule-Free methods; formalization of Schedule-Free GD as a nonautonomous dynamical system; proof of strict-saddle avoidance under an arbitrarily small one-time perturbation.
AI.result: Establish optimal worst-case convergence rates among first-order methods for smooth nonconvex objectives; prove strict-saddle avoidance under a negligible perturbation.
AI.conclusion: Theoretical results illuminate why Schedule-Free methods perform well in practice and extend understanding of nonconvex optimization without learning-rate schedules.

title: Dynamic Inverse Rendering for Enhanced Material-Lighting Decomposition
comment: Accepted at ECCV 2026. Project page: https://razayunus.github.io/DIR
summary: Decomposing outgoing surface radiance into material and illumination during inverse rendering is essential for applications such as relighting and augmented reality, yet it is severely ill-posed since multiple combinations can result in the same observed colour. Capturing an object under multiple lighting conditions usually helps resolve this ambiguity as it constrains the optimization towards correct solutions. In this work, we explore the potential of reconstructing rigidly moving objects -- which provides observations of diverse light-surface interactions -- to resolve the material-lighting ambiguity in inverse rendering. For this purpose, we introduce a relightable approach that marries object tracking and reconstruction with inverse rendering for general rigidly moving objects. Our experimental analysis on synthetic data demonstrates that motion can be an advantage for disentangling material and lighting: the reconstructed material is significantly more accurate when the object is observed under rigid motion than when it is static. Moreover, results on RGB videos of real hand-held objects show that our pipeline preserves this advantage even under noisy real-world conditions.

AI.tldr: Relightable inverse rendering for rigidly moving objects to resolve material-lighting ambiguity; motion improves material estimation and is robust to real-world noise.
AI.motivation: Inverse rendering is ill-posed: many material-illumination pairs produce the same observed radiance. Observing an object under multiple lighting helps, but exploiting motion–induced diverse light-surface interactions may provide additional constraints.
AI.method: A relightable framework that integrates object tracking and reconstruction with inverse rendering for general rigidly moving objects, enabling joint estimation of material and illumination across motion.
AI.result: On synthetic data, rigid motion yields significantly more accurate material estimates than static observation. On real RGB videos of hand-held objects, the advantage persists despite noise.
AI.conclusion: Motion provides valuable, additional cues for disentangling material and lighting in inverse rendering, improving material reconstruction under both synthetic and real-world conditions.

title: Application of machine learning to monster level prediction in tabletop RPG game design
summary: Designing balanced adversaries is a central but labor-intensive task in tabletop role-playing game (TTRPG) development. In systems such as Pathfinder, each monster is described by many numerical attributes that jointly determine its power, summarized as an ordinal level. We investigate whether machine learning can support designers by predicting this level from a monster's attributes, framing the task as tabular ordinal regression. We introduce what is, to our knowledge, the first dataset built specifically for TTRPG monster-level prediction, derived from publicly available Pathfinder Second Edition data. Using it, we compare classical regression models with rounding schemes, dedicated tabular ordinal regression algorithms, and neural networks with ordinal-aware losses. To mirror real design workflows, we evaluate all models under chronological and expanding-window protocols with several complementary metrics. Results show that tree-based ensembles outperform linear models and neural approaches, achieving near-perfect ordinal ranking and high predictive accuracy. Explainable AI analyses, such as feature importance and error distributions, show that the model is aligned with human intuition and follows patterns grounded in game rules. Together, these results show that machine learning can reliably approximate designer judgments and serve as an effective computer-aided tool for monster balancing and broader TTRPG system design.

AI.tldr: Dataset for predicting TTRPG monster level from attributes; tree ensembles best at ordinal ranking, suggesting ML can aid monster balancing.
AI.motivation: Reduce labor and subjectivity in balancing TTRPG monsters by predicting canonical level from attributes, enabling designer-aided workflows.
AI.method: Create a Pathfinder Second Edition-derived dataset for monster attributes and ordinal level; compare classical regression with rounding, ordinal regression algorithms, and neural networks; evaluate under chronological/ expanding-window protocols with multiple metrics; include explainability analyses.
AI.result: Tree-based ensembles achieve near-perfect ordinal ranking and high accuracy, outperforming linear and neural baselines; explanations align with human/game-rule intuition.
AI.conclusion: ML can reliably approximate designer judgments for monster balancing and can serve as an effective computer-aided design tool for TTRPG systems.

title: Simon-SR: Spatially Adaptive Modulation and Visual Prompt Adaptation for Text-Reinforced Super-Resolution
summary: Single Image Super-Resolution (SISR) reconstructs high-quality images from low-resolution inputs. While recent multi-modal methods improve perceptual quality, they remain sensitive to erroneous priors and require expensive annotations. To address these issues, we propose Simon-SR, a multi-modal SISR framework leveraging learnable prompts for efficient semantic mining and robust text-image fusion. Our approach combines Contrastive Prompt Learning with Prompt-Guided Spatially Adaptive Refinement to enhance multi-modal alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Simon-SR surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving maximum improvements of 0.50 dB in PSNR, 0.0133 in SSIM, and 0.0695 in LPIPS. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: A learnable-prompt multi-modal SISR framework (Simon-SR) that boosts image reconstruction quality by aligning text and image features and adaptively refining high-resolution outputs using prompts.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal SISR methods often rely on expensive annotations and are sensitive to incorrect priors. There is a need for efficient semantic mining and robust text-image fusion.
AI.method: Integrates Contrastive Prompt Learning with Prompt-Guided Spatially Adaptive Refinement to achieve improved multi-modal alignment and detail refinement in SISR.
AI.result: Reported state-of-the-art gains: PSNR up to +0.50 dB, SSIM up by +0.0133, LPIPS reduced by 0.0695. Claims superior performance on benchmarks; code will be released.
AI.conclusion: Simon-SR presents an effective, annotation-efficient framework for multi-modal SISR and promises practical release of code for reproducibility.

title: Interference and Retention in Continual Learning
summary:
Continual learning commonly relies on post-hoc mechanisms such as replay, elastic regularization, or distillation. This work argues that forgetting should instead be modeled directly as interference between tasks. In the frozen-feature regime, forgetting from learning a new task is exactly the interference energy induced on the old task. In deep networks, the same quantity is recovered through path-averaged curvature with minimal additional forward passes.
  When task supports are disjoint, forgetting can be eliminated structurally and when task supports overlap in conflicting directions, a non-zero distortion floor is unavoidable. The same geometry optimally merges models through task-aware orthogonalization. From this analysis we derive Interference-Gated Functional Allocation (IGFA), a replay-free, Fisher-free method that shares directions when tasks align and protects them when they conflict. Across benchmarks, IGFA achieves lossless retention when tasks are structurally separable and moves unavoidable cost from irreversible forgetting into deferred but recoverable plasticity when they are not. It matches the strongest replay-free structural baselines on dissimilar-task streams and improves on unconditional projection when similarity makes transfer worth preserving.

AI.tldr: Models forgetting as task interference and introduces IGFA, a replay-free, Fisher-free method that uses task-aware orthogonalization to share directions when tasks align and protect them when they conflict; achieves lossless retention for structurally separable tasks and recovers plasticity for overlapping tasks.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc replay/regularization methods are limited; forgetting can be understood as interference energy. In frozen-feature regimes, this energy equals forgetting; path-averaged curvature in deep networks captures this with few extra forward passes. Structurally separable tasks allow elimination of forgetting; conflicting directions impose a non-zero distortion floor. The work seeks a geometric, model-agnostic allocation mechanism.
AI.method: Theoretical interference-energy analysis; derive Interference-Gated Functional Allocation (IGFA); implement a replay-free, Fisher-free scheme that shares directions when tasks align and protects them when they conflict via task-aware orthogonalization. Uses path-averaged curvature concepts to guide allocation with minimal forward passes.
AI.result: IGFA achieves lossless retention when task supports are structurally separable; converts unavoidable forgetting into recoverable plasticity when supports overlap. It matches the strongest replay-free structural baselines on dissimilar-task streams and improves on unconditional projection when transfer is valuable.
AI.conclusion: IGFA provides a principled, geometry-driven continual-learning framework that reduces reliance on replay and Fisher-based constraints. Its performance depends on task support structure: perfect retention for separable tasks, recoverable forgetting for overlapping tasks, with a distortion floor unavoidable in conflicting directions.

title: CtrlVTON: Controllable Virtual Try-On via Visual-Instance-Prompt Segmentation
summary: Virtual try-on (VTO) has made significant progress in realistically transferring garments onto a target person. Yet most systems give the user little control over how a garment should be worn -- its size (loose or fitted), style (e.g., tucked in or untucked, open or closed), and spatial placement on the body. We address this gap with two complementary contributions. First, we define and solve Visual-Instance-Prompt Segmentation via VIP-SAM: given a flatlay image of a garment, segment that specific instance in a photograph of a person wearing it. This is an instance-level task, distinct from the typically studied category-level segmentation. Second, we introduce CtrlVTON, a controllable VTO framework that recasts try-on as an image editing problem and adds segmentation masks as pixel-level control over garment layout, including style, size, and spatial placement on the body. VIP-SAM and CtrlVTON each achieve state-of-the-art results on their respective tasks. In particular, CtrlVTON generates images that follow user-provided layouts far more faithfully than the strongest proprietary editing systems while matching them on garment fidelity.

AI.tldr: Introduce VIP-SAM for instance-level garment segmentation and CtrlVTON for controllable VTO via pixel-level masks; both achieve state-of-the-art; CtrlVTON preserves user layouts better than competing editors while maintaining garment fidelity.
AI.motivation: VTO lacks user-controllable garment wearing aspects (size, style, spatial placement); need instance-level segmentation and editing-driven control.
AI.method: VIP-SAM: Visual-Instance-Prompt Segmentation to segment a specific garment instance using a prompt; operates on flatlay garment to locate it in a person image. CtrlVTON: Recasts try-on as image editing and uses segmentation masks as pixel-level layout controls (style, size, placement).
AI.result: Both VIP-SAM and CtrlVTON achieve state-of-the-art on their tasks; CtrlVTON more faithfully follows user layouts than strongest proprietary editors while matching garment fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Presents complementary tools: an instance-level segmentation method for garments and a controllable VTO framework enabling precise user-directed garment layout control.

title: Temporal Knowledge Graph Forecasting under Distribution Shifts: A Synthetic Evaluation
summary: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) represent evolving relational systems, whose underlying data-generating processes often change over time. Yet, TKG forecasting models are commonly evaluated only on empirical benchmark datasets that provide limited insight into the models' robustness to such distribution shifts. Recognising this issue, we study TKG forecasting under controlled shift environments using a synthetic TKG generator that encodes three temporal and structural properties -- recurrence, homophily, and periodicity -- as data-generating mechanisms. This allows us to evaluate seven forecasting architectures under stationary and shifting regimes. Our experiments suggest that robustness in TKG forecasting is highly signal-dependent. Recurrence-based and periodic regularities are largely recoverable under stationary conditions, and simple memory-based baselines can be competitive when recurrence dominates the data. However, structural breaks reveal limitations in model adaptivity, with shifts in latent entity-community structure posing the strongest challenge in our study. Overall, our findings improve the understanding of the capabilities and limitations of current TKG models confronted with temporal distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: Synthetic evaluation of TKG forecasting under distribution shifts using a generator that encodes recurrence, homophily, and periodicity to compare seven models across stationary and shifting regimes; robustness is highly signal-dependent; recurrence/periodicity recoverable under stationarity; memory-based baselines strong when recurrence dominates; structural breaks, especially shifts in latent entity-community structure, challenge models; insights for robust TKG evaluation.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of understanding of how temporal distribution shifts affect TKG forecasting, and to disentangle how different temporal/structural signals (recurrence, homophily, periodicity) influence model robustness.
AI.method: Introduce a synthetic TKG generator that encodes three properties (recurrence, homophily, periodicity) as data-generating mechanisms. Generate data under stationary and shifting regimes, and evaluate seven forecasting architectures on the tasks of link/edge prediction over time, analyzing robustness to distribution shifts and adaptivity to structural breaks, with a focus on latent community structure changes.
AI.result: Robustness in TKG forecasting is highly signal-dependent. Recurrence-based and periodic regularities are largely recoverable under stationary conditions; simple memory-based baselines can be competitive when recurrence dominates. Structural breaks reveal limitations in model adaptivity, with shifts in latent entity-community structure posing the strongest challenge. Overall, the study clarifies capabilities and limitations of current TKG models when faced with temporal distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: The work advances understanding of TKG model robustness under temporal shifts, highlighting the importance of signal composition (recurrence, homophily, periodicity) and the need for models that adapt to structural breaks and evolving community structure; it informs more realistic benchmarking of TKG forecasting under distributional shifts.

title: SVF-CR: Synchronized Visual-Facial Cross-Refinement for Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition
summary: Ambivalence and hesitancy are subtle behavioral states that are expressed through a combination of verbal content, facial behavior, visual context, and acoustic cues. Effective recognition therefore requires not only extracting informative unimodal representations, but also modeling how temporally aligned behavioral evidence interacts across modalities. In this paper, we propose a synchronized visual-facial cross-refinement framework (SVF-CR) with pairwise multimodal evidence fusion for ambivalence and hesitancy recognition. The proposed method first extracts whole-video segment tokens and cropped-face segment tokens using the same temporal partition. The synchronized visual and facial tokens are refined through intra-modal self-attention and bidirectional visual-facial cross-attention, allowing whole-video context and local facial behavior to mutually refine each other before evidence construction. We then construct segment-level visual-facial evidence using consistency and discrepancy modeling, followed by temporal self-attention and attention pooling. Textual and acoustic features are lightly refined through context self-attention and are fused with the enhanced visual-facial evidence at the final decision stage using pairwise evidence fusion. Experiments on the BAH (Behavioral Ambivalence/Hesitancy) public evaluation split show that the proposed synchronized visual-facial cross-refinement improves public macro-F1 over both global visual-face token fusion and synchronized evidence baselines, achieving a public macro-F1 of 0.7156. Code is available at : https://github.com/hiinnnii/BAH-Challenge-ECCV2026\_SVF-CR.

AI.tldr: A synchronized visual-facial cross-refinement (SVF-CR) framework with pairwise multimodal evidence fusion improves ambivalence and hesitancy recognition by refining whole-video and facial tokens via intra-modal and bidirectional cross-attention, constructing segment-level visual-facial evidence through consistency/discrepancy modeling, and fusing with textual and acoustic cues, achieving a macro-F1 of 0.7156 on the BAH evaluation dataset.
AI.motivation: Ambivalence/hesitancy recognition requires integrated temporal context across modalities. Unimodal or naive fusion misses the interactions between full-video cues and localized facial behavior; synchronized cross-refinement can better capture inter-modal relationships.
AI.method: 1) Partition video into segments and extract whole-video tokens and cropped-face tokens with the same temporal partition. 2) Refine tokens via intra-modal self-attention and bidirectional visual-facial cross-attention to allow global context and local facial cues to mutually refine. 3) Build segment-level visual-facial evidence using consistency and discrepancy modeling, followed by temporal self-attention and attention pooling. 4) Lightly refine textual and acoustic features with context self-attention; finally fuse with enhanced visual-facial evidence via pairwise evidence fusion.
AI.result: On the BAH public evaluation split, SVF-CR improves macro-F1 to 0.7156, outperforming global visual-face token fusion and synchronized evidence baselines.
AI.conclusion: Synchronized cross-refinement of visual and facial tokens, along with segment-level evidence construction and pairwise fusion with text/audio cues, yields improved ambivalence/hesitancy recognition. Code is available at the provided repository.

title: All you need is SAMPAT
summary: The current state of the art in AI/ML rests on deep neural architectures, which, in general, suffer from a lack of interpretability. Interpretability is crucial to gleaning insights while analyzing experimental data, where quantitative predictions may not be adequate for a scientist. We present a three layer neural architecture, SAMPAT (Smooth Approximation via Multivariate Polynomials and Analytic Transformations), that can provably learn a continuous, everywhere differentiable function, that can approximate any smooth function arbitrarily closely. SAMPAT's approximant can be expressed as a closed and compact algebraic, analytic expression, providing complete interpretability. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets indicate that SAMPAT yields competitive performance with simpler representations. For many tasks, a two layer SAMPAT suffices. By imposing restrictions on the connectivity between neurons, SAMPAT may be used to provide a range of approximants, including regular and trigonometric polynomials, rational expressions, Gaussians, mixtures of Gaussians, as well as arbitrary combinations of the same; without restrictions, it learns a suitable structure. SAMPAT may be used to factorize polynomials and model nonlinear systems. With the addition of skip connections, a 4 to 6 layer SAMPAT is adequate to represent a substantive range of methods widely used in AI/ML, allowing the choice of a model's family, not just its parameters, to also be optimized as part of the learning process.

AI.tldr: Proposes SAMPAT, a three-layer neural architecture that provably learns a continuous, everywhere-differentiable approximant for any smooth function, expressed as a closed analytic form for interpretability; architecture supports various function families via connectivity constraints; demonstrates competitive performance with simpler representations; deeper variants with skip connections extend expressiveness to include common ML models.
AI.motivation: Address the interpretability gap in deep learning by providing closed-form, interpretable approximants with universal approximation capabilities; enable explicit control over the function family through architectural constraints.
AI.method: Introduce SAMPAT, a three-layer network whose differentiable, closed-form approximant can approximate any smooth function. By constraining neuron connectivity, it can realize regular/trigonometric polynomials, rational expressions, Gaussians, mixtures, or arbitrary combinations; without constraints, it learns flexible structures. A two-layer SAMPAT often suffices; adding skip connections yields 4–6 layers to cover a broader class of models. It also supports polynomial factorization and nonlinear system modeling.
AI.result: Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets show competitive performance with simpler representations, while providing complete interpretability via the closed-form analytic expression. In many tasks, a two-layer configuration suffices; the framework supports a spectrum of model families through connectivity choices; deeper variants with skip connections expand expressiveness.
AI.conclusion: SAMPAT offers an interpretable, universally approximating neural architecture with tunable expressiveness through connectivity, enabling selection of the model family as part of learning. It supports polynomial factorization and nonlinear system modeling; skip-connected versions extend to broader ML model classes.

title: Multimodal Scenario Similarity Search for Autonomous Driving
summary: Large-scale autonomous-driving datasets contain vast numbers of recorded scenarios, creating a need for efficient retrieval methods that can identify situations similar to a given query. Existing approaches typically rely on either visual representations or motion-based descriptions, making it difficult to understand their relative strengths and limitations for scenario retrieval. In this work, we present a multimodal framework for autonomous-driving scenario retrieval that combines visual and trajectory-based representations within a unified retrieval pipeline. We investigate two trajectory-based approaches: Exo-Trajectory, an explicit matching method based on surrounding-agent motion, and ScenarioFormer, a transformer-based representation learned from object trajectories using contrastive learning. We compare these approaches against strong vision-based baselines and analyze their behavior across a diverse set of driving scenarios. Experimental results show that trajectory representations provide strong retrieval performance for motion-centric events such as cut-ins, turning maneuvers, and traffic queueing, while visual embeddings excel when appearance cues are informative. Most importantly, combining visual and trajectory information consistently improves retrieval quality, yielding the best overall performance. These findings demonstrate that appearance and motion capture are complementary notions of scenario similarity and motivate multimodal retrieval systems for autonomous-driving data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.

AI.tldr: A multimodal retrieval framework for autonomous-driving scenarios that fuses visual and trajectory-based representations. Two trajectory methods are proposed: Exo-Trajectory (explicit motion-based matching) and ScenarioFormer (Transformer-based trajectory representation via contrastive learning). The framework is evaluated against vision baselines; trajectory data excels for motion-centric events, visuals for appearance cues, and multimodal fusion yields the best overall performance.
AI.motivation: Existing scenario retrieval methods typically rely on a single modality (vision or motion). There is a need to understand the complementary strengths and limitations of visual vs. trajectory representations in large-scale autonomous-driving datasets, and to develop efficient, accurate multimodal retrieval.
AI.method: A unified retrieval pipeline that integrates visual embeddings with trajectory-based representations. Two trajectory approaches are studied: (1) Exo-Trajectory, an explicit matching method using surrounding-agent motion; (2) ScenarioFormer, a transformer-based representation learned from object trajectories via contrastive learning. The methods are compared against strong vision-based baselines across diverse driving scenarios, with evaluation on retrieval quality.
AI.result: Trajectory-based representations perform strongly for motion-centric events (e.g., cut-ins, turns, queueing), while visual embeddings better capture appearance-informative cues. Importantly, fusing visual and trajectory information consistently improves retrieval performance, achieving the best overall results.
AI.conclusion: Appearance and motion capture are complementary notions of scenario similarity. Multimodal retrieval systems are advantageous for autonomous-driving data mining, dataset curation, and scenario-based validation.

title: Forget Narrowly, Retain Broadly: Unlearning as an Asymmetric Generalization Problem
summary: Machine unlearning in LLMs is the targeted removal of specific knowledge while preserving all other capabilities, critical for privacy and safety. Yet existing benchmarks measure it unreliably. They miss knowledge that resurfaces under paraphrased or indirect queries, a failure we call under-forgetting, and lack the semantic, syntactic, and lexical probes needed to verify that unrelated knowledge is preserved, a failure we call over-forgetting. Both failures reflect an asymmetric generalization problem. Forget evaluation must cover diverse query formulations of the same target facts, testing whether forgetting holds beyond exact training prompts. Retain evaluation must probe a far larger and implicitly defined set, namely every fact disjoint from the forget target. The retain set thus defines the effective forget set, yet current datasets provide no fine-grained annotation of this forget-retain boundary. We address this with SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that captures forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains. Methods trained on SUITE improve substantially, showing that training data is as important as algorithmic design. Building on the obtained insights, we introduce JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm that achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs, in both sequential and joint unlearning settings. Code and datasets are available at https://amitpeleg.github.io/forget-narrowly-retain-broadly

AI.tldr: Introduces SUITE for evaluating and training LLM unlearning with forget-retain structure; proposes JensUn++; shows improved forget-retain utility across LLMs.
AI.motivation: Current unlearning benchmarks are unreliable and miss under-forgetting and over-forgetting. There is a need to evaluate forgetting across diverse query formulations and for unknown, implicitly defined retain sets to ensure privacy and safety.
AI.method: Presents SUITE, an evaluation protocol and training corpus that captures forget-retain structure for real-world factual domains; introduces JensUn++, an unlearning algorithm; assesses performance on three LLMs in sequential and joint unlearning settings; analyzes the impact of training data.
AI.result: Methods trained on SUITE show substantial improvement; JensUn++ achieves the best forget-retain utility trade-off across three LLMs in multiple settings; code and datasets released.
AI.conclusion: Data-centric design (curated training data capturing forget-retain structure) is crucial, on par with algorithmic advances; SUITE provides a reusable benchmark and systematic approach to robust unlearning in LLMs.

title: Parameter-Efficient Vision-Language Adaptation with Continuous Metadata Conditioning for Animal Re-Identification
comment: This is the author's version of the paper accepted for publication in Expert Systems with Applications. The final authenticated version will be available from the publisher
summary: Long-term animal re-identification (ReID) must remain robust to gradual morphological evolution and seasonal appearance shifts. Although recent vision-language models provide strong pretrained visual representations, adapting them to longitudinal ecological settings remains challenging, particularly under identity and temporal distribution shifts. We present a parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation framework for animal ReID and introduce a continuous metadata-conditioning mechanism that incorporates numerical attributes directly into the prompt representation during training. While low-rank visual adaptation, prompt-based supervision, and cross-modal alignment provide the adaptation framework, the proposed metadata-conditioning strategy constitutes the primary methodological contribution. By preserving the continuous structure of numerical metadata rather than discretizing it into textual categories, the proposed approach enables smooth modulation of the embedding space during training while maintaining a purely visual inference pipeline. Experiments on a seven-year longitudinal fish dataset and multiple wildlife benchmarks demonstrate improved performance under closed-set, open-set, and time-aware evaluation protocols. The results demonstrate that continuous metadata conditioning improves robustness to longitudinal appearance variation and temporal distribution shifts, while parameter-efficient adaptation enables a purely visual inference pipeline without requiring metadata at test time. Code and evaluation splits can be found at: https://github.com/AnilOsmanTur/MetaPrompt-ReID.

AI.tldr: A parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation for long-term animal re-identification leveraging continuous numerical metadata conditioning in prompts to handle longitudinal appearance changes; achieves robustness across closed-set, open-set, and time-aware settings without requiring test-time metadata.
AI.motivation: Long-term re-identification must cope with gradual morphology evolution and seasonal appearance shifts. Adapting vision-language models to ecological longitudinal data poses identity and temporal distribution shifts while preserving a purely visual test-time pipeline.
AI.method: A framework combining low-rank visual adaptation, prompt-based supervision, and cross-modal alignment, with a continuous metadata-conditioning mechanism that injects numerical attributes into the prompt representation during training while preserving continuous metadata rather than discretizing it; enables smooth embedding modulation and a purely visual inference pipeline at test time.
AI.result: Improved performance on a seven-year longitudinal fish dataset and multiple wildlife benchmarks under closed-set, open-set, and time-aware evaluations; continuous metadata conditioning enhances robustness to longitudinal variation and distribution shifts; parameter-efficient adaptation allows a purely visual inference pipeline without test-time metadata.
AI.conclusion: Continuous metadata conditioning is the primary methodological contribution, enabling smooth modulation of the embedding space during training while avoiding test-time metadata, and demonstrating strong robustness in long-term ReID tasks; code available at the stated repository.

title: LionVote: Per-Layer Learning Rate Adaptation for Lion
summary: Per-layer diagnostics reveal that, at the prescribed learning rate, Lion's effective scale is 2.6-2.8x too high for attention and MLP parameters and ~2x too high for normalization layers on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100; this 32% cross-layer-type disparity cannot be reproduced by a single global rate. The measurement comes from LionVote, a per-layer learning rate mechanism in which each parameter tensor maintains a compound level, a persistent integer updated every c epochs by two diagnostics (gradient direction stability and momentum health) resolved by a validation loss tiebreaker. Voting thresholds derive from geometric identities, the EMA time constant, and a noise-floor estimate; cadence is bounded structurally and selected by ablation. On ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, LionVote achieves 69.7% top-1 accuracy vs. Lion's 69.0% (p < 0.02, Welch's t-test) and AdamW's 68.8%. Per-layer adaptation value depends on both architectural heterogeneity and task; on uniform CNN architectures tuned SGD with cosine annealing remains dominant, and on ViT architectures gains are task-dependent.

AI.tldr: A per-layer learning-rate mechanism (LionVote) improves optimization by assigning per-tensor compound learning-rate levels updated periodically, addressing cross-layer disparities; shows small but consistent gains on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100 over Lion and AdamW.
AI.motivation: Global learning rates cannot capture heterogeneous dynamics across layers (attention/MLP vs normalization). Need per-layer adaptation to improve training efficiency and generalization.
AI.method: Introduce LionVote: each tensor has a persistent integer 'compound level' updated every c epochs based on gradient direction stability and momentum health, resolved by validation loss. Voting thresholds derived from geometric identities, EMA time constant, and a noise-floor estimate. Cadence is structurally bounded and ablated. Evaluate on ViT-Tiny with CIFAR-100 and compare to Lion and AdamW.
AI.result: LionVote achieves 69.7% top-1 on ViT-Tiny/CIFAR-100, versus 69.0% for Lion and 68.8% for AdamW; p<0.02 (Welch's t-test). Per-layer adaptation values depend on architecture and task; across uniform CNNs tuned SGD with cosine annealing remains competitive; gains for ViT are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Per-layer adaptation via LionVote yields cross-layer-type disparities with effective scale adjustments; per-layer LR strategies can yield modest but robust gains with architectural-dependent behavior; not universally superior across all tasks/architectures.

title: Robustifying Vision-Language Models via Test-Time Prompt Adaptation
summary: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot generalization, but their performance degrades sharply under adversarial perturbations. Existing test-time adaptation methods typically rely on sample-level confidence heuristics, overlooking the intrinsic distributional structure of the data. This sample-centric approach limits robustness, as it fails to distinguish confident adversarial mispredictions from true semantic consistency. In this work, we observe that adversarial distortion is structurally brittle: while holistic representations are corrupted, semantic integrity is often preserved in the distribution of augmented views. Motivated by this insight, we propose RITA, a Robust test-tIme prompt-TAdaptation framework that shifts from sample-level estimates to distribution-level alignment. Specifically, RITA employs optimal transport to align the distribution of augmented visual features with textual prototypes, mitigating adversarial outliers and rectifying cross-modal semantic misalignment. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic cache to progressively accumulate reliable cues from the test stream for online refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RITA significantly improves adversarial robustness without compromising clean accuracy.

AI.tldr: RITA is a robust test-time adaptation method for vision–language models that uses distribution-level alignment via optimal transport between augmented visual features and textual prototypes, plus a dynamic test-stream cache, to improve adversarial robustness with minimal impact on clean accuracy.
