AI.motivation: Sample-level confidence heuristics in test-time adaptation fail to capture the distributional structure of data under adversarial perturbations; holistic features are brittle while semantic information remains in the data distribution across augmented views.
AI.method: Replace sample-wise confidence with distribution-level alignment by solving an optimal-transport problem between augmented visual-feature distributions and textual prototypes; update a dynamic test-time cache to progressively collect reliable cues for online refinement of prompts/adapters.
AI.result: Empirical evidence shows substantially improved adversarial robustness of pre-trained VLMs (e.g., CLIP-like models) with negligible or no degradation in clean accuracy, compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from sample-centric to distribution-centric test-time adaptation with OT alignment and online caching yields robust performance of vision–language models under adversarial perturbations.

title: Autoregressive latent diffusion for 3D molecule generation
summary: Three-dimensional (3D) molecule generation has been dominated by diffusion models, which achieve strong generation quality but typically require the molecular size to be specified a priori. Recent autoregressive approaches have substantially narrowed the performance gap while naturally supporting variable-length generation and conditioning on partial molecular context. However, balancing unconditional and context-conditioned generation remains challenging. We introduce KRONOS, a latent autoregressive diffusion framework that generates molecules in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, jointly modeling molecular graph topology and geometry, while retaining the flexibility of autoregressive generation. We further introduce a mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the Middle (FIM) paradigm, enabling both unconditional and fragment-conditioned molecular generation within a single left-to-right autoregressive model. Experiments on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs demonstrate that KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods, while remaining competitive with diffusion models. Moreover, fragment-conditioned generation is achieved with negligible impact on unconditional generation performance, demonstrating that both generation paradigms can be supported within a single architecture.

AI.tldr: KRONOS presents a latent autoregressive diffusion model operating in the latent space of a pre-trained 3D molecular autoencoder, enabling a single left-to-right model to perform both unconditional and fragment-conditioned generation; it achieves state-of-the-art unconditional performance among autoregressive methods and competitive results with diffusion models on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs.
AI.motivation: To combine the strengths of diffusion models (high-quality generation) with the flexibility of autoregressive schemes (variable-length and conditioning) while reducing the need to fix molecular size in advance; to model both topology and geometry jointly in 3D molecular generation.
AI.method: A latent autoregressive diffusion framework (KRONOS) that operates in the latent space of a pre-trained molecular autoencoder to jointly model graph topology and 3D geometry. A mixed training strategy inspired by Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) enables both unconditional and fragment-conditioned generation within a single left-to-right autoregressive model.
AI.result: Experiments on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs show that KRONOS achieves leading unconditional generation performance among autoregressive methods and remains competitive with diffusion models. Fragment-conditioned generation incurs negligible impact on unconditional generation performance, demonstrating that both capabilities can be supported within one architecture.
AI.conclusion: KRONOS demonstrates that a single latent-space autoregressive model can jointly support unconditional and fragment-conditioned 3D molecule generation with strong performance, balancing generation quality and conditioning flexibility while leveraging latent diffusion in a pre-trained autoencoder.

title: Super-Tuning: From Activation-Aware Pruning to Sparse Fine-Tuning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) remain expensive to fine-tune because full-parameter updates require substantial memory, compute, and per-task storage. We study whether saliency signals originally developed for pruning can be reused to choose where a model should adapt. We propose Super, a sparse parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method that fixes a small trainable support using a Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude score [Sun et al., 2023] computed from a calibration pass. We then introduce Supra, a hybrid adapter that combines this sparse update with LoRA while preserving a matched trainable-parameter budget through a simple budget-splitting rule. In single-seed Math17K arithmetic experiments on Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B, the best Super/Supra variants achieve the highest average accuracy among the tested schedule-selected adapter configurations. We also include a PaFi-style magnitude-only support as a closest training-free sparse baseline and find that low-score supports under both magnitude and Wanda-style orderings can be effective. These results suggest that simple pruning-inspired orderings can provide useful fixed sparse supports for PEFT, especially when combined with low-rank adapters.

AI.tldr: Super and Supra propose pruning-inspired sparse PEFT by fixing a small trainable support using Wanda-style activation-weighted magnitude scores and combining with LoRA; they outperform other adapter configurations on Math17K tasks in Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B.
AI.motivation: Reduce the cost of fine-tuning large language models by reusing saliency signals from pruning to guide where adaptation should occur, enabling fixed sparse supports and budget-aware hybrids.
AI.method: Introduce Super (sparse update with a fixed trainable support selected via activation-weighted magnitude scoring from a calibration pass) and Supra (a hybrid adapter that couples this sparse update with LoRA under a simple budget-splitting rule); compare against a PaFi-style magnitude-only sparse baseline; evaluate on single-seed Math17K arithmetic tasks using Llama-3.2-1B and Meta-Llama-3-8B; report average accuracy across schedule-selected adapters.
AI.result: Best Super/Supra variants achieve the highest average accuracy among the tested schedule-selected adapter configurations; low-score supports under both magnitude and Wanda-style orderings can be effective; PaFi-style magnitude-only supports are a close training-free baseline; overall, pruning-inspired orderings provide useful fixed sparse supports for PEFT, especially when combined with low-rank adapters.
AI.conclusion: Pruning-inspired sparse orderings can be effective fixed sparse supports for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, particularly when paired with low-rank adapters like LoRA to manage parameter budgets.

title: Foveation-Guided Dynamic Token Selection for Robust and Efficient Vision Transformers
summary: The human visual system (HVS) employs foveated sampling and eye movements to achieve efficient perception, conserving both metabolic energy and computational resources. Drawing inspiration from this robustness and adaptability, we introduce the Foveated Dynamic Transformer (FDT), a foveation-guided dynamic token-selection architecture that integrates these mechanisms into a vision transformer framework. The FDT exhibits strong resilience to various types of noise and adversarial attacks, despite not being explicitly trained for such challenges. This inherent robustness is achieved through the use of fixation and foveation modules: the fixation module identifies fixation points to filter out irrelevant information, while the foveation module generates foveated embeddings with multi-scale information. At the 50% fixation-budget setting, FDT achieves higher accuracy than DeiT-S (81.9% vs. 80.9%) while reducing multiply-accumulate operations by 34.57%, highlighting one operating point on its accuracy-efficiency trade-off. These attributes position FDT as an HVS-inspired step toward artificial neural networks that combine adaptive computation with improved resilience.

AI.tldr: A foveation-guided dynamic transformer (FDT) uses fixation and foveation to enable adaptive computation in vision transformers, achieving robustness and efficiency gains (e.g., 81.9% accuracy at 50% fixation-budget vs 80.9% for DeiT-S with a 34.57% MAC reduction).
AI.motivation: Emulate human visual efficiency and resilience by combining fixation-based filtering and multi-scale foveated embeddings to reduce computation without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Introduce FDT with a fixation module that selects fixation points to filter irrelevant information and a foveation module that produces multi-scale, foveated embeddings, enabling dynamic token selection within a ViT framework.
AI.result: At 50% fixation-budget, FDT outperforms DeiT-S (81.9% vs 80.9%) and reduces MAC by 34.57%; additionally, the model shows robustness to noise and adversarial attacks even without explicit training for such challenges.
AI.conclusion: FDT demonstrates an HVS-inspired approach that combines adaptive computation with enhanced resilience, representing a step toward efficient, robust vision models.

title: Risk-Aware General-Utility Markov Decision Processes
summary: We study general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) with risk-aware objectives. In this framework, an agent aims to optimize a risk measure of the distribution of objective values, where the objective function depends on the frequency of visitation of states induced by the agent's policy. First, we motivate, propose, and formalize risk-aware GUMDPs, which enable agents and decision makers to trade off expected performance by risk aversion while benefiting from the rich set of objectives that can be cast under the framework of GUMDPs. We focus our attention on the entropic risk measure (ERM). Second, we show how we can solve risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM objectives by resorting to online planning techniques. In particular, we propose an approach based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to provably solve risk-aware GUMDPs up to any desired accuracy. Third, we provide a set of experimental results showcasing that our approach is successful when optimizing for a spectrum of risk-aware behaviors in the context of GUMDPs under diverse tasks (standard MDPs, maximum state entropy exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs).

AI.tldr: Introduces risk-aware General-Utility MDPs (GUMDPs) with entropic risk measure (ERM), and provides a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based online planner to solve them with provable accuracy; demonstrates risk-sensitive behavior across various tasks.
AI.motivation: Enable trade-offs between expected performance and risk within the flexible GUMDP framework, allowing decision-makers and agents to adopt risk-averse behaviors while leveraging diverse objective formulations.
AI.method: Formalize risk-aware GUMDPs using ERM as the objective; develop an online planning approach based on Monte Carlo Tree Search that provably converges to within any desired accuracy; apply to standard MDPs, entropy-driven exploration, imitation learning, and multi-objective MDPs.
AI.result: A principled, provably convergent MCTS-based method for solving risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM, accompanied by experiments showing effective risk-sensitive behavior across a spectrum of tasks.
AI.conclusion: Risk-aware GUMDPs with ERM extend the GUMDP framework to incorporate risk preferences; the proposed MCTS-based planner provides theoretical guarantees and practical performance across diverse problem settings.

title: Decoupling Language Guidance from Backbones for Text-Guided Medical Segmentation
summary: Text-guided medical image segmentation leverages clinical semantics to improve lesion delineation, yet many existing models bind cross-modal fusion, supervision, and decoder design into a task-specific architecture. Such tight coupling makes it difficult to reuse language guidance modules across heterogeneous vision and text backbones, and often requires redesigning the network when the encoder pair changes. This paper presents BTHA, a backbone-transferable hierarchical adapter framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. BTHA is built around a stable feature-level interface: given multi-scale visual features and a text representation, it injects semantic guidance through shape-preserving adapters while maintaining the decoder-side tensor contract. To make this interface effective, we introduce a Hierarchical Coarse-to-Fine Supervision Strategy that decomposes learning into global image-text alignment, multi-scale auxiliary localization, and boundary-aware final mask refinement. We further design a Scale-Adaptive Gated Semantic Guidance (SAGSG) adapter, where resolution-specific gates adaptively control textual injection and channel recalibration suppresses redundant cross-modal responses. Evaluations across diverse vision and text backbones show that the same adapter and supervision design remains effective across convolutional and transformer-based visual encoders as well as different language encoders. Experiments on four public datasets further demonstrate that BTHA improves strong text-guided baselines with modest computational overhead.

AI.tldr: Backbone-transferable, hierarchical adapters enable text-guided medical image segmentation across diverse backbones with stable interface; achieves improvements with modest overhead.
AI.motivation: Current text-guided segmentation models tightly couple cross-modal fusion, supervision, and decoders to a specific architecture, hindering reuse of language guidance across backbones.
AI.method: Introduce BTHA: a feature-level interface with shape-preserving adapters injected into multi-scale visual features guided by text; Hierarchical Coarse-to-Fine Supervision (global alignment, multi-scale localization, boundary refinement); Scale-Adaptive Gated Semantic Guidance (SAGSG) adapter with resolution-specific gates and channel recalibration; designed to be compatible with various encoders and language models.
AI.result: Demonstrates effectiveness of the same adapter and supervision across convolutional and transformer vision encoders and different language encoders; improves strong text-guided baselines on four public datasets with modest computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: BTHA enables reusable, efficient, and effective text-guided segmentation across heterogeneous backbones, reducing architectural redesign needs while delivering performance gains.

title: SigLIP-HD by Fine-to-Coarse Supervision
summary: High-quality visual representation is a long-standing pursuit in computer vision. In the context of multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), feeding higher-resolution images can produce more fine-grained visual tokens. However, it introduces additional computational and design complexity, due to multiple forward passes and post-processing of increased tokens. Before simply adopting a higher resolution, have we truly unlocked the model's full perception capability at a standard resolution? Therefore, we study an interesting problem: how to achieve fine visual perception under lower cost without larger images. We present SigLIP-HD in this work. The core is a highly simple fine-to-coarse supervision design. We enforce the coarse feature of a mid-resolution image to mimic the fine-grained feature of its high-resolution version. We build this framework on the advanced SigLIP 2 model. Our final model produces better visual tokens at exactly the same inference budget. It is validated on extensive MLLM benchmarks and consistently delivers stronger results than our baseline model, especially on OCR-related tasks.

AI.tldr: Fine-to-coarse supervision to boost fine-grained visual perception at standard resolution, yielding better visual tokens at the same inference budget.
AI.motivation: Reduce computational cost of high-resolution inputs in multimodal LLMs while preserving fine-grained perception; questions whether higher resolution is necessary for full perception.
AI.method: A simple fine-to-coarse supervision that makes mid-resolution coarse features mimic the fine-grained features of a high-resolution image, built on SigLIP-2.
AI.result: Achieves better visual tokens at the same inference budget and consistently outperforms the baseline, especially on OCR-related tasks across extensive MLLM benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: High-quality perception can be attained without larger images via simple supervision; the approach is effective and may generalize beyond the base model.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Scalable and Transferable Node Centrality Approximation
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a learning-based framework for approximating graph quantities that are expensive to compute exactly. This paper investigates GNNs for scalable approximation of betweenness and closeness centrality, formulated as a node-ranking problem. Exact centrality values are used as supervision, and ranking quality is evaluated using Kendall's tau rank correlation. We study whether message-passing GNNs can learn transferable structural representations across different graph topologies rather than only fitting the distribution used during training. On unseen Erdos renyi graphs, the proposed models achieve tau = 0.851 for betweenness and tau = 0.894 for closeness. A large-scale betweenness model trained on graphs with N = 5,000 nodes achieves tau = 0.938, demonstrating scalability. Mixed-distribution training on Erdos renyi, Barabasi-Albert, and Gaussian Random Partition graphs improves betweenness transfer across graph families. In contrast, closeness centrality remains more sensitive to community-structured graphs and shows reduced transfer to real-world topologies. Finally, GNN inference achieves up to a 97.7x speedup over exact computation. These results show that mixed-distribution training can improve structural transfer in GNN-based centrality approximation, while identifying closeness centrality's sensitivity to topology as an open challenge.

AI.tldr: GNN-based scalable approximation of betweenness and closeness centrality with transfer learning across graph topologies; achieves high Kendall's tau and substantial speedups; mixed-distribution training improves cross-family transfer, while closeness is topology-sensitive.
AI.motivation: Centrality measures are expensive to compute on large graphs. GNNs offer a learning-based, scalable approach. A key question is whether GNNs can learn transferable, topology-agnostic representations across graph families, not just fit the training distribution.
AI.method: Supervised, message-passing GNNs trained to predict exact centrality values; evaluation via ranking quality using Kendall's tau. Experiments on unseen Erdos-Renyi graphs to assess transfer. A large 5,000-node betweenness model demonstrates scalability. Mixed-distribution training across Erdos-Renyi, Barabasi-Albert, and Gaussian Random Partition graphs to improve transfer across graph families.
AI.result: On unseen Erdos-Renyi graphs: tau=0.851 for betweenness, tau=0.894 for closeness. Large-scale betweenness model (N=5,000) achieves tau=0.938. Mixed-distribution training improves betweenness transfer across graph families. Closeness is more sensitive to community structure, showing reduced transfer to real-world topologies. Inference speedup up to 97.7x over exact computation.
AI.conclusion: GNNs can learn transferable structural representations for centrality ranking and offer scalable approximations. Mixed-distribution training helps cross-family transfer for betweenness, but closeness centrality remains challenging due to topology sensitivity.

title: What VGGT Knows About Overlap: Probing Geometric Foundation Models for Co-Visibility
summary: A fundamental challenge in 3D reconstruction and robotic localization is co-visibility: determining which image pairs share overlapping visible surfaces, particularly in scenarios with minimal overlap. We demonstrate that VGGT implicitly encodes co-visibility as an emergent behavior: without any supervision for this task, its internal representations exhibit a clear hierarchical structure mirroring that of large language models, i.e. early layers build a 3D-aware scene representation, while late layers act as dedicated co-visibility reasoners. In particular, we identify layer L17 as a negative anchor that consistently routes non-co-visible pairs for this backbone, regardless of the evaluation setting, providing task-grounded evidence of layer specialization in a geometry-grounded foundation model. Building on this, we introduce Co-VGGT, which freezes VGGT and trains only a lightweight layer-wise mixture-of-experts head (less than 7.5M parameters) to classify co-visibility from RGB alone, treating each layer as a specialized expert whose geometric abstraction is adaptively weighted per input pair. On the Co-VisiON benchmark, Co-VGGT surpasses the human annotation baseline and improves over prior work by more than 25% pairwise and 10% multiview. Pairwise predictions are well-calibrated (ECE=0.030), enabling direct use as edge weights in visibility graphs for downstream SfM and SLAM pipelines without post-hoc correction. Code and data are available.

AI.tldr: VGGT shows emergent co-visibility understanding; Co-VGGT enhances this with a lightweight mixture-of-experts head, achieving superior, calibrated co-visibility classification from RGB and usable edge weights for SfM/SLAM.
AI.motivation: Co-visibility determination is key for robust 3D reconstruction and localization, especially with limited image overlap. The work investigates whether a geometry-grounded foundation model implicitly encodes co-visibility and whether a small adapter can leverage this for practical tasks.
AI.method: The authors analyze VGGT's internal representations, identify layer L17 as a negative anchor for non-co-visible pairs, and freeze VGGT while training a small layer-wise mixture-of-experts head (<7.5M parameters) to classify co-visibility from RGB. Each layer acts as a specialized expert, with input-dependent weighting.
AI.result: On Co-VisiON, Co-VGGT surpasses human annotations by >25% in pairwise and ~10% in multiview tests. Pairwise predictions are well-calibrated (ECE=0.030) and suitable as edge weights in visibility graphs for downstream SfM/SLAM without post-hoc correction.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that geometry-grounded foundation models can be efficiently specialized for co-visibility via a compact mixture-of-experts head, enabling calibrated, RGB-only co-visibility classification and practical integration into SLAM pipelines. Code and data are available.

title: Mach-Mind-4-Flash Technical Report
summary: We present Mach-Mind-4-Flash, a 35B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model with 3B activated parameters. Through post-training optimization alone without scaling pre-training compute, the model achieves performance on par with or surpassing that of 100B-parameter-class models. By introducing scalable agentic interaction environments for large-scale reinforcement learning, the model attains significant performance gains on real-world application tasks. Our pipeline comprises three stages: (1) a unified RL/OPD training infrastructure with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration, delivering 17\% end-to-end training speedup; (2) multiple domain-specific RL experts trained in parallel across Reasoning, General, and Agent tracks, then fused into a single generalist via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) -- a routed reverse-KL objective that eliminates the see-saw degradation of mixed-reward RL; (3) Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO), a single-stage token-efficiency method that compresses reasoning chains by 19--46\% with $\le$0.7 percentage-point accuracy loss. Mach-Mind-4-Flash scores 92.70 on AIME'26, 82.82 on IFBench, 80.74 on Behavioral-SafetyBench, 75.80 on BFCL-v4, 72.31 on BrowseComp-zh, and 84.20 on ClawBench -- leading or matching models with 10--30$\times$ its activated size at a fraction of the inference cost.

AI.tldr: 35B MoE model Mach-Mind-4-Flash uses only 3B active parameters to match or exceed 100B-class models via post-training optimization, enabled by a three-stage pipeline: RL/OPD infra with multi-teacher scheduling, Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO).
AI.motivation: Demonstrate that large-scale RL agentic performance can be achieved without scaling pre-training compute, by optimizing activation sparsity and using modular domain-specific experts fused into a generalist.
AI.method: Stage 1: Unified RL/OPD training with dynamic multi-teacher scheduling and operator-level acceleration for 17% end-to-end speedup. Stage 2: Train multiple domain-specific RL experts in parallel across Reasoning, General, and Agent tracks; fuse into a single generalist via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) using a routed reverse-KL objective to avoid mixed-reward see-saw degradation. Stage 3: Hybrid Median-length Policy Optimization (HMPO), a single-stage token-efficient method compressing reasoning chains by 19–46% with ≤0.7 percentage-point accuracy loss.
AI.result: Achieves state-the-art-like scores across multiple benchmarks: AIME'26 92.70; IFBench 82.82; Behavioral-SafetyBench 80.74; BFCL-v4 75.80; BrowseComp-zh 72.31; ClawBench 84.20; claims to lead or match models with 10–30× smaller activated size and lower inference cost.
AI.conclusion: A three-stage pipeline leveraging MoE, MOPD, and HMPO yields high-performance, efficient agentic models without increasing pre-training compute, enabling scalable real-world RL applications.

title: DGSfM: Depth-Guided Scale-Aware Global Structure-from-Motion
summary: Global Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is an efficient paradigm for recovering camera poses and sparse 3D structure from unordered images. However, its reliance on scale-ambiguous epipolar geometry makes global positioning sensitive to noisy baseline estimates and weak view-graph constraints, while false edges from visually ambiguous pairs can further degrade reconstruction. We propose DGSfM, a depth-aware global SfM pipeline that uses monocular depth maps as a scalable prior while preserving explicit multi-view optimization. For each image pair, we use a depth-aware relative pose solver to convert scale-ambiguous epipolar constraints into scale-aware relative pose constraints. We further improve robustness through view-graph filtering and depth-consistency-based correspondence pruning, which suppress false edges and matches that remain plausible under epipolar geometry alone. Finally, global scale averaging and depth-guided pose-point initialization align monocular depth maps into a common reconstruction scale and provide stable initialization for global positioning and bundle adjustment. Experiments on ETH3D and IMC2021 show that DGSfM consistently improves over strong global SfM baselines across sparse and dense matching front-ends, achieving substantial gains in pose accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/sithu31296/DGSfM.

AI.tldr: A depth-aware global SfM method (DGSfM) integrates monocular depth priors to convert scale-ambiguous epipolar constraints into scale-aware relative poses, with view-graph filtering and depth-consistency pruning, yielding improved pose accuracy over strong global SfM baselines on ETH3D/IMC2021; code available.
AI.motivation: Global SfM is hampered by scale-ambiguous, noisy geometry and false edges from ambiguous image pairs, which degrade pose estimation and reconstruction quality. A scalable depth prior can stabilize scale and improve robustness.
AI.method: Introduce a depth-aware relative pose solver to convert scale-ambiguous epipolar constraints into scale-aware ones for each image pair. Apply view-graph filtering and depth-consistency-based pruning to suppress false edges/matches. Use global scale averaging and depth-guided initialization to align depth maps to a common scale and provide stable initialization for global optimization and bundle adjustment.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on ETH3D and IMC2021 shows consistent improvements over strong global SfM baselines across sparse and dense matching pipelines, with substantial gains in pose accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating monocular depth priors and depth-consistency pruning into global SfM yields more robust and accurate global reconstructions, demonstrated on challenging benchmarks; code is released for reproducibility.

title: Learning Physics-Informed Surrogate Model of Linear Elastic Displacement Fields from Geometry
summary: This work aims to develop a fast and physically consistent surrogate model for real-time structural health monitoring of fractured elastic domains. We propose a physics-informed DeepONet framework that predicts displacement fields from both boundary conditions and fracture geometry, using a dedicated encoding strategy for the latter and without relying on finite-element-generated training data. The traction-free condition on the fracture boundary is imposed weakly through a localized penalty term. The presented numerical example focuses on one representative fracture geometry, demonstrating the feasibility of the formulation and laying the groundwork for extensions to surrogate modeling across diverse fracture geometries.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed DeepONet surrogate for real-time SHM in fractured elastic media, predicting displacement fields from boundary conditions and fracture geometry without FE-generated training data, enforcing traction-free fracture boundaries via a localized penalty, demonstrated on a single fracture geometry with plan for generalization.
AI.motivation: Enable fast, physically consistent real-time monitoring of fractured structures; traditional FE surrogates require extensive data and may not generalize well across varying fracture geometries. A geometry-aware, physics-informed surrogate is needed to handle diverse fractures efficiently.
AI.method: A DeepONet framework that encodes fracture geometry with a dedicated input pathway and takes boundary conditions as inputs; trains without FE-generated data; enforces traction-free conditions on fracture boundaries weakly using a localized penalty term; validated on one representative fracture geometry to establish feasibility.
AI.result: Feasibility demonstrated: the surrogate produces displacement fields consistent with the governing physics for the chosen fracture geometry in real time, showing promise for extension to other fracture geometries.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for surrogate modeling across diverse fracture geometries in real-time SHM, with future work aimed at broadening geometry coverage, refining penalty enforcement, and validating on more complex fracture networks.

title: Seeing is Free, Speaking is Not: Uncovering the True Energy Bottleneck in Edge VLM Inference
comment: Accepted to ACM MM 2026. 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the perceptual backbone of embodied AI, but their energy footprint on edge hardware remains poorly understood. Existing efficiency efforts focus predominantly on reducing visual tokens, implicitly treating visual processing as the dominant energy cost. We overturn this implicit assumption through the first systematic energy profiling of on-device VLM inference, spanning five models across three architecture families, four input resolutions, and two hardware platforms (NVIDIA RTX 3070 and Jetson Orin NX). Our analysis yields three findings. First, average inference power is a model-intrinsic constant, invariant to input resolution, image complexity, and prompt type, with less than 5% variation across all conditions. This means that all energy variation across inputs must arise from variation in inference time, not from variation in power draw. Second, each output token costs 11 to 39x more wall-clock time than each input token due to the compute-bound and memory-bound asymmetry between prefill and decode, making output token count the dominant driver of both latency and energy. Third, image complexity, measured by the number of objects in an image, induces up to 4.1x energy differences at identical resolution. This variation arises not from increased visual processing cost, but from differences in output length. These findings expose a fundamental limitation of visual token pruning: even removing all visual tokens saves at most 10% of total energy for fixed-token models. Across models spanning 1 billion to 8 billion parameters, controlling output length saves up to 97% of total energy, with the energy dominance of decoding growing stronger at larger model scale. In short, the true energy bottleneck in edge VLM inference is not what the model sees, but how much it says.

AI.tldr: On-device Vision-Language Models: energy is dominated by decoding rather than visual input. Inference power is largely constant across resolutions and inputs; per-output-token costs are 11–39x higher than input tokens; image complexity affects energy mainly via longer output, not vision compute; token pruning yields limited gains (~10%), while controlling output length can save up to 97% of energy, especially for larger models.
AI.motivation: Quantify the on-device energy profile of VLM inference across architecture families, input resolutions, and hardware to identify true energy bottlenecks and guide efficiency strategies.
AI.method: Empirical energy profiling of five VLMs (three architecture families) across four input resolutions and two hardware platforms (NVIDIA RTX 3070, Jetson Orin NX). Measured power and wall-clock time for inference, separated into prefill and decode stages; varied image complexity (object count) and prompt types; compared visual-token pruning vs. output-token-dominant costs.
AI.result: - Inference power is an intrinsic constant per model with <5% variation across input resolution, image complexity, and prompt type. - Output tokens incur 11–39× more wall-clock time than input tokens; decoding dominates latency and energy. - Image complexity (object count) affects energy up to 4.1× at the same resolution due to longer outputs, not increased visual computation. - Visual token pruning yields at most ~10% energy savings for fixed-token models. - Across 1B–8B parameter models, controlling output length saves up to 97% of total energy; energy cost of decoding grows with model size.
AI.conclusion: Energy bottleneck in edge VLMs lies in the length of the model's generated output rather than the vision input processing; decoding is the primary driver of energy, and strategies should focus on output-length management and decoding efficiency, especially for larger models.

title: Fully Trainable Deep Differentiable Logic Gate Networks and Lookup Table Networks
summary: We introduce a novel method for both partial and full optimization of the connections in deep differentiable logic gate networks (LGNs) and lookup table networks (LUTNs). Our training method utilizes a probability distribution over a set of connections per gate/lookup table (LUT) input pin, selecting the connection with highest merit, all whilst the optimal gate types or LUT-entries are learned in parallel. We show that the connection-optimized LGNs outperform standard fixed-connection LGNs on the Yin-Yang, MNIST Handwritten Digits and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks, while requiring only a fraction of the number of logic gates. We achieve 98.92% on the MNIST dataset with two layers of 8000 gates. With only one layer of 8000 gates, we obtain 98.45%, showing that our method requires almost 50 times fewer gates compared to fixed-connection LGNs. Training stability up to ten layers has been ensured by employing a high learning rate, straight-through estimators and trimming constant-output gate types. Additionally, we present a LUT neuron description that enables stable training with backpropagation, tested up to 6-layer deep networks. The model requires four times fewer trainable parameters and still achieves a higher accuracy compared to the fixed-connection LGN training algorithm. Our connection-training algorithm also works well for the LUTNs, achieving an accuracy of 98.88% for two layers of 2000 6-input LUTs.

AI.tldr: Trainable probabilistic connection optimization for LGNs and LUTNs with hard selection per input pin, learning gate/LUT types in parallel; achieves state-like accuracy with far fewer gates and stable training up to 10 layers.
AI.motivation: Reduce model size and improve training stability of differentiable logic networks by jointly optimizing connections and gate types.
AI.method: Maintain a probability distribution over connections for each gate/LUT input pin and select the highest-merit connection (hard selection). Simultaneously learn optimal gate types or LUT entries. Use straight-through estimators and trimming of constant-output gate types for stability; introduce a LUT neuron description enabling backpropagation in multi-layer LUTNs.
AI.result: Outperforms fixed-connection LGNs on Yin-Yang, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST. 98.92% MNIST with two layers of 8000 gates; 98.45% with one layer. About 50x fewer gates than fixed-connection LGNs. Stable training up to ten layers. LUT neurons achieve 98.88% with two layers of 2000 six-input LUTs and fourfold fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed connection-training approach enables efficient, scalable, and accurate LGNs and LUTNs, reducing parameter counts while maintaining high performance and training stability across multiple depths.

title: ALICE: Learning a General-Purpose Pathology Foundation Model from Vision, Vision-Language, and Slide-Level Experts
summary: Foundation models are reshaping computational pathology, yet their capabilities remain shaped by pretraining objectives, data sources, and spatial scales, fragmenting complementary expertise across separate backbones. Here we present ALICE, a unified foundation model trained through multi-stage agglomerative distillation that sequentially distills eight vision-only, vision-language, and slide-level teacher models into dedicated modules of a single backbone. ALICE is pretrained on 24,985,184 tile-level pathology images and 155,604 high-resolution images, and evaluated across 21 task scenarios, 96 downstream tasks, and 48 data sources, spanning region-of-interest tissue analysis, vision-language multimodal evaluation, and whole-slide clinical assessment. In all three evaluation settings, ALICE achieved the best average rank among task-matched pathology foundation models. These results demonstrate that agglomerative distillation can consolidate complementary capabilities from specialized models into a unified backbone for broad computational pathology applications. The model is available at https://github.com/WonderLandxD/ALICE.

AI.tldr: ALICE is a unified foundation model for computational pathology obtained via multi-stage agglomerative distillation, integrating eight specialized teacher models into a single backbone; trained on massive tile- and high-res image datasets; evaluated broadly and outperformed task-matched baselines; code available.
AI.motivation: To address fragmentation of capabilities across separate backbones and to consolidate complementary expertise into a single scalable model for diverse pathology tasks.
AI.method: Sequential distillation from eight teacher models (vision-only, vision-language, slide-level) into dedicated modules within one backbone, across multi-stage agglomerative distillation; large-scale data: ~25M tile images and ~156k high-res images; evaluation across 21 task scenarios, 96 downstream tasks, 48 data sources, including ROI analysis, multimodal evaluation, and whole-slide clinical assessment.
AI.result: ALICE achieved the best average rank among task-matched pathology foundation models across three evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Agglomerative distillation enables consolidation of specialized capabilities into a unified pathology backbone, enabling broad applications; code available on GitHub.

title: On-Device Adaptive Battery Power Prediction for Electric Vehicles
comment: 6 pages, 3 tables, 5 figures; Accepted to IEEE EdgeCom 2025
summary: Adaptive power management in Electric Vehicles (EVs) requires accurate power prediction. Although deep learning models have emerged as highly effective for time-series forecasting in this domain, their performance is prone to degradation when exposed to data with distributions different from the training data. We introduce a novel approach that enables on-device learning in resource-constrained EV systems to continuously adapt pretrained battery prediction models to new, unseen data. We leverage existing pretrained models by transforming them into adaptable versions that retain critical hyperparameter knowledge from their initial training. We comprehensively investigate both online and offline model adaptation strategies. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in forecasting performance across various models and time horizons, achieving mean absolute error reductions of up to 7.49\% and 14.88\% with online and offline adaptation techniques, respectively. This study highlights the substantial benefit of on-device adaptation, resulting in enhanced battery power predictions than unadapted model deployments in real-world EV scenarios.

AI.tldr: On-device continual adaptation of pretrained battery-prediction models for EV power forecasting using online and offline strategies, achieving MAE reductions up to 7.49% and 14.88% respectively.
AI.motivation: Data distribution shifts in EV battery power forecasting degrade DL model performance; need on-device, resource-aware adaptation to maintain accuracy without offloading data.
AI.method: Transform pretrained models into adaptable versions that preserve initial hyperparameter knowledge; evaluate online and offline adaptation strategies for on-device deployment.
AI.result: Significant forecasting improvements across models/time horizons; MAE reductions up to 7.49% (online) and 14.88% (offline).
AI.conclusion: On-device adaptation effectively improves battery power predictions in real-world EV scenarios; demonstrates practical viability of continual, resource-constrained learning.

title: The Count Is There, but Misaligned: Understanding and Correcting Counting Failures in VLMs
summary: Despite strong performance on many multimodal tasks, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with basic object counting. We investigate whether this reflects missing internal knowledge or a gap between internal representations and verbalized outputs. Training simple probes on activations from four VLMs across five counting datasets reveals that nonlinear probes can reliably detect counting errors, suggesting that VLMs often encode the correct count even when they output the wrong answer. SVCCA analysis shows that probes trained on ground-truth counts and probes trained on model outputs occupy a partially shared activation subspace but read out along misaligned directions. We further validate our findings using a causal steering intervention, proving that strengthening the direction of count-identified probes does improve model counting performance. Motivated by this result, we propose a detector-guided self-correction method that selectively re-prompts the model only when an internal error detector predicts failure. This simple inference-time intervention improves counting accuracy by up to 15.6 absolute percentage points, without any parameter updates. Our results establish activation-based error probing as both a practical tool for improving VLM counting and a mechanistic lens on the gap between internal knowledge and model outputs.

AI.tldr: Activation-based error probing reveals internal counting knowledge in VLMs, but misalignment between internal representations and verbal outputs; detector-guided self-correction at inference time substantially improves counting without parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Understand whether counting failures in vision-language models stem from missing internal knowledge or from a mismatch between internal representations and the model’s verbal outputs; explore practical ways to leverage internal signals to improve performance.
AI.method: Train nonlinear probes on activations from four VLMs across five counting datasets. Use SVCCA to compare subspaces of probes trained on ground-truth counts vs. model outputs. Conduct causal steering to test if strengthening count-related directions improves counting. Develop detector-guided self-correction that re-prompts only when an internal error detector signals failure. Evaluate counting accuracy gains without parameter updates.
AI.result: Nonlinear probes reliably detect counting errors, indicating encoded counting knowledge even when outputs are wrong. Probes for ground-truth counts and model outputs share a subspace but are read out along misaligned directions. Causal steering improves counting when the relevant directions are strengthened. Detector-guided re-prompting yields up to 15.6 percentage points absolute gain without parameter updates.
AI.conclusion: Activation-based error probing provides a practical mechanism to diagnose and fix counting in VLMs, offering a mechanistic view of the gap between internal knowledge and emitted outputs and enabling effective inference-time corrections.

title: Data-Efficient Deep Learning: Empirical Guidelines for Training Set Size Estimation in Inertial Sensor Classification
summary: Deep learning models dependency on large-scale inertial datasets presents a significant bottleneck in inertial sensor-based classification tasks, such as human activity recognition and smartphone location recognition. In these domains, data collection requires massive recording campaigns that are complex, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Currently, data-driven guidelines for determining the minimum sample size required to reach a desired accuracy level do not exist. To address this gap, this study presents a systematic empirical evaluation of learning curve convergence rates in inertial classification. We introduce a unified framework that analyzes classification performance under both binary and multi-class scenarios, and derive an empirical formula to estimate performance relative to dataset size. Testing across six diverse, real-world datasets totaling 102.7 hours of inertial measurements demonstrates that accuracy follows a consistent logarithmic growth pattern, regardless of task complexity. Leveraging this finding, we propose a quantitative stability point metric, defined as the sample size required for the learning curve to stabilize within a predefined mean absolute percentage deviation of its asymptotic maximum. Our analysis reveals that models often reach practical stability with substantially fewer samples than traditional heuristics suggest. Ultimately, we offer a generalizable framework to extrapolate total data requirements from small-scale pilot studies, optimizing the tradeoff between recording effort and model reliability. These findings shift the prevailing paradigm from maximizing data volume toward optimizing data efficiency, offering concrete, data-backed guidelines for planning recording campaigns in inertial sensing applications.

AI.tldr: Inertial-sensing learning curves follow a logarithmic growth pattern; a stability-point metric estimates practical data needs, enabling extrapolation of total data from small pilots and favoring data-efficient design over sheer volume.
AI.motivation: DL models for inertial classification are bottlenecked by the need for large datasets; there are no data-driven guidelines for minimum sample size to achieve target accuracy in inertial sensing tasks.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation across six real-world inertial datasets (totaling 102.7 hours) using a unified framework for binary and multi-class tasks; derive an empirical formula linking performance to dataset size; introduce a stability-point metric defined by mean absolute percentage deviation from the asymptotic maximum.
AI.result: Accuracy exhibits consistent logarithmic growth with increasing data across tasks; practical stability is reached with far fewer samples than traditional heuristics; provides a framework to estimate total data requirements from small pilot studies.
AI.conclusion: Shifts the paradigm toward data efficiency in inertial sensing; offers concrete, generalizable guidelines for planning data collection and recording campaigns, enabling extrapolation of data needs from pilot studies.

title: TCLA: Training-Free Class-wise Logit Adaptation for Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical Vision-Language Models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot performance, yet their effectiveness still declines on out-of-distribution (OOD) data due to domain shifts and class bias inherited from large-scale pretraining. Existing few-shot adaptation methods typically introduce additional trainable components, which can be unstable in extremely low-data regimes (e.g., 1-shot), and lack robustness on different medical data. We present TCLA, a purely training-free few-shot adaptation method for Medical VLMs, which is fast and model-agnostic. TCLA corrects inference logits based on a small set of support samples, boosting pretrained VLMs performance by improving inter-class deconfusion and reducing domain shift. Extensive experiments on nine datasets across multiple medical imaging modalities including X-ray, Ultrasound, MRI, CT, Histopathology, demonstrate that TCLA consistently improves OOD performance of Medical VLMs and, in most of cases, outperforms existing training-based adaptation methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes TCLA, a training-free, few-shot adaptation method for medical VLMs that uses a small support set to calibrate logits, improving OOD performance across multiple modalities and often outperforming training-based adapters.
AI.motivation: Medical Vision-Language Models suffer from OOD degradation due to domain shifts and class bias from large-scale pretraining. Existing few-shot methods add trainable components, which can be unstable in ultra-low-data regimes and lack full robustness across medical data.
AI.method: TCLA operates without additional training. It uses a small support set to adjust inference logits, enhancing inter-class separation and reducing domain shift. The approach is model-agnostic and fast, aiming to be robust across diverse medical imaging modalities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on nine datasets spanning X-ray, Ultrasound, MRI, CT, and Histopathology show consistent OOD performance gains for medical VLMs, with TCLA outperforming many training-based adaptation methods in most cases.
AI.conclusion: A fast, model-agnostic, training-free adaptation technique that improves OOD robustness of medical VLMs with few-shot support, suitable for diverse medical imaging tasks without additional training.

title: SYNRARE: Synthetic Rare Disease EHR Generation for ML Benchmarking
comment: Intended for submission to the Application Notes Bioinformatics Journal
summary:
Motivation: Rare disease (RD) diagnosis is frequently delayed due to the similarities in symptoms to common disease variants. Machine Learning Algorithms applied to Electronic Health Records show promise for accelerating the diagnosis; however, legal and privacy concerns pose significant barriers. To address these issues, Synthetic Data Generation is an alternative method for obtaining Electronic Health Records and can be applied with any Machine Learning algorithm for benchmarking and development purposes. Despite the availability of Synthetic Data Generation algorithms, support for generating a subset of patients that differ in a definable degree from the majority to simulate patients with RD is often lacking.
  Results: We present SYNRARE, a graphical user interface based on the Synthea framework that enables easier modification and generation of synthetic Electronic Health Records of RD patients, which differ only to a definable degree from patients with common diseases, thereby enabling the benchmarking and testing of algorithms under controlled technical conditions. SYNRARE enables researchers to rapidly benchmark their Machine Learning algorithms across any scenario.
  Availability and implementation: SYNRARE, including detailed instructions for installing, is available at https://gitlab.sdu.dk/screen4care/synrare.

AI.tldr: SYNRARE is a GUI tool that extends Synthea to generate synthetic EHRs with RD-like deviations from common diseases, enabling controlled benchmarking of ML algorithms while preserving privacy.
AI.motivation: RD diagnosis is often delayed due to symptom overlap with common diseases. Synthetic data can circumvent legal/privacy barriers for ML development and benchmarking. Existing SDG tools often lack a way to generate subpopulations that differ by a definable degree from the majority to simulate RD.
AI.method: A GUI-based extension of the Synthea framework that allows users to modify and generate synthetic EHRs for RD patients, with a definable degree of difference from those with common diseases, facilitating controlled ML benchmarking.
AI.result: SYNRARE enables rapid benchmarking of ML algorithms across defined scenarios by providing controllable RD-like synthetic datasets.
AI.conclusion: SYNRARE fills a gap in synthetic data generation by offering targeted subpopulation generation for RD simulation, and is available with installation instructions at the specified GitLab repository for researchers.

title: Wan-Dancer: A Hierarchical Framework for Minute-scale Coherent Music-to-Dance Generation
summary: Generating long-duration, high-definition, and rhythmically synchronized dance videos directly from music remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the temporal constraints of current diffusion models, which typically fail beyond 20 seconds. Existing approaches, whether they rely on intermediate 3D skeletons or on end-to-end video synthesis, suffer from temporal drift, identity inconsistency, and repetitive motion patterns when extended to longer horizons. To address these limitations, we propose a novel hierarchical framework for minute-scale coherent music-to-dance generation. Our method decouples the process into global keyframe planning and local temporal refinement, leveraging full-track musical context to ensure long-range coherence. Key innovations include dynamic frame rate adaptation via time-mapped RoPE embeddings for precise alignment, an optical-flow-based loss function to enhance motion continuity, and motion-speed control to preserve high-fidelity details during rapid movements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework surpasses the conventional duration barrier, generating stable, 720p/30fps videos exceeding one minute with superior temporal stability. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust versatility across five distinct dance genres, conditioned on both audio and textual prompts, establishing a new state-of-the-art in coherent, long-form dance video synthesis.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical music-to-dance generation framework extending diffusion-based methods to minute-scale videos, splitting global planning and local refinement. It uses time-mapped RoPE embeddings for dynamic frame-rate alignment, an optical-flow loss for motion continuity, and motion-speed control to preserve detail during rapid moves. It produces 720p/30fps videos over a minute, robust across five dance genres, conditioned on audio and text prompts, achieving state-of-the-art long-form coherence.
AI.motivation: Overcome diffusion models' limited temporal horizon (~20 seconds) and issues such as temporal drift, identity inconsistency, and repetitive motion when generating long-form dance videos.
AI.method: Decouple generation into global keyframe planning and local temporal refinement. Employ time-mapped RoPE embeddings to adapt frame rate to track length. Introduce an optical-flow-based loss to enforce motion continuity. Incorporate motion-speed control to maintain fidelity during rapid movements. Condition on both audio and textual prompts to guide style and correspondence.
AI.result: Generates stable minute-scale, 720p/30fps dance videos (>60s) with strong temporal stability. Demonstrates robustness across five dance genres and surpasses conventional duration barriers, achieving state-of-the-art performance in coherent long-form dance video synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Presents a scalable, practical framework for long-form music-to-dance generation that fuses global planning with local refinement, improving long-horizon coherence and visual fidelity and enabling versatile, multi-modal control.

title: Similarity search generalisation in contrastive learning with InfoNCE loss
summary: Similarity search is a primary application of embedding models trained by contrastive learning. For one of the most popular contrastive learning loss functions, InfoNCE, we show that the population risk with $k$ negative samples is $O(1/k)$ close to an expected cross-entropy which quantifies deviation between i) a softmax similarity search over unseen data using the learned embedding function, and ii) an idealised softmax search over the same data but using similarity implicitly represented in the positive sample generator. This complements existing interpretations of InfoNCE in the $k\to\infty$ limit which are phrased in terms of mutual information, and alignment versus uniformity in embeddings. To quantify generalisation performance, we introduce a new continuity bound for the InfoNCE loss, obtained via Gâteaux differentiation. The bound preserves the structure of averaging over negative samples present in the loss function and features an ``inverse temperature'' parameter which can be tuned to account for the algorithmic temperature. For embedding functions which are Lipschitz in a parameter, this yields a simple demonstration that the averaging effect of $k$ negative samples in the InfoNCE loss carries over to stabilisation of the generalisation error as $k$ grows.

AI.tldr: InfoNCE with k negatives yields population risk within O(1/k) of an expected cross-entropy between a softmax search on unseen data using the learned embedding and an idealized softmax search using the positive-sample generator; finite-k interpretation complements MI-based views.
AI.motivation: Clarify finite-k behavior of InfoNCE beyond the asymptotic k→∞ mutual information perspective and its relation to alignment and uniformity in embeddings; quantify how negative sampling affects generalisation.
AI.method: Derive a population-risk bound showing O(1/k) proximity to a cross-entropy term. Introduce a continuity bound for the InfoNCE loss via Gâteaux differentiation, preserving the negative-sample averaging structure and including an inverse temperature parameter. Consider Lipschitz embedding functions to show how averaging over negatives stabilises generalisation as k grows.
AI.result: Establishes a finite-k interpretation of InfoNCE as an expected cross-entropy close to, and bounded by, a term that mirrors the softmax similarity search under the generator. Provides a bound that links negative-sample averaging to generalisation stability and introduces a tunable temperature to reflect algorithmic temperature.
AI.conclusion: The finite-k analysis complements the conventional k→∞ mutual-information viewpoint, offering practical guidance on how the number of negatives and the temperature affect generalisation stability and the alignment of learned embeddings.

title: Promptable Concept Segmentation from Above: Evaluating SAM 3's Zero-Shot and One-Shot Capabilities in Remote Sensing
summary: The deployment of large-scale foundation models, such as the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3), promises a transition toward open-vocabulary, training-free computer vision. However, their capacity to generalize out-of-distribution to the complex, top-down geometric structures of Earth Observation imagery remains largely unquantified. Driven by SAM 3's performance disparities in highly specialized domains, we present a comprehensive, multi-task empirical evaluation across remote sensing scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation under strict zero-shot and one-shot constraints. To achieve this, we introduce a structural adaptation of SAM 3 by repurposing its decoupled binary presence head into a standalone zero-shot classifier. Furthermore, by systematically isolating textual and visual prompt modalities across five configurations, we explicitly diagnose the alignment mechanics within the model's multimodal decoder. Our findings reveal severe cross-modal interference: while visual prompts successfully align the decoder to complex remote sensing geometry, textual prompts inject misaligned, ground-level semantic bias, actively degrading coordinate regression. To benchmark these capabilities without resource-intensive training, we formulate a novel training-free proxy evaluation protocol for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks (scene classification and instance segmentation). Ultimately, our results demonstrate that SAM 3 avoids the overfitting commonly seen in legacy domain-adapted models, achieving high Harmonic Mean scores in segmentation tasks. However, it remains fundamentally constrained by sub-pixel resolution limits and overhead semantic blind spots, charting a definitive mandate for parameter-efficient geospatial fine-tuning of its multimodal decoder.

AI.tldr: SAM 3 shows competitive segmentation in EO with training-free evaluation but struggles with cross-modal alignment in top-down geometry; visual prompts help geometry, while textual prompts inject ground-level bias that harms coordinate regression; introduces a training-free proxy for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks; overall performance limited by sub-pixel resolution and semantic blind spots, prompting parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the multimodal decoder.
AI.motivation: Evaluate out-of-distribution generalization of large foundation models (SAM 3) to Earth Observation imagery across scene classification, object detection, and instance segmentation under strict zero-shot and one-shot constraints, and diagnose cross-modal alignment between vision and language prompts.
AI.method: Adapt SAM 3 by turning its decoupled binary presence head into a standalone zero-shot classifier; systematically vary textual and visual prompts across five configurations to diagnose alignment in the multimodal decoder; conduct multi-task zero-shot and one-shot evaluation on remote sensing tasks (scene classification, detection, segmentation); develop a training-free proxy evaluation protocol for Generalized Zero-Shot tasks to benchmark without retraining—emphasizing cross-modal interference analysis.
AI.result: Visual prompts effectively align the decoder to complex EO geometry; textual prompts introduce misaligned, ground-level semantic bias, degrading coordinate regression; SAM 3 avoids overfitting seen in legacy domain-adapted models and yields high Harmonic Mean scores in segmentation, but is limited by sub-pixel resolution and overhead semantic blind spots.
AI.conclusion: To fully exploit SAM 3 for geospatial tasks, pursue parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the multimodal decoder and improved cross-modal alignment strategies for textual prompts, alongside robust, training-free evaluation protocols to quantify generalized zero-shot capabilities.

title: Action-Factored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Scalable Quantum Device Tuning
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning is well suited to problems with large parameter spaces and exploitable local structure, such as the tuning of electrostatically-defined quantum-dot arrays. However, if parameter cross-talk is strong, a non-stationary environment from the perspective of any individual agent can destabilize learning - the same effect that plagues manual tuning of such systems. We propose using a factored representation of the action space, learned online, to decouple agents and minimize their interference. Our framework, QADAPT, uses this factorization to efficiently learn shared policies based on local measurements and rewards. With this modular strategy, we achieve zero-shot generalization to unseen quantum device sizes and maintain an approximately constant number of convergence steps to reach target regimes. This work provides a scalable route toward the rapid calibration of large-scale quantum processors.

AI.tldr: QADAPT uses online learned action-space factorization to decouple agents in cooperative MARL for calibrating large quantum-dot arrays, enabling zero-shot generalization to larger devices with stable convergence.
AI.motivation: In cooperative MARL for quantum-device calibration, strong parameter cross-talk creates non-stationarity that destabilizes learning; a modular decoupling approach is needed to scale to large arrays.
AI.method: Proposes QADAPT, which learns an online factorization of the action space to decouple agents, enabling shared policies based on local measurements and rewards; modular architecture.
AI.result: Demonstrates zero-shot generalization to unseen quantum-device sizes and maintains approximately constant convergence steps to reach target regimes; supports scalable rapid calibration of large-scale quantum processors.
AI.conclusion: Online action-space factorization enables decoupled learning in cooperative MARL, offering scalable calibration for large quantum devices; approach likely applicable to systems with cross-talk and local structure.

title: 4DR360: State Reasoning for Joint 3D Detection and Occupancy Prediction in 4D Radar-Camera Full-Scene Perception
summary: Reliable autonomous driving requires full-scene perception that couples foreground objects with dense semantic layout. Recently, 4D millimeter-wave radar has emerged as a robust and affordable sensor, yet its sparse returns make radar-camera fusion necessary for comprehensive scene understanding. Existing radar-camera methods mainly optimize detection, while dual-task systems usually decode boxes and occupancy with limited interaction. To address this gap and advance radar-based multi-task learning, we propose \method, a 4D radar-camera framework for 360$^\circ$ full-scene perception, which models semantic occupancy as a persistent scene state rather than a terminal output. \method{} follows a cross-modal state reasoning paradigm, where the occupancy state is modeled and propagated through stages for coarse-to-fine feature aggregation. Specifically, State-guided BEV Enhancement (SBE) strengthens intra-frame BEV representation, while Doppler-guided Temporal Fusion (DTF) preserves state evidence over longer temporal horizons. Beyond the model, we further extend ManTruckScenes with satellite-map-based generated occupancy labels and pair it with OmniHD-Scenes in a unified cross-dataset detection-and-occupancy protocol. The resulting experiments cover accuracy, robustness, ablation, and efficiency under one radar-camera multi-task evaluation framework. Code and labels will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A 4D radar-camera framework for 360° full-scene perception that treats semantic occupancy as a persistent state, using cross-modal state reasoning with SBE and DTF for coarse-to-fine fusion, plus cross-dataset occupancy labeling to enable unified detection-and-occupancy evaluation.
AI.motivation: Address sparse 4D radar returns and the need for robust full-scene perception by coupling radar with camera, shifting occupancy from a terminal output to a controllable scene-state that can be propagated over time.
AI.method: Cross-modal state reasoning that propagates an occupancy state through stages for coarse-to-fine feature aggregation. Key components: State-guided BEV Enhancement (SBE) to strengthen intra-frame BEV features; Doppler-guided Temporal Fusion (DTF) to preserve state evidence across longer temporal horizons. Extension of datasets with satellite-map-based generated occupancy labels; unified cross-dataset protocol combining ManTruckScenes and OmniHD-Scenes for detection-and-occupancy tasks.
AI.result: Experiments evaluate accuracy, robustness, ablations, and efficiency under a radar-camera multi-task framework; code and labels to be released.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a novel radar-camera multi-task framework that treats occupancy as a persistent state and validates it across datasets, showing potential gains in robust 360° perception with 4D radar.

title: Active rejection enables reliable generalization of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
summary: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) bridge quantum-mechanical accuracy and large-scale molecular dynamics, but the cost of high-accuracy calculations such as r$^2$SCAN limits training to datasets that remain small relative to the open materials space. Strong average benchmark performance also does not guarantee reliable energy--force predictions for every structure. We propose Adaptive Multi-Teacher Routing (ATR), which reformulates high-fidelity data construction as a structure-wise decision problem under uncertainty. Using a small set of real r$^2$SCAN labels, ATR calibrates multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers and combines structural descriptors, teacher identity, and inter-teacher disagreement to estimate the reliability of each structure--teacher pair. It selects high-confidence predictions for pseudo-label generation and rejects structures for which no teacher is sufficiently reliable. With real r$^2$SCAN labels for only 0.2\% of candidate structures, ATR distils 2.89 million traceable r$^2$SCAN-level pseudo-labels for pretraining. On held-out r$^2$SCAN structures and the MP-r$^2$SCAN benchmark, a lightweight CHGNet trained on the ATR-generated dataset consistently outperforms the baseline and non-routed controls. Finite-temperature molecular dynamics further shows that ATR improves dynamical robustness across multiple material systems, maintaining stable trajectories where baseline simulations undergo catastrophic structural collapse. These results establish active rejection as an effective mechanism for converting multiple pretrained uMLIPs into a scalable and reliable data-construction system for high-fidelity uMLIPs.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Multi-Teacher Routing (ATR) uses an uncertainty-aware, structure-level routing strategy to select high-confidence pseudo-labels from multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers, enabling scalable high-fidelity data generation with only 0.2% real r2SCAN labels. It trains CHGNet on ATR-generated data, achieving improved accuracy and dynamical robustness across materials.
AI.motivation: Bridge quantum-chemical accuracy and scalable MD by reducing reliance on expensive r2SCAN data; ensure energy–force predictions are reliable for diverse structures, not just benchmarked averages.
AI.method: Calibrate multiple pretrained uMLIP teachers; for each structure-teacher pair estimate reliability using structure descriptors, teacher identity, and inter-teacher disagreement; accept high-confidence predictions for pseudo-labeling and discard unreliable cases; use a tiny real-label set (0.2%) to generate a large pseudo-labeled dataset (2.89 million labels); train CHGNet on this dataset; validate on held-out r2SCAN structures and MP-r2SCAN benchmark; assess dynamical stability via finite-temperature MD.
AI.result: ATR-generated data enabled CHGNet to surpass baseline and non-routed controls on held-out tests and MP-r2SCAN; 0.2% real labels yielded 2.89M pseudo-labels; MD simulations showed improved dynamical robustness, with stable trajectories where baselines failed.
AI.conclusion: Active rejection-based routing across multiple tutors is effective for scalable, reliable construction of high-fidelity uMLIPs, enabling robust predictive performance beyond standard benchmark metrics.

title: All Explanations are Wrong, But Many Are Useful: Exploring the Rashomon Explanation Set with Large Language Models
summary: Explaining machine-learning models is increasingly important for decision-making and consumer trust, yet it is widely believed to come at a cost: existing Explainable AI (XAI) methods suffer from a persistent accuracy-explainability trade-off. We argue that this trade-off is not fundamental, but an artifact of treating explanation and prediction as separate objectives; when properly coupled, they become complementary, so that equipping a model to explain itself improves, rather than degrades, its accuracy. We introduce the Rashomon Explanation paradigm, which builds a set of faithful, prediction-guiding explanations rather than a single one, and prove that this set is generally non-empty and that explanation fidelity bounds the performance of the models it guides. To explore this set, we propose RashomonLLM, an Explanation-Prediction-Reflection agentic workflow that generates explanations in natural language by iteratively aligning them with predictions, and we prove it converges and recovers the full set. Across customer-churn classification, clinical survival regression, and industrial click-through prediction on large-scale live-streaming logs, RashomonLLM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art prediction and XAI baselines on both accuracy and explanation quality, with gains driven by explanation fidelity and robust to distribution shifts, temporal splits, and seeds. Our framework thus advances business performance while laying the groundwork for consumer trust.

AI.tldr: Proposes Rashomon Explanation paradigm and RashomonLLM to couple explanations with predictions, yielding a non-empty set of faithful explanations; improves accuracy and explanation quality across tasks; shows convergence and robustness; reframes explainability as a synergistic objective rather than a cost.
AI.motivation: Explainable AI methods often trade accuracy for interpretability. The paper argues that this trade-off is not fundamental if explanations are grounded in the model's predictions and can guide improvement.
AI.method: Introduce Rashomon Explanation paradigm to build a set of faithful, prediction-guiding explanations. Develop RashomonLLM, an Explanation-Prediction-Reflection agentic workflow that generates natural-language explanations by iteratively aligning them with predictions; prove non-emptiness, fidelity bounds on model performance, convergence, and recovery of the full explanation set.
AI.result: Empirical results across customer churn classification, clinical survival regression, and industrial click-through prediction show RashomonLLM outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both predictive accuracy and explanation quality; explanations are faithful and robust to distribution shifts, temporal splits, and seeds.
AI.conclusion: The framework enhances business performance while enabling consumer trust by treating explanations as a constructive component of predictive modeling rather than a separate post-hoc add-on.

title: The Effects of Synthetic Data and Label Distribution on Canola Branch Counting
summary: Collecting annotated plant images for automated phenotyping is often slow and expensive. Plant models simulating growth and development can generate unlimited synthetic images with exact labels. However, previous work has established that whether incorporating synthetic data improves performance depends on the ratio of synthetic to real images and the label distribution of the synthetic dataset. To systematically quantify both factors, we train ResNet-18 models on a canola branch-counting task using a calibrated L-system plant model. We vary each factor independently. Synthetic-to-real ratios of 1:5 to 1:22 broadly improve performance; the best ratio (1:7) reduces mean absolute difference by 7.6% over real-only training. For label distribution, a uniform synthetic distribution is strongly suboptimal (abs. diff. of approximately 1.70); interpolating 90% toward the real distribution yields abs. diff. 0.927, whereas Gaussian smoothing of the real label distribution yields the best overall result (abs. diff. 0.912, a 14.7% improvement over real-only). A minimum of 10 synthetic images per label offers a simpler alternative with modest gains, while 100 per label over-corrects and hurts performance.

AI.tldr: Synthetic canola branch-counting with a calibrated L-system; optimal performance depends on synthetic-to-real image ratio and label distribution. Best ratio ~1:7; Gaussian smoothing of real label distribution outperforms other strategies; 10 synthetic images per label helps modestly, 100 per label hurts.
AI.motivation: Quantify how synthetic data quantity and label distribution affect model performance in automated plant phenotyping, addressing inconsistent findings in prior work.
AI.method: Train ResNet-18 on a canola branch-counting task using a calibrated L-system plant model to generate synthetic images. Systematically vary synthetic-to-real image ratio (1:5 to 1:22) and explore label distributions: uniform, 90% interpolation toward the real distribution, and Gaussian smoothing of the real distribution. Also compare per-label synthetic counts (e.g., 10 vs 100). Evaluate with mean absolute difference between predicted and true counts.
AI.result: Synthetic-to-real ratio of 1:7 yields the largest improvement, reducing mean absolute difference by 7.6% over real-only training. Uniform synthetic label distribution performs poorly (abs. diff ≈ 1.70). Interpolating 90% toward the real distribution yields abs. diff ≈ 0.927, while Gaussian smoothing of the real distribution achieves the best result with abs. diff 0.912 (a 14.7% improvement over real-only). A minimum of 10 synthetic images per label provides modest gains; 100 per label over-corrects and worsens performance.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can improve performance in plant phenotyping, but gains are contingent on both the synthetic-to-real ratio and the alignment of synthetic labels with real data. An approximately 1:7 ratio and a label distribution shaped by Gaussian smoothing of the real distribution yield the best results; small synthetic counts per label are beneficial, while excessive per-label counts can degrade performance.

title: Neural Collapse Is Forbidden: Information Floors in Language Models
summary: Within-class variance in language-model representations is commonly read as incomplete neural collapse. We argue it is allocated information storage, and that the allocation obeys a law. A one-line centering identity voids a family of simplex equiangular-tight-frame claims, including our own earlier ones; in dimensionless variance shares across 14 models, macro-category structure carries only 4-12% of representational variance and within-token context carries 79-91%, stable across a 100x parameter range. On the theory side, token-level weight decay penalizes a category in proportion to its type count, not its occurrence mass, reducing next-token prediction to an imbalanced K-class problem whose optimum orders category norms by type count. A converse floor, proved for binary categories, forces within-category dispersion to be at least proportional to the conditional mutual information I(token; context | category).
