The law holds: identity dispersion, not total variance, tracks this information across every tested model and partition, under a model-free estimate and even across models, where one model's information predicts another's dispersion; and over pretraining the category share overshoots, decays, and partially recovers, because the information it must carry never left.

AI.tldr: The abstract posits a law-like relationship governing how information is distributed in language-model representations: most variance arises from within-token context rather than macro-category structure, identity dispersion tracks information across models, and token-level weight decay creates an imbalanced K-class optimization; a converse floor ties it to conditional mutual information.
AI.motivation: Clarify what within-class variance in neural representations means and formalize a law for information distribution across tokens, contexts, and categories in language models, challenging purely geometric neural-collapse interpretations.
AI.method: Theoretical derivations plus model-free empirical estimates across 14 models and a wide parameter range; analysis of token-level weight decay; a converse floor proven for binary categories; cross-model information transfer; and pretraining-category-share experiments to study information persistence.
AI.result: Macro-category structure accounts for 4–12% of representational variance; within-token context accounts for 79–91%. A one-line centering identity invalidates a broad family of simplex equiangular-tight-frame claims. Token-level weight decay shifts emphasis to category type count. A converse floor ties dispersion to conditional mutual information I(token; context | category). Identity dispersion tracks information across models and partitions, robust under model-free estimates and across architectures; information persists even when pretraining category shares change.
AI.conclusion: The proposed law—identity dispersion as the carrier of information—best explains cross-model and cross-partition behavior, with total variance being a poor proxy for information; the phenomenon is robust across models, contexts, and pretraining regimes, indicating persistent information that survives substantial architectural changes.

title: Revisiting Euler-Angle Regression with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary: In many real-world systems, including articulated robots and biomechanical models, rotations are defined in joint space and naturally parameterized by Euler angles with bounded ranges. Yet regressing Euler angles remains challenging, as their discontinuities and singularities often destabilize training. In this work, we revisit Euler-angle regression and show that its effectiveness depends critically on the interaction between rotation representation, regression architecture, and domain constraints. We introduce a new framework that combines range-aware Euler modeling with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which replace fixed node-wise activations with learnable univariate functions on edges. We further provide theoretical analysis indicating that bounded Euler ranges motivate a near-additive structure in the regression function, which favors the additive functional form of KAN, and we confirm this trend empirically. Extensive experiments on controlled rotation regression, object pose estimation, and robotic and human inverse kinematics demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, convergence, and efficiency. The code will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: Range-aware Euler modeling paired with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks improves regression of bounded Euler angles by exploiting an near-additive regression structure, yielding consistent gains across rotation-related tasks.
AI.motivation: Euler-angle regression suffers from discontinuities and gimbal-lock-like singularities. Understanding how rotation representation, regression architecture, and domain constraints interact can guide better design.
AI.method: Introduce range-aware Euler modeling and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) that use learnable univariate edge functions instead of fixed node activations; provide theoretical analysis showing bounded Euler ranges induce near-additive structure favorable to KAN; validate with experiments on rotation regression, object pose estimation, and robotic/human inverse kinematics.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in accuracy, convergence speed, and computational efficiency across tasks; empirical support for the near-additive effect and the suitability of KAN for this setting; code to be released.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses Euler-angle regression challenges by leveraging range-aware representations and KAN, with both theoretical and empirical support, suggesting broad applicability to rotation-related regression problems.

title: Evolution of Accuracy and Visual-Cognitive Errors in a Decade of Vision-Language AI Models
summary: Vision language models (VLMs) have made remarkable progress in visual reasoning during the last decade. Most evaluations have used simple scenes (MS-COCO) that do not showcase complex human interactions or behaviors, only a handful of non-curated human descriptions as a benchmark, and have not focused on understanding the model's error types. Here, we introduce the Complex Social Behavior (CSB) dataset, containing 100 images depicting complex social interactions/behaviors. We analyze the progression of scene descriptions over a decade (2017-2025) of VLMs (four pre-Multimodal Large Language Models, MLLMs, and five MLLMs). We evaluate the accuracy of the models and 20 human descriptions relative to a gold standard on the CSB dataset and on a sample from MS-COCO. We analyzed five visual-cognitive error types: object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence. The CSB dataset showed a more pronounced improvement than MS-COCO in scene description accuracy, with pre-MLLMs achieving much lower accuracy than the bottom-ranked human descriptions and MLLMs attaining accuracies similar to the top-ranked human descriptions. We show that MLLMs have eliminated the gap in scene description accuracy between simpler MS-COCO scenes and scenes depicting complex behaviors (CSB). MLLMs have almost eliminated all error types in our tested datasets, except for occasionally relying on different image regions for scene descriptions than humans do (spatial dependence error). We also show that detection, recognition, and hallucination errors have the highest impact on scene description accuracy. Together, our findings provide a more thorough evaluation of how visual language models have advanced over the last decade.

AI.tldr: Introduces CSB dataset (100 images) to evaluate VLMs on complex social behavior; shows MLLMs close to top human descriptions on CSB, with some residual spatial-dependence errors; detection/recognition/hallucination drive accuracy.
AI.motivation: MS-COCO-style datasets are too simple to capture complex social interactions and error types; there is a need to track VLM progress over the last decade (2017-2025) and quantify error types.
AI.method: Construct the Complex Social Behavior (CSB) dataset; evaluate four pre-Multimodal LMs (pre-MLLMs) and five MLLMs; compare model descriptions and human references against a gold standard on CSB and a MS-COCO sample; analyze five visual-cognitive error types: object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence.
AI.result: CSB shows a more pronounced improvement over time than MS-COCO; pre-MLLMs are significantly less accurate than bottom-ranked humans; MLLMs reach accuracies similar to top-ranked humans on CSB; gap between simple MS-COCO and CSB has narrowed for CSB; most errors are eliminated by MLLMs, except spatial-dependence where models sometimes use different regions than humans; detection, recognition, and hallucination errors have the highest impact on accuracy.
AI.conclusion: CSB enables a thorough evaluation of visual-language model progress in complex social scenarios; MLLMs have substantially reduced most error types and closed the performance gap with humans on CSB, though spatial-dependence remains a residual challenge and datasets continue to be essential for fine-grained error analysis.

title: TSAI-MetaFraud: A Benchmark Dataset for Financial Fraud Transaction and Behavioral Risk Detection in Metaverse Ecosystems
summary: The emergence of metaverse platforms has created virtual economies that introduce new challenges related to fraud, bot activity, and illicit financial behavior. Despite growing interest in trustworthy metaverse analytics, existing datasets typically focus on user behavior, authentication, or financial transactions in isolation, limiting the development and reproducible evaluation of multimodal fraud detection methods. To address this gap, we present TSAI-MetaFraud, a multimodal, multi-task benchmark dataset for fraud analytics in virtual economies. TSAI-MetaFraud integrates behavioral, transactional, and graph-structured information while incorporating realistic fraud and automated bot scenarios. We define benchmark tasks including transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, and weakly supervised fraud detection, and provide baseline evaluations using machine learning models and graph neural networks. By jointly capturing behavioral activity, financial interactions, and relational structure within a unified virtual economy, TSAI-MetaFraud provides a benchmark for advancing multimodal learning, graph mining, fraud analytics, and trustworthy AI in emerging metaverse ecosystems.

AI.tldr: Introduces TSAI-MetaFraud, a multimodal, multi-task benchmark for fraud analytics in virtual economies, integrating behavioral, transactional, and graph data with baseline evaluations on multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation of existing datasets that isolate data modalities, hindering reproducible evaluation and development of multimodal fraud detection in metaverse environments; aims to capture realistic fraud and bot activity within a unified virtual economy.
AI.method: Constructs a multimodal dataset combining behavioral traces, financial transactions, and graph-structured relations; simulates realistic fraud and bot scenarios; defines tasks (transaction fraud detection, cross-modal node classification, temporal link prediction, weakly supervised fraud detection); provides baseline evaluations using machine learning and graph neural networks.
AI.result: Provides a unified benchmark with baseline models across multiple tasks, demonstrating feasibility of multimodal fraud analytics in metaverse settings and enabling reproducible evaluation for graph mining and multimodal learning.
AI.conclusion: TSAI-MetaFraud offers a comprehensive benchmark to advance multimodal learning, graph mining, fraud analytics, and trustworthy AI within emerging metaverse ecosystems.

title: OpenLongTail: Generative Scaling of Long-Tail Driving Data
summary: Scaling robust driving policies is fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of edge cases in curated datasets. While the real world continuously captures these critical events, such long-tail events remain underutilized when collected from heterogeneous sources. Specifically, diverse but valuable in-the-wild long-tail videos lack the full view coverage required for training policy models, often missing multi-view poses or originating solely from monocular dash cameras. This modality gap prevents these ubiquitous observations from being converted into scalable training data for long-tail generalization. We introduce OpenLongTail, an open-source generative data engine for scaling autonomous driving policies under long-tail events. To transform heterogeneous data sources into view-aligned and temporally coherent multi-view assets that are useful for policy learning, we develop a pose-informed extrapolative view synthesis pipeline that generates the missing views. We further enhance cross-view consistency and the temporal alignment for the newly generated views by injecting Plücker ray geometry into the scalable generation engine. By synthesizing heterogeneous long-tail data, we observe a significant improvement in closed-loop driving robustness in handling long-tail events. By measuring the extrapolative view synthesis and pose metrics, we validate the effectiveness of OpenLongTail in visual fidelity, cross-view consistency, and ego-trajectory recovery.

AI.tldr: OpenLongTail is an open-source generative data engine that scales autonomous driving policies for long-tail events by converting heterogeneous, long-tail in-the-wild video sources into view-aligned, temporally coherent multi-view data using a pose-informed extrapolative view-synthesis pipeline and Plücker ray geometry for cross-view consistency.
AI.motivation: Long-tail edge-case data are scarce in curated datasets; in-the-wild observations are diverse and often monocular, yielding a modality gap that hinders scalable policy learning for rare driving events.
AI.method: A pose-informed extrapolative view-synthesis pipeline that generates missing views to create view-aligned, temporally coherent multi-view assets from heterogeneous sources; cross-view consistency and temporal alignment are reinforced by injecting Plücker ray geometry into the generation engine.
AI.result: OpenLongTail-achieved data synthesis quality with improved visual fidelity, cross-view consistency, and ego-trajectory recovery; empirical evaluation shows significant improvements in closed-loop driving robustness when trained on the synthesized long-tail data.
AI.conclusion: OpenLongTail provides a scalable, open-source pathway to leverage heterogeneous long-tail driving data for robust policy learning, enabling better generalization to long-tail events through extrapolative, pose-aware, multi-view data generation.

title: Statistically Undetectable Backdoors in Deep Neural Networks
summary: We show how an adversarial model trainer can plant backdoors in a large class of deep, feedforward neural networks. These backdoors are statistically undetectable in the white-box setting, meaning that the backdoored and honestly trained models are close in total variation distance, even given the full descriptions of the models (e.g., all of the weights). The backdoor provides access to invariance-based adversarial examples for every input, mapping distant inputs to unusually close outputs. However, without the backdoor, it is provably impossible (under standard cryptographic assumptions) to generate any such adversarial examples in polynomial time. Our theoretical and preliminary empirical findings demonstrate a fundamental power asymmetry between model trainers and model users.

AI.tldr: Trainers can implant statistically undetectable backdoors in deep feedforward nets, enabling invariant adversarial behavior; users cannot efficiently generate such attacks without the backdoor, under standard cryptographic assumptions; reveals a fundamental trainer-user power asymmetry.
AI.motivation: Understand security implications of undetectable backdoors and their impact on robustness and trust in neural networks.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis under cryptographic hardness assumptions; construction of backdoors in a large class of deep, feedforward networks; preliminary empirical evaluation.
AI.result: Backdoors are statistically indistinguishable from benign models in white-box metrics (e.g., total variation distance); they enable access to invariance-based adversarial examples that map distant inputs to similar outputs; in the absence of the backdoor, generating such adversarials is computationally infeasible in polynomial time under standard assumptions; empirical results support theory.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a fundamental trainer-versus-user power asymmetry and motivates auditing, verification, and defenses against hidden, hard-to-detect backdoors in ML systems.

title: Scalable Visual Pretraining for Language Intelligence
summary: The rapid progress of large foundation models has been driven predominantly by pretraining on large-scale text corpora. However, many forms of knowledge are conveyed through visual representations, where figures, typeset equations, and page layouts carry rich information that cannot be faithfully or completely captured by text alone. Yet current pretraining approaches discard these visual cues by converting visually rich sources, such as documents and web pages, into plain text for learning language intelligence. This paper challenges the default assumption that language models must be trained on text-only representations and shows that Visual Pretraining is a scalable learner for foundation model intelligence. To this end, we conduct a systematic study of unsupervised visual pretraining paradigms that directly leverage visual documents without text extraction. Across multiple backbones and benchmarks, visual pretraining on the same underlying corpora consistently outperforms text-only pretraining, offering an efficient pathway to scalable language intelligence.

AI.tldr: Visual pretraining on raw visual documents without OCR outperforms text-only pretraining on the same data, suggesting a scalable route to language-like intelligence.
AI.motivation: Text-only pretraining ignores rich visual cues embedded in documents and layouts; leveraging visual information could unlock stronger foundation model capabilities.
AI.method: Systematic study of unsupervised visual pretraining paradigms that operate directly on visual documents without text extraction; evaluation across multiple backbones and benchmarks using the same underlying corpora.
AI.result: Visual pretraining consistently surpasses text-only pretraining on the same corpora, indicating scalability and efficiency in enhancing foundation-model intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Reconsider data representations for pretraining; visual cues from documents provide valuable signals, offering a scalable path to more capable language-aware models.

title: GatedLinear: Adaptive Routing of Complementary Linear Bases for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Time series forecasting requires models to capture diverse, often mutually exclusive, temporal dynamics, from smooth trend continuation to nonstationary drift and strict phase-aligned recurrence. While recent deep learning models have improved accuracy, they typically force these diverse patterns through a single computational backbone governed by fixed algorithmic inductive biases (e.g., self-attention or spectral filtering). This single-mechanism approach often struggles with the profound heterogeneity of real-world series, where different variables and forecast horizons necessitate fundamentally different predictive treatments. To address this, we propose GatedLinear: a lightweight framework that frames forecasting as the adaptive routing of complementary linear bases. GatedLinear leverages a pool of three specialized mechanisms: a global trend-seasonal basis for smooth projection, a difference-based incremental basis for nonstationary drift, and a phase-aligned recurrence basis for explicit cyclic reuse. To dynamically orchestrate these distinct behaviors, we introduce a Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate that disentangles routing decisions into channel-specific preferences, horizon-aware offsets, and phase-indexed biases derived from known future time marks. This design allows the model to perform highly granular, point-wise soft routing across different predictive regimes without stacking computationally heavy neural modules. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive accuracy against recent complex foundational models, while offering explicitly interpretable routing patterns and operating with a substantially smaller parameter footprint.

AI.tldr: Proposes GatedLinear, a lightweight time-series forecasting framework that routes through three specialized linear bases (trend-seasonal, incremental drift, phase-aligned recurrence) via a Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate for channel-, horizon-, and phase-aware routing; achieves competitive state-of-the-art results with fewer parameters and interpretable routing.
AI.motivation: Real-world time series exhibit heterogeneous, often mutually exclusive dynamics (trend, drift, cycles). Single backbones with fixed inductive biases struggle to capture this heterogeneity; a flexible, interpretable, lightweight routing mechanism is desirable.
AI.method: Introduce three complementary linear bases: (1) global trend-seasonal basis for smooth projection, (2) difference-based incremental basis for nonstationary drift, (3) phase-aligned recurrence basis for explicit cyclic reuse. Use a Tri-Factorized Fusion Gate to disentangle routing into channel-specific preferences, horizon-aware offsets, and phase-indexed biases derived from known future time marks. Forecasting is done via point-wise soft routing across bases without heavy neural modules.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on standard benchmarks shows state-of-the-art or highly competitive accuracy compared to recent foundational models, while achieving a substantially smaller parameter footprint and offering interpretable routing patterns.
AI.conclusion: GatedLinear provides an interpretable, efficient alternative to heavy neural architectures for time-series forecasting by decoupling predictive regimes into specialized linear bases and routing decisions, achieving competitive performance with fewer parameters.

title: PanoWorld: Real-World Panoramic Generation
summary: In this work, we aim to address the challenge of long-range memory in panoramic world models by exploiting the rotation-equivariant property of omnidirectional representations, where rotation can be treated as an implicit geometric transformation.Building on this insight, we propose PanoWorld, which simplifies camera trajectories into translations via fixed headings for both current-action modeling and long-range memory through Dense Panoramic Ray-Conditioning (DPRC) and Geometry-aware Memory Augmentation (GMA).Then, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize each component. To better evaluate physical consistency under large-scale spatial variations and diverse illumination conditions, where existing datasets are relatively stable, we construct World360, a large-scale dataset consisting of both real-world video clips collected via panoramic unmanned aerial vehicles and high-quality simulated clips generated by AirSim360.Extensive experiments on World360 demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoWorld, outperforming alternative methods by a large margin.Our models, training code, and dataset will be publicly available. More information can be found on our project page: https://lihaoy-ux.github.io/panoworld-page/.

AI.tldr: PanoWorld leverages rotation-equivariant panoramic representations to address long-range memory in panoramic world models, introducing Dense Panoramic Ray-Conditioning (DPRC) and Geometry-aware Memory Augmentation (GMA) within a three-stage training pipeline, and validating on a new World360 dataset comprising real UAV panoramas and AirSim360 simulations; results show large performance gains with public release of code and data.
AI.motivation: Long-range memory and viewpoint variability hinder panoramic world models. By exploiting rotation-equivariant properties of omnidirectional representations, the paper treats rotation as an implicit geometric transform to simplify trajectory modeling and memory integration, aiming to improve consistency across large spatial scales and diverse illumination conditions.
AI.method: PanoWorld simplifies camera trajectories to translations via fixed headings for current-action modeling and long-range memory. It introduces Dense Panoramic Ray-Conditioning (DPRC) to condition on panoramic ray information and Geometry-aware Memory Augmentation (GMA) to incorporate geometry into memory. A three-stage training pipeline progressively optimizes each component.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on World360 show that PanoWorld outperforms alternative methods by a large margin. The World360 dataset combines real panoramic videos captured by panoramic UAVs with high-quality simulated clips from AirSim360. The authors will release training code and the dataset publicly.
AI.conclusion: PanoWorld demonstrates that rotation-equivariant, panorama-focused designs with explicit memory augmentation and ray-conditioned context can significantly improve long-range memory and physical consistency in large-scale panoramic understanding tasks. The World360 benchmark provides a valuable testbed for evaluating robustness under spatial variation and illumination changes.

title: CoCoT-EEG: Contrastive-Pretrained Multiscale Convolutional Transformer for EEG Decoding
summary: Self-supervised pretrained foundation models (FM) have shown early promise for non-invasive electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding applications. Many recent large-scale models converged on the approach of tokenizing raw EEG followed by masked reconstruction pretraining. However, this recipe has been shown to be suboptimal for data, like EEG, with high noise amplitude and information confined to limited dimensions such as narrow frequency bands. Building on this insight, we develop a novel contrastive-pretrained EEG model with multiscale temporal convolution input layers and Transformer encoder blocks (CoCoT). CoCoT matches or beats state-of-the-art reconstruction-pretrained EEG models on extensive benchmark decoding tasks with heterogeneous electrode configurations. Furthermore, CoCoT trained from scratch outperforms previous single-task decoding models and even rivals pretrained models, showcasing the architecture's flexibility and data efficiency. Through systematic ablations, including model architecture and pretraining objective, we demonstrate the viability of contrastive learning for building EEG FMs while suggesting key architectural design considerations, prompting further investigations in alternative large-scale pretraining strategies.

AI.tldr: Introduces CoCoT, a contrastive-pretrained EEG model with multiscale temporal conv inputs and Transformer encoder; rivals reconstruction-pretrained models and shows data efficiency and strong single-task performance.
AI.motivation: EEG data are highly noisy with information concentrated in narrow frequency bands; masked reconstruction pretraining is suboptimal for such data, motivating alternative pretraining objectives and architectures for EEG foundation models.
AI.method: Proposes CoCoT using multiscale temporal convolution input layers feeding Transformer encoder blocks; employs contrastive pretraining; evaluates both pretrained and from-scratch training; extensive ablations on architecture and pretraining objective across heterogeneous electrode setups.
AI.result: CoCoT matches or surpasses state-of-the-art reconstruction-pretrained EEG models on diverse benchmarks; models trained from scratch outperform prior single-task decoders and approach pretrained model performance, showing data efficiency and architectural benefits.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive learning is a viable pretraining strategy for EEG foundation models; architectural and objective design choices critically influence performance; results encourage exploration of additional large-scale pretraining strategies for EEG.

title: Graph-Regularized Low-Rank Matrix Completion by Variable Projection
summary: We address the low-rank matrix completion problem by incorporating graph regularization into the existing Riemannian Trust-Region Matrix Completion (RTRMC) framework. The latter uses the geometry of the low-rank constraint to remodel the problem as an unconstrained optimization problem on a single Grassmann manifold. Our approach, named Graph-Regularized RTRMC (GR-RTRMC), exploits the inherent relationships between rows and columns of the matrix. By using these relationships, we aim to improve the accuracy and robustness of matrix completion, particularly in scenarios where the underlying data exhibits strong correlations between rows or columns.

AI.tldr: Graph-Regularized RTRMC (GR-RTRMC) extends RTRMC by adding graph-based regularization to exploit row/column relationships, aiming to improve low-rank matrix completion on the Grassmann manifold in data with strong correlations.
AI.motivation: Standard low-rank matrix completion under regularization may fail when data exhibit strong intra-row or intra-column correlations. Incorporating graph structure provides additional priors that can improve recovery robustness and accuracy.
AI.method: Integrate graph regularization terms into the RTRMC framework, solving an unconstrained optimization on a single Grassmann manifold. Likely involves row/column graphs with Laplacian-based penalties and Riemannian trust-region optimization to learn a low-rank factorization under graph-regularized constraints.
AI.result: The abstract does not report experimental results or quantitative findings; it focuses on the proposed problem formulation and method.
AI.conclusion: GR-RTRMC proposes a principled combination of low-rank geometry on the Grassmann manifold with graph-based priors to enhance matrix completion in correlated settings; effectiveness and trade-offs (e.g., computational cost, graph construction) are not disclosed in the abstract.

title: Semantic Pareto-DQN: A Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Framework for Financial Anomaly Detection
comment: BRACIS 2026 - 36th Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems
summary: Financial anomaly detection suffers from extreme class imbalance, causing traditional single-objective algorithms to exhibit ``fraud collapse'', defaulting to the majority class and failing to balance anomaly interdiction with customer friction. To overcome this without distortive data resampling, we propose the Semantic Pareto-DQN, a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework. Our approach synthesizes heterogeneous transaction features into cohesive natural-language narratives, encoded by large language models, thereby producing a robust, scale-invariant state representation. The agent optimizes a vectorial reward that explicitly decouples financial efficacy, operational friction, and semantic discovery. By mapping the continuous Pareto frontier, the system dynamically navigates the asymmetric costs of missed anomalies versus false positives. Empirical evaluations across E-Commerce fraud and UCI Credit datasets show that semantic Pareto-DQN successfully shatters the zero-recall trap. It achieves superior minority-class recall compared to scalarized baselines, providing an alternative to trade bounded operational friction for financial anomaly discovery.

AI.tldr: Multi-objective reinforcement learning for fraud detection using Semantic Pareto-DQN; uses LLM-generated narratives for state representation; optimizes vector reward across financial efficacy, operational friction, semantic discovery; maps Pareto frontier to balance missed anomalies with false positives; demonstrates improved minority recall on E-Commerce fraud and UCI Credit datasets without resampling.
AI.motivation: Financial anomaly detection suffers from extreme class imbalance leading to fraud collapse when optimizing a single objective; resampling is undesirable due to distortions. There is a need for a scale-invariant, multi-objective framework that balances detection efficacy, user friction, and semantic discovery.
AI.method: Proposes Semantic Pareto-DQN, a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework. Heterogeneous transaction features are synthesized into cohesive natural-language narratives via large language models to form a robust state representation. The agent learns a vector-valued reward that decouples financial efficacy, operational friction, and semantic discovery. It maps the continuous Pareto frontier to navigate the costs of missed detections versus false positives. Evaluations on E-Commerce fraud and UCI Credit datasets.
AI.result: Demonstrates shattering of the zero-recall trap; achieves superior minority-class recall compared to scalarized baselines; shows robustness and scale-invariant state representation through NLP narratives; provides a practical alternative to trading off bounded friction for anomaly discovery.
AI.conclusion: Semantic Pareto-DQN is a promising approach to imbalance-driven fraud detection, offering a multi-objective, resampling-free framework that balances financial gains, customer friction, and semantic discovery. Further work should investigate computational costs, robustness to prompts and prompts-induced biases, and broader generalization across datasets.

title: SolarChain-Eval: A Physics-Constrained Benchmark for Trustworthy Economic Agents in Decentralized Energy Markets
summary: As agentic AI systems are increasingly applied to cyber-physical environments, their evaluation requires assessment of both task performance and trustworthiness. In decentralized energy markets, autonomous agents may improve market utility, but may also exploit invalid physical data, create artificial liquidity, and produce unstable governance decisions. Therefore, we propose SolarChain-Eval, a physics-constrained benchmark for evaluating trustworthy economic agents. It formulates market governance as a Gymnasium-compatible Markov Decision Process, where agents make hourly decisions. SolarChain-Eval evaluates each policy across multiple dimensions, including market utility, physical safety, slippage, action smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability. To support agentic evaluation, SolarChain-Eval incorporates an LLM-based Planner/Auditor layer. The Planner defines episode-level action bounds and audit rules, while the Auditor reviews and revises high-risk actions. All interventions are recorded through structured logs, including trigger signals, proposed actions, revised actions, and audit rationales. Experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies reveal a clear utility-safety trade-off. RL agents improve market utility but can still produce unsafe behavior. When the physics penalty is removed, reward-maximizing agents exploit invalid generation and increase artificial liquidity. The LLM Planner/Auditor improves auditability and mitigates selected risks, but it cannot fully compensate for a misspecified reward function. These results indicate that trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires both physical constraints and transparent intervention traces. We release data and code as open access on GitHub for replicability.

AI.tldr: SolarChain-Eval is a physics-constrained, Gymnasium-like MDP benchmark to evaluate trustworthy economic agents in decentralized energy markets, featuring an LLM-based Planner/Auditor and open-source data/code.
AI.motivation: Evaluate agentic AI in cyber-physical environments, balancing task performance and trustworthiness, and mitigating exploitation risks in energy markets.
AI.method: Formulates market governance as a hourly-decision Gymnasium-compatible MDP; evaluates policies across utility, safety, slippage, smoothness, spatial fairness, and auditability; introduces an LLM Planner/Auditor layer that logs interventions and rationales; experiments with static, random, myopic, RL, and RL+LLM policies.
AI.result: RL improves market utility but can be unsafe; removing physics penalties enables exploitation via invalid generation and liquidity manipulation; LLM Planner/Auditor enhances auditability and mitigates some risks but cannot fully compensate for misspecified rewards; emphasizes need for physical constraints and transparent intervention traces.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy agentic AI evaluation requires physics-based constraints and comprehensive auditability; open-source data and code enable replicability.
